**Summary.** The paper presents an alternative Quantum Phase Estimation algorithm for cQED that bypasses the need for deep circuits and inverse Quantum Fourier Transforms. It achieves optimal Heisenberg scaling by encoding phase information into a bosonic mode and reading it out through sequential binary threshold measurements. This offers a significantly more practical route toward high-precision quantum computation on superconducting circuit platforms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses hardware overhead in quantum algorithms by mapping a complex algorithmic requirement (QFT) onto a physical measurement process inherent to cavity QED systems, making high-precision computation more feasible on current platforms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Conventional Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) suffers from high circuit depth due to deep controlled-unitary operations and the inverse QFT.

**Main result.** The authors propose a novel protocol achieving Heisenberg scaling in precision by replacing ancilla qubits and the inverse QFT with iterative binary threshold tests on a bosonic mode.

**Method.** Phase extraction is performed sequentially through repeated homodyne measurements of a bosonic mode, determining one bit of the phase at each stage via adaptive frequency setting.

**Model / system.** The protocol is implemented on a Circuit Quantum Electrodynamics (cQED) platform. The system dynamics are governed by a dispersive coupling Hamiltonian involving a bosonic mode acting as quantum memory.

**Key observables.** The sign of the phase-space rotation ($	ext{sign}(\Delta_j)$) determined via homodyne detection provides the binary digit $\phi_j$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Heisenberg scaling in precision ($O(2^{-n})$), exponentially suppressed failure probability ($\delta$), and total evolution time $T \sim O(1/\epsilon)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes high-fidelity dispersive readout techniques are available, and it neglects decoherence and bosonic-mode loss.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares standard QPE circuits to the proposed cQED binary threshold test. Figure 2 illustrates the iterative protocol using a binary test tree, showing probability distributions related to the phase estimation path.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the limitations of conventional QPE, details the novel bosonic-based protocol involving sequential binary tests and homodyne measurements, analyzes the scaling laws for precision and failure probability, and concludes with numerical examples demonstrating optimal time complexity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum phase estimation is a cornerstone algorithm for determining eigenvalues of unitary operators or Hamiltonians with Heisenberg-limited precision. Conventional implementations rely on deep controlled-unitary operations together with an inverse quantum Fourier transform, resulting in substantial circuit depth and hardware overhead. Here, we propose a conceptually simple and experimentally feasible alternative that exploits the toolbox of circuit quantum electrodynamics. The protocol extracts the phase through a sequence of binary threshold tests, eliminating the need for an inverse quantum Fourier transform. A bosonic mode serves as an efficient quantum memory in which the binary digits of the phase are encoded into the direction of phase-space rotations. These digits are then read out sequentially via high-fidelity homodyne measurements. We show that the protocol achieves Heisenberg scaling in estimation precision while simultaneously providing exponentially suppressed failure probability. By replacing the ancillary circuit with a bosonic degree of freedom, the scheme significantly reduces hardware complexity and offers a practical route toward implementing high-precision quantum phase estimation on circuit quantum electrodynamics platforms.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes using permanent electric dipoles within a qubit coupled to a cavity to suppress Purcell decay. By exploiting the dipole's ability to create channel-selective field displacements, it achieves significant protection against radiative loss while maintaining necessary readout signals. This offers a pathway for building high-fidelity quantum devices by engineering dissipation itself.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides an advanced theoretical tool for engineering dissipation channels in superconducting or solid-state qubits, moving beyond simple filtering to utilize intrinsic material properties (dipoles) for quantum control.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is Purcell decay, a loss mechanism in cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) that limits fast qubit readout.

**Main result.** Permanent electric dipoles can provide an internal, channel-selective form of Purcell protection, significantly increasing the qubit lifetime and reducing readout error rates.

**Method.** The analysis uses open-system quantum dynamics by calculating dressed decay rates derived from a Lindblad master equation in the system's eigenbasis.

**Model / system.** The model involves a qubit coupled to a cavity resonator, incorporating an additional interaction term mediated by a permanent electric dipole moment. The Hamiltonian includes transverse ($g_x$) and longitudinal ($g_p$) coupling terms.

**Key observables.** Normalized lifetime ($\kappa T_1$), single-shot readout error ($\epsilon_{tot}$), and the decay rates ($\Gamma_i$) for different coupling regimes.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimensionless longitudinal coupling $\eta = g_p / \omega_c$, which controls the degree of dipole-induced field displacement.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis compares results from a simplified displaced Rotating-Wave Approximation (RWA) against a more rigorous full-transverse model, noting that the RWA zero is not physically exact.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the competition between transverse and longitudinal couplings, showing how the decay rate suppression shifts from an analytical RWA zero ($\eta=\sqrt{2}$) to a larger operating point ($\eta_{FT}=2.60$) in the full model.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of Purcell decay, develops a Hamiltonian incorporating dipole coupling, calculates open-system decay rates using dressed states, and benchmarks performance improvements by comparing RWA predictions against full-transverse calculations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Reading out a qubit often requires coupling it to a resonator, but that same resonator can also give the qubit an extra path to decay. Here, we study a way to reduce this loss using a built-in permanent electric dipole. The dipole shifts the cavity field in different directions for the qubit ground and excited states. This shift makes the relevant wave functions overlap less, which weakens the transverse qubit--cavity exchange that causes Purcell decay. In a simplified displaced rotating-wave model, this exchange vanishes at $η=\sqrt{2}$. In the full transverse model, this exact zero is lifted, but strong suppression remains at a larger dipole-induced displacement. Using dressed open-system decay rates, we find an operating point where the cavity-mediated decay is strongly reduced while the longitudinal readout signal remains finite. For the benchmark studied here, at fixed pointer separation, the normalized lifetime increases from $κT_1=11.1$ to $47.3$, and the estimated single-shot readout error drops from $0.21$ to $0.07$. These results show that permanent electric dipoles can provide an internal, channel-selective form of Purcell protection.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes speech from psychosis patients by quantifying the temporal organization of semantic meaning using Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (DFA) on word embedding similarities. The authors found that patients exhibit abnormally high scaling exponents, suggesting excessive persistence and a departure from optimal 'critical' dynamics. This links linguistic pathology to known deviations from criticality observed in other complex physical systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** Although applied to linguistics, the methodology—using DFA to test for deviations from critical scaling ($\alpha$) in a complex temporal process—is directly relevant to characterizing non-equilibrium dynamics in open quantum systems or biological processes modeled by statistical physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether deviations from a scale-invariant 'pink noise' regime characterize the temporal organization of semantic relations in psychosis, drawing parallels with pathology seen in other complex systems.

**Main result.** Patients exhibited significantly elevated DFA scaling exponents ($\alpha$) compared to controls, indicating abnormally strong and excessive long-range temporal correlations in their semantic fluctuations.

**Method.** Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (DFA) was applied to continuous cosine-similarity time series derived from BERT embeddings of clinical speech transcripts.

**Model / system.** The system analyzed is the temporal evolution of semantic relationships within human language production, modeled as trajectories through a high-dimensional semantic space using word embeddings.

**Key observables.** DFA scaling exponent ($\alpha$), which quantifies long-range temporal correlations; cosine similarity time series.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The critical regime (associated with pink noise/scale-invariance); the threshold for excessive persistence ($\alpha > 0.5$); minimum continuous stretch length (>100 words).

**Assumptions / limitations.** That deviations from criticality in language dynamics mirror pathological departures observed in physiological or neural systems; that DFA is an appropriate tool to characterize multi-timescale organization of meaning.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 shows DFA scaling exponents ($\alpha$) across diagnostic groups (Zürich, Izmir, Marburg datasets); subsequent figures show partial Spearman correlations between $\alpha$ and symptom scores for different cohorts.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical framework by comparing noise regimes in pathology. It then details the application of DFA to semantic similarity time series from multiple clinical datasets (Zürich, Izmir, Marburg), presenting group comparisons and correlation analyses with symptom severity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The notion of pink noise refers to 'scale-invariant' temporal dynamics, where fluctuations exhibit similar statistical structure across time scales. Departures from a regime associated with such scale-free organization toward uncorrelated 'white' noise or overly persistent 'brown' noise have been widely identified as markers of pathology across physiological and cognitive domains. Whether comparable alterations characterize the temporal organization of language remains largely unexplored. We address this question in the domain of psychosis, where language anomalies are pervasively documented. Specifically, we apply detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) to quantify temporal scaling in BERT-derived continuous cosine-similarity time series capturing trajectories through semantic space, using clinical transcripts from patients and controls across three independent datasets. DFA scaling exponents were extracted to characterize the strength of long-range temporal correlations. Across all datasets, patients exhibited significantly elevated scaling exponents relative to controls, indicating abnormally strong long-range correlations with excessive persistence in semantic fluctuations. This temporal analysis opens a window into the multi-timescale organization of meaning as it unfolds in discourse. The results reveal a signature of altered temporal scaling in speech, consistent with deviations from criticality in physiological domains, paralleling known departures from criticality in brain function in psychosis and suggesting possible links between these two domains.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper develops a theoretical model for open quantum systems exhibiting bistability driven by first-order phase transitions. It shows that these systems can sustain stable Limit Cycles characterized by periodic fluctuations. These LCs are robustly linked to the system's tipping points, which manifest as sharp spikes in dynamical susceptibility and energy dissipation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous quantum mechanical framework for understanding how far-from-equilibrium processes—like those seen in climate or ecology—can generate sustained, coherent oscillations (LCs) using fundamental concepts of critical slowing down and dissipation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how non-equilibrium fluctuations and long-range correlations can be sustained by engineering a quantum limit cycle in systems undergoing first-order absorbing-state phase transitions.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that stable Limit Cycles (LCs) emerge from the interplay between bistability, multiplicative quantum noise, and periodic passage through tipping points, which are marked by sharp spikes in dynamical susceptibility and entropy production.

**Method.** The analysis employs a combination of Lindblad master equations, semiclassical continuum approximations leading to coupled Langevin equations, Floquet analysis for stability, and path integral methods for calculating entropy production.

**Model / system.** The model is a generic quantum contact system involving active and inactive emitters, exhibiting bistability. Dynamics are governed by coupled stochastic differential equations derived from the master equation, describing the evolution of active ($ho$) and total ($n$) densities.

**Key observables.** Dynamical susceptibility (showing transient spikes), energy dissipation rate/dynamical entropy production (showing stepwise accumulation), and spatial correlation functions $S_{k,t}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** System rates ($\Gamma, \kappa, \lambda, b$), noise characteristics, and the control parameter $\lambda$ which dictates the transition between stationary states and LC regimes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on semiclassical continuum limits, Markovian noise assumptions, and linearization techniques (e.g., around mean-field trajectories) to analyze fluctuations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate Mean-Field phase diagrams showing APTs; time series show periodic oscillations of correlations ($S_{k,t}$) peaking near the tipping point; and entropy production ($\partial t S$) shows a sharp peak coinciding with the transition.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the physical system via master equations to deriving effective classical/stochastic dynamics. It then analyzes phase transitions (APT) using mean-field theory, followed by linearizing fluctuations around the trajectory and applying Floquet analysis to confirm LC stability and characterize correlation peaks linked to thermodynamic signatures like entropy production.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nonequilibrium systems maintain spatiotemporal order through energy dissipation and entropy production. Here, we demonstrate this principle by engineering a quantum limit cycle that emerges from the interplay between a first-order absorbing-state phase transition and feedback mechanism coupling order and control parameters. The quantum limit cycle manifests dynamical correlations driven by multiplicative quantum noise and periodic traverses through tipping points, which act as a robust early-warning signal for state transitions. This periodic crossing results in the enhanced dynamical susceptibility and transient rise of long-range correlations near each tipping event and their subsequent disappearance away from it. These critical transitions are accompanied by a sharp increase in the energy dissipation rate, leading to a stepwise accumulation of dynamical entropy production over time. Our results provide a way for realizing dynamical fluctuations and long-range correlations in strongly interacting driven-dissipative open quantum systems.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper reveals that Andreev reflection, typically associated with superconducting interfaces, can emerge microscopically in a purely lattice system by introducing a duality defect into the transverse-field Ising chain. This mechanism is mathematically equivalent to a specific one-site translation of Majorana fermions, providing a unified theoretical framework for understanding boundary physics across different quantum impurity models.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep microscopic understanding of topological boundary phenomena, linking concepts from condensed matter (Kitaev chains, SPT phases) to fundamental quantum impurity physics (Kondo effect) via lattice symmetries and defects.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to determine the universal mechanism behind Andreev reflection (a charge-conjugating boundary condition) when it appears in seemingly unrelated quantum impurity problems, such as those related to the two-channel Kondo effect.

**Main result.** Andreev reflection is shown to emerge naturally from a purely lattice duality defect—specifically, it corresponds to a one-site translation of Majorana operators within the folded transverse-field Ising chain model.

**Method.** The authors use theoretical mapping techniques, transforming the Ising Hamiltonian into a Majorana representation and analyzing scattering dynamics by 'folding' the system at an impurity site.

**Model / system.** The primary model is based on the transverse-field Ising chain, which is analyzed via its Majorana fermion formulation. The defect introduces an effective boundary condition analogous to those found in the Emery–Kivelson (EK) model or at interfaces between Kitaev-chain SPT phases and gapless chains.

**Key observables.** Scattering dynamics of wavepackets, charge fluctuation ($\delta n(x)$), comparison between free vs. EK boundary conditions, and conservation laws for axial $U(1)_A$ symmetry.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The system is analyzed in the continuum limit and at the interface between a Kitaev-chain SPT phase and gapless chains; the two-channel Kondo problem serves as a key physical realization.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The identification of Andreev reflection with a one-site translation defect is termed 'emergent' because it is not an exact microscopic equality on the lattice, but rather a low-energy statement.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the mapping from the Ising chain to the folded geometry, comparing scattering results for free vs. EK boundaries, and showing the physical realization of Andreev reflection via Majorana impurity defects acting as chiral fermion-parity defects.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by establishing the lattice model (Ising $	o$ Majorana), analyzing the boundary defect structure through folding, deriving the continuum limit connection to Dirac fermions, and finally connecting this mechanism to known physical boundaries like those in the two-channel Kondo problem.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Andreev reflection converts an incoming fermion into an outgoing hole and is usually tied to a superconducting interface. We show that an analogous charge-conjugating boundary condition emerges from a purely lattice duality defect. Starting from a Majorana representation of the transverse-field Ising chain, we construct a folded lattice model in which a boundary Majorana impurity implements a one-site translation of a staggered Majorana chain. In the continuum, this translation becomes a chiral fermion-parity defect: it flips the sign of the only left-moving Majorana mode while leaving the right-moving mode unchanged. When the two Majorana modes are recombined into a complex fermion in the folded geometry, this sign flip becomes the Andreev-like boundary condition. Our lattice formulation gives a microscopic interpretation of the Emery--Kivelson boundary of the two-channel Kondo problem and of Maldacena--Ludwig monopole scattering, while identifying the boundary as the interface between a Kitaev-chain SPT phase and a gapless chain. The same Majorana translation defect also provides a lattice realization of an axial $U(1)_A$-symmetric charge-flip boundary.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the transport and fluctuation properties of self-propelled particles whose motion is governed by a complex, age-dependent phase-switching mechanism.

**Main result.** The system exhibits giant fluctuations at the critical point ($a=1$), where the variance scales anomalously as $	ext{Var}(x_T) \propto T^2 / \log T$, indicating a marginal breakdown of the Central Limit Theorem.

**Method.** The analysis employs generating-function methods and discrete-time moment recurrences, utilizing spatial Fourier and temporal z-transforms to derive exact expressions for the propagator and its asymptotic moments.

**Model / system.** The model describes a particle switching between two phases: a memoryless downstream phase ($\sigma_t = +1$) and an upstream phase ($\sigma_t = -1$) whose switching probability depends on the age $c$ via a hazard function $a/(b+c)$.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the transport and fluctuation properties of self-propelled particles whose motion is governed by an age-dependent phase-switching mechanism. The dynamics alternate between a Markovian downstream phase with a constant switching probability $r$ and a semi-Markovian upstream phase in which the age-dependent hazard probability $a/(b+c)$ decays with the internal clock $c$, representing persistent orientation. The time-averaged velocity, as an order parameter, shows a continuous transition at $a=1$ which separates an upstream-dominated ballistic regime ($a<1$) from an ergodic diffusive regime ($a>1$). Through generating-function methods and discrete-time moment recurrences, we derive exact expressions for the propagator and determine the long-time asymptotics of the mean displacement and variance. At the critical point $a=1$, the system exhibits giant fluctuations, with the variance scaling ballistically up to a logarithmic correction, $\mathrm{Var}(x_T) \propto T^2 / \log T$. These results demonstrate how slowly decaying reorientation probabilities lead to a marginal breakdown of the Central Limit Theorem, enabling unusually high-variance exploratory dynamics in biased environments.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents novel, efficient protocols for learning the generator of open quantum system dynamics (Lindbladians) using only limited measurements like product-state preparations. By combining advanced techniques such as Semidefinite Programming with structural assumptions on interactions, it achieves rigorous sample complexity guarantees that scale favorably with system size $n$ when the underlying physics is sparse or local.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it provides the theoretical tools necessary to characterize complex quantum dynamics in realistic settings where full tomography is impossible. The focus on $k$-locality and sparsity directly addresses resource limitations inherent in experimental quantum physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is developing efficient, data-driven protocols to reconstruct an unknown $k$-local Lindbladian generator ($\mathcal{L}$) governing open quantum system dynamics.

**Main result.** The authors provide sample complexity bounds for learning the coefficients of $\mathcal{L}$ using limited measurements, achieving significant improvements when exploiting sparsity assumptions. They also establish lower bounds proving the necessity of these sample complexities.

**Method.** The methodology combines techniques from quantum process tomography (using product-state preparations and short-time evolution) with advanced mathematical tools like Semidefinite Programming (SDP) to project noisy estimates onto the space of physically valid Lindblad generators.

**Model / system.** The system is an open quantum system of $n$ qubits evolving under a Markovian master equation, $rac{d}{dt}ho(t) = \mathcal{L}(ho(t))$. The generator $\mathcal{L}$ is assumed to be $k$-local, meaning interactions are confined to small subsets of qubits.

**Key observables.** The primary observables are the Pauli-GKSL coefficients ($\chi_{P,Q}$) defining the Lindbladian structure, and the measured quantities are related to the Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM) elements derived from short-time evolution.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Key parameters include the accuracy $\epsilon$, failure probability $\delta$, locality $k$, system size $n$, and the weighted intersection strength $\alpha$ which bounds local interactions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The protocol assumes a constant bound on the interaction strength ($\alpha=O(1)$) for general learning, and relies heavily on exploiting sparsity structures (e.g., via supplied influential coefficients $\Omega$) to improve scaling from polynomial to logarithmic in $n$.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops a multi-stage pipeline: first, estimating raw coefficients from measurements; second, using SDPs to project these estimates onto the space of valid Lindbladians; and finally, deriving rigorous sample complexity bounds (both upper bounds for the protocol and lower bounds proving their necessity) based on locality assumptions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present an efficient protocol for learning an unknown $k$-local Lindblad generator on $n$ qubits using only product-state preparations, short-time evolution, and single-qubit Pauli measurements, without prior knowledge of the interaction structure. For fixed $k$ and bounded weighted interaction strength, the protocol estimates all Hamiltonian and dissipative Pauli--GKSL coefficients to entrywise accuracy $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$ using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_k(\varepsilon^{-2}n^{2k}\log(1/δ))$ samples and polylogarithmically many evolution times. A semidefinite projection converts these estimates into a valid $k$-local Lindblad generator with diamond-norm error at most $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_k(\varepsilon^{-2}n^{4k}\log(1/δ))$ samples and polynomial-time classical postprocessing. If a suitable set of influential coefficients is supplied and satisfies a stable sparsity condition, the dependence on $n$ can improve from polynomial to logarithmic; in particular, exact supports of bounded intersection degree require only $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_k(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ samples, with analogous reductions in system-size dependence for sufficiently decaying long-range interactions. We also provide a robust structure-learning procedure, extend the guarantees to model misspecification, and prove complementary sample-complexity lower bounds. To our knowledge, these are the first efficient learning guarantees for general $k$-local dissipative quantum dynamics under such limited experimental control.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates dipolar effects and the miscibility transition within a quantum-degenerate Bose-Bose mixture of Dysprosium isotopes.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated efficient thermalization in the mixture and provided evidence for an interaction-driven spatial reorganization, consistent with tuning across a miscible-immiscible crossover.

**Method.** Experiments involved evaporative cooling followed by atom-loss spectroscopy as a function of magnetic field to probe interspecies interactions and center-of-mass separation measurements.

**Model / system.** The platform is a quantum-degenerate Bose-Bose mixture of $^{162}	ext{Dy}$ and $^{164}	ext{Dy}$, which possesses large magnetic dipole moments, making it ideal for studying dipolar interactions in ultracold gases.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Efficient thermalization is assumed, although isotope-specific three-body losses were noted as a potential limitation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate population control via detuning ($\delta EOM$), compare mixture vs. single-species atom-loss spectra to find resonances, and plot relative vertical displacement ($\Delta y$) versus magnetic field to show phase separation behavior.

**Paper structure.** The work progresses from establishing the stable cooling and thermalization of the dual-isotope mixture, to mapping out interspecies Feshbach resonances using loss spectroscopy, culminating in measurements that probe spatial reorganization indicative of a miscibility crossover.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We report on the realization of a quantum-degenerate Bose-Bose mixture of 162Dy and 164Dy. Owing to the near-identical mass and polarizability of the two isotopes, the mixture thermalizes efficiently, with evaporation trajectories closely following those of the single-isotope case. Using a broad interspecies Feshbach resonance, we explore a miscible-immiscible transition between the two Bose-Einstein condensates. The tunability of the interspecies interaction, combined with the large magnetic dipole moment of Dy, makes this platform well suited for exploring dipolar effects in ultracold mixtures, including multi-component supersolidity.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores how residual quantum information, specifically anomalous scalar coherence that persists after entanglement vanishes due to decoherence, can leave detectable imprints on the background of induced gravitational waves. Instead of predicting a simple spectral shift, the authors predict a unique correlated tensor background characterized by non-trivial covariance and phase structure. This offers a novel probe for primordial quantum correlations beyond standard entanglement measurements.

**Why it may be interesting.** The focus on discord and coherence as robust quantum measures surviving decoherence provides a theoretical framework applicable to any system where initial quantum correlations are expected but might be masked by environmental coupling or classical averaging.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether residual quantum-information properties, beyond simple entanglement, survive decoherence in the scalar sector and leave measurable imprints on induced gravitational waves.

**Main result.** The primary signature is not a universal shift in the spectrum, but rather a correlated tensor background characterized by nontrivial covariance and phase structure, sourced by anomalous scalar coherence contractions.

**Method.** The analysis employs the covariance-matrix formalism and uses continuous-variable Gaussian quantum state descriptions to derive transfer relations between scalar and induced tensor correlations.

**Model / system.** The system models gravitational waves induced at second order from primordial curvature perturbations ($\zeta$), treating $\zeta$ as a decohered two-mode squeezed Gaussian state. The analysis tracks the evolution of quantum correlations (discord, coherence) through this process.

**Key observables.** Connected power covariance $\kappa(k)$, opposite-mode tensor coherence $\gamma_k$, and phase-sensitive strain correlators $\Gamma_h(k)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Decoherence parameter ($\epsilon_{	ext{dec}}$), squeezing parameters ($r_k$), and the effective residual-coherence amplitude ($\alpha_{	ext{coh}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on leading order (Wick contractions) approximations for calculating four-point functions, assuming Gaussian dynamics.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the decay of entanglement versus the survival of discord and anomalous coherence, showing how this residual coherence sources off-diagonal tensor correlations.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the quantum measures (discord vs. entanglement) in the scalar sector; then deriving the transfer relations connecting these residual coherences to the induced tensor covariance matrix components ($\gamma_k$); finally, identifying measurable observables like $\kappa(k)$ and $\Gamma_h(k)$ for future detection.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Scalar-induced gravitational waves are usually modeled as a classical stochastic background sourced by primordial curvature perturbations. We investigate whether residual quantum-information properties of the scalar sector can survive decoherence and leave imprints in the induced tensor background. Using the covariance-matrix formalism, we describe primordial curvature perturbations as decohered two-mode squeezed Gaussian states and identify the anomalous scalar coherence that may remain after scalar entanglement has vanished. We then derive the leading scalar-to-tensor transfer relations for opposite-momentum induced tensor modes. The ordinary tensor power is sourced by scalar power contractions, whereas the opposite-mode tensor coherence is sourced by anomalous scalar-coherence contractions. This tensor coherence controls the induced Gaussian discord and generates connected and phase-sensitive observables, including a connected power covariance $κ(k)\propto |γ_k|^2/α_k^2$. Thus the robust signature is not a universal shift of the gravitational-wave spectrum, but a correlated tensor background with nontrivial covariance and phase structure. We discuss phenomenological templates and provide an illustrative Fisher estimate for future gravitational-wave observations. Our results suggest that scalar-induced gravitational waves may offer a new probe of primordial quantum correlations beyond entanglement.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically analyzes High-Harmonic Generation driven by bright squeezed vacuum light to study entanglement generation. Using tools like covariance matrices and logarithmic negativity, the authors show that while the system often remains Gaussian, strong squeezing can induce non-classical correlations. This positions HHG as a promising platform for engineering quantum states of light.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges nonlinear optics (HHG) with advanced quantum information concepts (entanglement, squeezing). It shows how a fundamental physical process can serve as an engineered platform for generating complex entangled states of light in the extreme UV regime.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how High-Harmonic Generation (HHG) driven by Bright Squeezed Vacuum (BSV) light modifies the quantum statistical properties of the emitted harmonics, specifically looking for entanglement generation.

**Main result.** Bichromatic driving with BSV light can generate non-classical multimode Gaussian entanglement in the even harmonic field. The analysis systematically characterizes the transition regimes where this description holds or breaks down into genuinely non-Gaussian states.

**Method.** The authors employ quantum characteristic functions, covariance matrix analysis, and entanglement measures like logarithmic negativity to characterize the generated quantum state.

**Model / system.** The physical system is HHG in atomic systems driven by a combination of a strong coherent field ($\omega$) and a perturbative BSV field ($2\omega$). The theoretical framework models the evolution using approximations derived from the time-dependent dipole moment.

**Key observables.** Gaussian entanglement structure, covariance matrix elements, quantum teleportation fidelity, logarithmic negativity, and Wigner functions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Squeezing parameter (r), effective coupling parameter ($\varrho$), harmonic order ($2\omega, 3\omega, \dots$), and the ratio of driving field strengths.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on low-depletion approximations for the propagator element and often utilizes simplified one-quadrature models for the BSV driver state.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate quadrature variances comparing different models, show entanglement quantification via logarithmic negativity across harmonic orders, and display Wigner functions demonstrating the transition from Gaussian to non-Gaussian states as squeezing increases.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework using characteristic functions for HHG. It then analyzes specific driving configurations (bichromatic) to derive the state's properties, quantifying entanglement via covariance matrices and fidelity benchmarks before mapping out the transition regimes where Gaussianity breaks down.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

High harmonic generation (HHG) is a highly nonlinear optical process in which radiation from a strong driving field is up-converted into its high-order harmonics. In atomic systems, this nonlinearity manifests itself through the intensity scaling of the emitted harmonics with the driving field strength. Despite the highly nonlinear nature of HHG, when the driving field is prepared in a classical Gaussian state and atomic depletion remains negligible, the quantum statistical properties of the generated harmonics retains classical Gaussian quantum statistics. Driving HHG with bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) light challenges this paradigm, as its enhanced field fluctuations can modify the statistical properties of the generated harmonics. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which BSV-driven HHG gives rise to non-classical Gaussian states, and identify the regimes where this Gaussian description breaks down. For bichromatic driving by a strong coherent field at frequency $ω$ and a perturbative BSV field at $2ω$, the even-harmonic response is approximately linear in the BSV quadrature, leading to non-classical multimode Gaussian entanglement in the harmonic field. We show that this state can be described as a distributed collective squeezed mode over the even-harmonic manifold, and characterize its covariance matrix, entanglement structure, and quantum teleportation fidelity as an operational benchmark. Our results highlight the potential of non-classically driven HHG as a platform for engineering Gaussian and non-Gaussian states of light in the extreme ultraviolet regime.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a novel geometric framework to interpret multidimensional spectroscopy in open quantum systems. It argues that environmental coupling causes continuous 'transport' of amplitude among spectroscopically defined pathways within Liouville space. By quantifying this transport using concepts like Liouvillian curvature and holonomy, the authors show how spectral distortions can be mapped back to the underlying structural misalignment between different physical bases.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful geometric lens to analyze complex quantum dynamics in the presence of dissipation, connecting fundamental concepts like Berry phase/holonomy directly to measurable spectroscopic signatures in open systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Standard interpretations of multidimensional spectroscopy fail in open quantum systems because environmental interactions cause continuous amplitude redistribution among Liouville pathways, which is not accounted for by treating pathways as fixed objects.

**Main result.** The paper develops a geometric framework showing that pathway transport is governed by a Liouvillian connection and curvature, reinterpreting spectral distortions as measurable signatures of this curved geometry rather than mere broadening corrections.

**Method.** It employs the language of differential geometry (connections, curvature, holonomy) applied to the Liouville space propagator, utilizing Duhamel expansions to derive reconstruction procedures for transport operators.

**Model / system.** The system is an open quantum system undergoing spectroscopic measurements, modeled by a Liouvillian $\mathcal{L}(t)$ that includes Hamiltonian evolution ($\mathcal{L}_H$), external field interactions ($V(t)$), and environmental dissipation ($\mathcal{D}_{	ext{bath}}$).

**Key observables.** Spectral distortions, peak shifts, and the observational holonomy derived from nonlinear spectroscopic response.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Basis misalignment angle ($\theta$) between the Hamiltonian eigenbasis and the environment-selected pointer basis.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes that environmental interactions induce a measurable transport structure in Liouville space due to basis incompatibility, allowing for geometric reconstruction from observables.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate how spectral responses (real/imaginary components) are structured by the misalignment angle $\theta$, and demonstrate the high accuracy of second-order Duhamel expansions in reconstructing these signals up to maximal misalignment ($\theta = \pi/2$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the failure of fixed pathway assumptions in open systems, developing a geometric framework using Liouvillian connections and curvature, deriving reconstruction procedures via Duhamel expansion, and finally demonstrating that spectral features are determined by amplitude transport rather than just existing pathways.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Liouville pathways provide the conceptual foundation for interpreting multidimensional spectroscopies, yet are typically treated as fixed objects that evolve independently between optical interactions. In open quantum systems, this picture is incomplete. Environmental interactions continuously redistribute amplitude among pathways during every free-evolution interval, generating transport that leaves measurable signatures in the nonlinear spectroscopic response. We develop a geometric framework in which pathway transport is governed by a Liouvillian connection, its associated curvature, and the resulting observational holonomy. The framework applies to open quantum systems in which the environment selects a pointer basis distinct from the observational basis used to construct the spectroscopic response. This basis incompatibility induces transport among Liouville pathways, generating characteristic spectral distortions and a nontrivial Liouvillian curvature. Using a Duhamel expansion of the Liouvillian propagator, we derive a reconstruction procedure that identifies the transport operators responsible for the observed redistribution of pathway weight, accurate throughout the full range of basis misalignment. This perspective reframes spectral features as determined not only by which pathways exist but by how amplitude is transported among them. Spectral distortions, peak shifts, and otherwise-forbidden pathway contributions become geometric signatures of a curved Liouville-space manifold rather than phenomenological broadening corrections, identifying pathway geometry as a complementary layer of organization in nonlinear spectroscopy.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces a novel gauge-propagation approach to approximate the conversion of general tensor networks into isometric forms. By developing a structured local decomposition, it provides a systematic way to manage non-isometric residuals in higher dimensions. The method is shown to effectively reduce errors when applied to models like the Kitaev spin liquid, offering a powerful tool for variational optimization.

**Why it may be interesting.** The development of robust, systematic methods for enforcing physical constraints (like isometry) within tensor network representations is crucial for accurately simulating strongly correlated quantum materials where standard contractions fail due to gauge redundancy.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of converting generic tensor-network states into an isometric form (isoTNS) by developing a gauge-propagation approach.

**Main result.** A structured local decomposition method is proposed that allows for controlled approximation of non-isometric tensors, showing significant error reduction when applied to models like the Kitaev spin liquid.

**Method.** The core technique involves defining a propagation-compatible local decomposition where complex residuals are approximated as sums of structured terms, enabling iterative refinement via truncation.

**Model / system.** The method is tested on random tensors and specifically on the loop-gas tensor representation used for describing the Kitaev spin liquid (KSL) on honeycomb lattices. It applies to general tensor network states (e.g., MPS/PEPS).

**Key observables.** Local residuals, accumulated propagation errors ($\Delta_\ell$), normalized overlap ($O_\ell$), and truncation error bounds ($\epsilon_m$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The local cluster size (e.g., 2-in-2-out up to 6-in-2-out) and the number of retained structured terms ($m$) are key parameters controlling approximation quality.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the residual factor can be approximated by a sum of absorbable, structured local tensors; in higher dimensions, this requires an approximation due to structural obstructions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate gauge propagation geometry on 1D and 2D lattices. Benchmarks compare decomposition methods for random and LG tensors, showing error reduction upon increasing the number of retained terms or enlarging the local cluster size.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the goal (isoTNS via gauge propagation), contrasts exact 1D propagation with obstructed higher-dimensional cases, develops the structured local decomposition approximation, analyzes its convergence using multi-term truncation bounds, and finally validates it by simulating error accumulation on a finite honeycomb lattice.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We introduce a gauge-propagation approach for approximately converting generic tensor-network states into an isometric tensor-network state form with a prescribed orthogonality center. In one dimension, this propagation is exact because the non-isometric factor produced by a QR or singular-value decomposition is supported on a single virtual bond. In higher-dimensional networks, however, a local step can have several outgoing directions, and the residual factor is generally not separable into independent single-bond contributions. We address this local obstruction by approximating a local tensor, or a contracted local cluster, by structured terms consisting of an isometric factor multiplied by a tensor product of output-leg factors. The isometric factor is retained at the current site or cluster, while the output-leg factors are absorbed into neighboring tensors along the propagation directions. This construction provides a local truncation criterion for gauge propagation and a practical route to refinement by increasing the number of retained terms or enlarging the local cluster. Benchmarks on random tensors and on the loop-gas tensor representation of the Kitaev spin liquid show that this refinement reduces both local residuals and accumulated propagation errors. For the loop-gas tensor, two structured terms reduce the local residual to numerical precision, and enlarging the local object from 2-in-2-out to 4-in-2-out and 6-in-2-out clusters lowers both local truncation errors and accumulated errors in finite honeycomb gauge propagation. These results identify propagation-compatible local decomposition as a useful building block for approximate isometrization and as a potential initializer or preconditioner for variational isoTNS algorithms.

</details>

**Summary.** The research addresses how to optimize parametric amplifiers for fast, multi-qubit readout of superconducting qubits. The authors propose a novel strategy that prioritizes improving the performance of the single slowest qubit channel (the bottleneck). This approach experimentally demonstrated a significant reduction in overall readout time compared to optimizing for average performance across all qubits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it tackles practical engineering constraints (readout speed) in superconducting circuits by optimizing the coupling element (parametric amplifier) based on system bottlenecks rather than simple averages.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop a pump optimization strategy for parametric amplifiers used in superconducting qubit readout chains to minimize the total multiplexed readout time.

**Main result.** By optimizing the amplifier pump condition based on the limiting (slowest) qubit channel rather than the average SNR, the authors achieved a significant reduction in the overall multiplexed readout time (e.g., 25% reduction).

**Method.** The study experimentally calibrates the parametric amplifier by sweeping its frequency and power while comparing two optimization metrics: maximizing average $\Delta	ext{SNR}$ versus maximizing $\Delta	ext{SNR}$ for the bottleneck qubit.

**Model / system.** The system involves superconducting qubits (e.g., five tunable transmon qubits) whose readout signals are amplified by a Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier (TWPA). The performance is governed by the interplay between amplifier gain, noise, and qubit relaxation times ($T_1$).

**Key observables.** Multiplexed Readout Time ($T_{	ext{MPX}}^{	ext{RO}}$), Signal-to-Noise Ratio ($	ext{SNR}$), $\Delta	ext{SNR}$, and required readout time ($	ext{TRO}$) for individual qubits.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Target SNR of 3 is chosen as the optimal point where further SNR improvement yields diminishing returns due to $T_1$ relaxation; the limiting qubit dictates $T_{	ext{MPX}}^{	ext{RO}}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that setting a fixed target $	ext{SNR}$ (e.g., 3) is optimal because increasing it further does not improve fidelity due to relaxation effects, and that readout time is limited by the slowest channel.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate how different pump conditions affect gain profiles across multiple qubits; one figure compares the required readout times ($	ext{TRO}$) for both optimization strategies, showing a clear reduction in $T_{	ext{MPX}}^{	ext{RO}}$ when targeting the limiting qubit.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem of minimizing multiplexed readout time set by the slowest channel. It then compares conventional average-optimization against the proposed limiting-channel optimization strategy, demonstrating quantitative improvements using experimental measurements on a multi-qubit array.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Low-noise parametric amplifiers are widely used as the first-stage amplifier in qubit readout chains. The performance of parametric amplifiers depends sensitively on the choice of the pump condition. We propose a strategy for determining the pump condition that is tailored for fast multiplexed readout. Choosing the amplifier pump to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement at the readout frequency of the limiting qubit--the qubit that requires the longest readout time to reach a target SNR--minimizes the total multiplexed readout time. We demonstrate our pump calibration strategy experimentally on a five-qubit multiplexed readout chain with a traveling-wave parametric amplifier. Using our strategy, we reduce the multiplexed readout time by 320 ns compared to optimizing the average SNR improvement on all qubits, without degrading the target SNR for any qubit.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors propose an advanced interferometric test to search for evidence of Continuous Spontaneous Localization (CSL) by monitoring the loss of coherence in a nanoparticle pointer. By utilizing the pointer reversibly, they aim to achieve sensitivities that surpass current direct matter-wave bounds. The work is significant because it outlines a pathway to probe fundamental physics theories using state-of-the-art trapped-matter quantum optics techniques.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, high-precision proposal for testing fundamental physics theories like objective collapse models using mesoscopic quantum systems, which is highly relevant to AMO research in quantum measurement and decoherence.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper proposes an interferometric test to search for deviations from standard quantum mechanics predicted by Continuous Spontaneous Localization (CSL) theory.

**Main result.** The proposed measurement-like protocol yields sensitivity estimates ($\lambda_{\min}$) that significantly improve upon existing direct matter-wave CSL bounds, although they do not surpass the strongest non-interferometric limits.

**Method.** The test uses a trapped nanoparticle as a reversible mesoscopic pointer to temporarily store which-branch information from a microscopic superposition. Coherence loss is measured by comparing the visibility after recombination against predictions from standard QM versus CSL.

**Model / system.** The system involves a two-branch quantum state interacting with a harmonic oscillator (the nanoparticle) via opposite weak forces, leading to conditional displacements. The dynamics are governed by modified Hamiltonians incorporating the CSL collapse rate ($\lambda$) and correlation length ($r_c$).

**Key observables.** Visibility loss of microscopic coherence read out interferometrically after recombination; the minimum detectable CSL rate ($\lambda_{\min}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Nanoparticle mass ($m \approx 10^{-18} 	ext{ kg}$), differential force ($F \approx 10^{-21} 	ext{ N}$), correlation length ($r_c$), and the ordinary loss budget ($\Lambda_{	ext{loss}} \lesssim 0.1$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on approximations valid in the small-separation regime ($D(t) \ll r_c$) and assumes that technical noise sources (like residual gas or timing mismatch) can be controlled below a specified threshold.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares projected sensitivities ($\lambda_{	ext{chosen}}$ vs $\lambda_{	ext{aggressive}}$) against various theoretical bounds, demonstrating the improvement over direct interferometric tests.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces CSL and the experimental setup using a nanoparticle pointer. It derives the expected coherence loss from CSL theory, calculates the required sensitivity based on noise budgets (including systematic errors), and finally compares the achievable limits to existing theoretical bounds.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose a measurement-like interferometric test of Continuous Spontaneous Localization (CSL), in which a trapped nanoparticle acts as a reversible mesoscopic pointer rather than as the initially prepared microscopic superposition. A microscopic two-branch system applies opposite weak forces to the nanoparticle, temporarily amplifying which-branch information into branch-conditioned pointer displacements. After one weak-trap period the pointer positions and momenta recombine, so ordinary quantum mechanics predicts recovery of the microscopic coherence, whereas CSL predicts an irreversible visibility loss accumulated while the pointer mass distributions were separated.   For a $10^{-18},{\rm kg}$ nanoparticle driven by a $10^{-21},{\rm N}$ differential force at $T=0.4,{\rm K}$, including thermal breathing and an ordinary loss budget $Λ_{\rm loss}\lesssim 0.1$, we find $λ_{\min}\simeq 1.4\times 10^{-10},{\rm s}^{-1}$ at $r_c=100,{\rm nm}$ with $10^5$ shots. A more aggressive lower-frequency point reaches $λ_{\min}\simeq 8.7\times 10^{-12},{\rm s}^{-1}$.   These sensitivities would improve over digitized direct matter-wave CSL bounds by about $7\times 10^3$ and $10^5$, respectively, while remaining above the strongest non-interferometric bounds. The proposal is therefore aimed at a substantially stronger direct visibility-loss test of CSL, and at a reversible measurement-like realization of collapse sensitivity, rather than at the strongest overall exclusion curve.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the Haldane phase of the S=1 BLBQ chain by comparing two methods to study edge spin dynamics: angular-time evolution derived from the entanglement Hamiltonian, and direct simulation using an effective magnetic field. The authors successfully demonstrate that both approaches yield consistent results regarding the dominant oscillation mode, confirming a deep link between the system's entanglement structure and its boundary physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a powerful theoretical tool—the angular-time evolution—to probe boundary physics in gapped quantum magnets, offering an alternative to standard real-time dynamics calculations. This connection between entanglement structure and physical observables is highly relevant for understanding topological phases.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the relationship between angular-time evolution, derived from entanglement Hamiltonians, and real-time edge-spin dynamics in the Haldane phase of the S=1 bilinear-biquadratic chain.

**Main result.** The analysis confirms that the dominant oscillation mode extracted from both correlation functions (angular-time) and effective edge-spin protocols matches, demonstrating a robust connection between entanglement structure and boundary physics away from specific points like the AKLT limit.

**Method.** The authors employ Matrix Product States (MPS) to calculate ground state properties, defining an angular-time evolution operator $U_l(	au) = e^{-i	au K_l}$ using the entanglement Hamiltonian $K_l$. They compare this theoretical evolution with dynamics derived from applying a uniform magnetic field to the edge spin.

**Model / system.** The system is the S=1 bilinear-biquadratic (BLBQ) quantum spin chain, characterized by the Hamiltonian $H_{eta} = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} (S_i \cdot S_{i+1} + eta(S_i \cdot S_{i+1})^2)$. The analysis focuses on the Haldane phase under open boundary conditions.

**Key observables.** Angular-time spin correlation functions $\langle S_{\alpha}^n(	au)S_{\alpha}^{n'}(0)angle$, entanglement spectrum eigenvalues ($\epsilon_i$), and effective edge-spin autocorrelation functions $G_{\alpha}^l(	au)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The coupling parameter $eta$ (ranging from 0 to approaching 1/3), the subsystem length $l$, and the correlation length $\xi$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on approximating the angular-time evolution by projecting onto the ground state sector using an approximate identity operator ($I_\chi$), which is assumed accurate away from the AKLT point.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the entanglement spectrum showing bulk degeneracy and boundary splitting, compare correlation functions for different subsystem sizes ($l=6$ vs $l=40$), and show semilog plots demonstrating that amplitude decay rates are consistent between the two dynamic measurements.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by establishing the theoretical framework using MPS to define angular-time evolution via entanglement Hamiltonians. It then calculates correlation functions, compares these results against a known edge-spin protocol (magnetic field), and finally analyzes the scaling of amplitudes with subsystem size ($l$) across different coupling regimes ($eta$).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the angular-time evolution -- a parameter-time evolution generated by the entanglement Hamiltonian -- for the bipartitioned ground state of the S=1 bilinear-biquadratic chain under the open boundary condition with the up edge spin. Using a matrix-product-state representation of the ground-state wavefunction, we calculate the angular-time spin correlation functions $\langle S_n^{α}(τ)S_{n'}^{α}(0)\rangle$ in the Haldane phase, and extract its dominant oscillation mode attributed to the nearly two-fold-degenerate entanglement spectrum associated with the $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry. We also compute the effective edge-spin dynamics under a uniform magnetic field applied to the system part and numerically verify its correspondence to the dominant angular-time mode by precisely comparing the subsystem-size dependence of their amplitudes.

</details>

**Summary.** The research presents an innovative method to generate polarization-entangled photon pairs using $	ext{3R-MoS}_2$ integrated directly within standard optical fibers. By exploiting the material's nonlinear properties and coupling it with precise polarization control, the authors achieve deterministic tuning of the entanglement state in the telecom band. This development is crucial for realizing practical, long-distance quantum key distribution systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work represents a significant engineering advance in quantum optics, moving entanglement sources from complex free-space setups into robust, chip-scale, fiber-integrated components suitable for real-world quantum communication networks.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to develop a highly tunable, compact, and fully integrated source of polarization-entangled photon pairs compatible with standard near-infrared telecommunication optical fiber infrastructure.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated deterministic control over the generated two-photon polarization state by manipulating the incident pump polarization within an in-line $	ext{3R-MoS}_2$ thin film, achieving high entanglement fidelity and a record Coincidences-to-Accidentals ratio.

**Method.** Polarization-resolved coincidence measurements are used to map the generated two-photon state $|\psi_Gangle$ as a function of pump polarization angle ($\varphi_P$) and retardance ($\delta_P$).

**Model / system.** The system utilizes Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) in a submicron $	ext{3R-MoS}_2$ thin film placed directly between standard fiber connectors. The physics relies on the second-order nonlinear susceptibility tensor ($\chi^{(2)}$) of this van der Waals material.

**Key observables.** Coincidence rates ($I_{HH}, I_{DD}, I_{RR}$), entanglement fidelity ($\mathcal{F}$), concurrence ($C$), and the Coincidences-to-Accidentals ratio (CAR).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Near-infrared telecom band operation ($\sim 1560 	ext{ nm}$), pump wavelength ($\lambda=780 	ext{ nm}$), and polarization control parameters ($\varphi_P, \delta_P$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on modeling the state evolution using unitary transformations derived from fiber birefringence measurements, assuming a self-consistent description of the entire optical network.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup for polarization tuning (using controllers and splitters), show coincidence rate mappings confirming state tunability based on pump parameters, and display density matrix estimations comparing measured states to target Bell states.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform ($	ext{3R-MoS}_2$ in fiber) to detailing the measurement techniques (polarization tomography via coincidence rates), deriving the relationship between these rates and fundamental source parameters ($\varphi_P, \delta_P$), and finally demonstrating state control by mapping measured results onto theoretical entangled states like Bell pairs.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a tunable, single-mode-optical-fiber-based source of polarization entangled photon pairs for the near-infrared telecommunication band that is deployable in standard infrastructure. The photon pairs are generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in a submicron-scale thin film of the inversion-broken rhombohedral polytype of the transition metal dichalcogenide molybdenum disulfide (3R-MoS$_2$), located between two fiber connectors. By exploiting the intrinsic symmetries of the second-order nonlinear susceptibility tensor of 3R-MoS$_2$, this hybrid approach offers control over the generated two-photon polarization state through the incident pump polarization. Most notably, two of the four maximally entangled Bell states, as well as fully co-polarized pairs can be produced. This represents a substantial improvement in terms of tunability and simplicity over established fiber-integrated sources, which require additional optical elements, precise alignment, or careful engineering of design parameters. Additionally, a nonlinear drop in the background photoluminescence signal of 3R-MoS$_2$ is observed at low pump powers, allowing us to reach a coincidences-to-accidentals ratio (CAR) of $(8.3\pm1.8)\times10^{3}$, the highest value recorded for SPDC in van der Waals materials to date.

</details>

The authors characterize how these engineered interactions dictate the droplet's stability, shape anisotropy, and dynamic behavior during collisions. It demonstrates that controlling these long-range forces allows for rich control over quantum matter wave properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides detailed theoretical insights into controlling quantum matter waves using engineered long-range interactions (DDIs) via microwave dressing, which is crucial for realizing novel quantum states like supersolids in ultracold atomic systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study systematically explores how dual microwave fields affect the formation and dynamics of self-bound quantum droplets (QDs) in dipolar molecular condensates, focusing on non-axisymmetric dipole-dipole interactions.

**Main result.** The research reveals that QD properties exhibit pronounced non-monotonic dependencies on non-axisymmetric DDI strength, and collisions between QDs show strong directional dependence ranging from rebound to fragmentation.

**Method.** The dynamics are modeled using the extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation incorporating Lee-Huang-Yang corrections. Stability and structure are analyzed via imaginary-time methods and direct simulations of perturbed evolution.

**Model / system.** The system is an ultracold Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of polar molecules whose interactions are dominated by tunable, non-axisymmetric dipole-dipole interactions (DDIs). The governing equation is the extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation with LHY corrections.

**Key observables.** Chemical potential ($\mu$), total energy ($E$), effective volume ($V$), peak density, and geometric anisotropy ratios ($\eta_{zy}, \eta_{xy}$)

**Important parameters / regimes.** Non-axisymmetric DDI strength ($\epsilon^{(2)}_{	ext{dd}}$), s-wave scattering length ($a_s$), and particle number ($N$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a regime dominated by non-axisymmetric DDIs, and the study uses mean-field approximations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate isodensity profiles of QDs under varying $\epsilon^{(2)}_{	ext{dd}}$, map out the existence region in the $(N, \epsilon^{(2)}_{	ext{dd}})$ plane, and show density cross sections for collisions along different axes ($x, y, z$).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using the eGPE with non-axisymmetric DDIs. It then characterizes the existence region and structural properties of stable QDs by analyzing how $\mu$ and $E$ depend on interaction parameters. Finally, it investigates the complex dynamics of QD collisions along different spatial directions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Recent advances in the work with ultracold condensates of polar molecules have enabled the realization of highly tunable self-bound quantum droplets (QDs), with the help of dual microwave fields dressig the dipole-dipole interactions (DDIs) It has been reported that symmetry properties and the equilibrium phase diagram of such QDs can be controlled by parameters of the two microwave fields. However, the effect of these fields on the formation and dynamics of the QD has not yet been systematically explored. Here we address self-bound QDs in a regime dominated by non-axisymmetric DDIs and governed by the extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation with the Lee-Huang-Yang corrections. Within this framework, we identify the existence region of the self-bound QDs and characterize their chemical potential, total energy, effective volume, peak density, and geometric anisotropy. The results reveal a pronounced nonmonotonous dependence on the non-axisymmetric DDI strength, whereas the increase of the number of particles in the condensate leads to tighter bound and more anisotropic QDs. Furthermore, reducing the s-wave scattering length drives a transition from stable self-bound states to the collapse. Collisions between QDs moving along different directions reveal a strong directional dependence, with outcomes ranging from quasi-elastic rebound and merger to fragmentation.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a technique called local basis rotation sampling to overcome the 'support mismatch' problem encountered in Variational Monte Carlo simulations. This bias arises when local quenches force certain quantum configurations to have zero amplitude, causing numerical instability. By rotating the sampling basis locally, the authors restore these missing contributions, allowing for accurate simulation of long-time dynamics and spectral properties in various spin models.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial, general numerical tool for simulating non-equilibrium quantum dynamics in strongly correlated systems where standard VMC estimators fail due to nodal structure or local quenching operators.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is resolving 'support mismatch' bias in Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) simulations when calculating real-time dynamics after a local quench by a charged operator.

**Main result.** A novel local basis rotation sampling scheme successfully resolves this support-mismatch problem, enabling accurate variational calculations of long-time quantum dynamics and dynamical structure factors.

**Method.** The authors propose augmenting the variational state with a helper state and applying a one-site unitary rotation to the sampling basis. This restores contributions from zero-amplitude configurations without altering the underlying physics.

**Model / system.** The method is tested on various models, including the XY model (1D and 2D) and the Heisenberg chain, simulating local-operator quenches in these quantum spin systems.

**Key observables.** Dynamical structure factors (DSF), quench-site magnetization $\langle S_{z}^i(t) angle$, and energy drift ($\Delta E/|E|$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dynamics are studied over long time scales ($t_{	ext{max}}=40$) and in various dimensions (1D, 2D).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The support mismatch is an artifact of the chosen sampling basis, which can be corrected by a local rotation.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare standard tVMC/p-tVMC simulations that freeze at $t=0$ due to bias against those using rotation sampling (rot-tVMC/rot-p-tVMC), showing the latter accurately tracking exact or reference results for magnetization and spectra.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the support mismatch problem in tVMC, then introduces the local basis rotation as a solution. It validates this approach by benchmarking against known solvable models (XY chain) and comparing spectral functions with established methods (ABACUS). The technique is shown to be applicable both for real-time dynamics and ground-state optimization.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Real-time dynamics after a local quench by a charged operator encodes the response functions measured in spectroscopic experiments, yet they have long posed a challenge for variational Monte Carlo calculations. The obstacle is a support mismatch: the projective action by a charged local operator forces an exponentially large number of configurations to vanish, but these configurations may still contribute to the dynamics, biasing the estimators and freezing the evolution at the very first step. This difficulty is an artifact of the chosen sampling basis, and the support mismatch generated by a charged local operator is itself local. We demonstrate that the missing support can be restored by a local rotation of the sampling basis, without changing the underlying variational dynamics. We propose a local basis-rotation sampling scheme that resolves the support-mismatch problem and can be readily incorporated into existing variational Monte Carlo algorithms. Benchmarks show that rotation sampling accurately captures long-time quantum dynamics, enabling variational Monte Carlo calculations of dynamical structure factors in one dimension and unbiased local-operator quench dynamics in two dimensions. We also show that this resolution of the support-mismatch problem extends beyond real-time dynamics, and may also be helpful for ground state variational Monte Carlo calculations.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents an experimental Quantum Random Number Generator (QRNG) utilizing continuous variables and QPSK modulation. It achieves state-of-the-art randomness certification by employing advanced mathematical tools like Semidefinite Programming to bound the conditional Shannon entropy in a semi-device-independent setting. This work is significant for realizing high-speed, provably secure quantum random number sources.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges advanced quantum information theory (SDP bounds on entropy) with cutting-edge photonic hardware implementation, providing a tangible, high-performance realization of fundamental security principles.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing a Quantum Random Number Generator (QRNG) framework that provides strong security guarantees while maintaining high randomness generation rates using practical physical assumptions.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated a QRNG achieving 0.223 bits per measurement, setting a record for continuous-variable semi-device-independent QRNGs, and reaching a rate of 55.6 Mbit/s.

**Method.** Randomness certification is achieved by bounding the conditional Shannon entropy using Semidefinite Programming (SDP) relaxations, which are extended to handle non-i.i.d. finite-size regimes via Entropy Accumulation Theorems.

**Model / system.** The protocol uses a prepare-and-measure scheme with four-state coherent-state constellations (QPSK modulation), measured by a low-loss integrated photonic heterodyne receiver.

**Key observables.** Certified Shannon entropy per measurement, observable witness value $W$, and the vacuum component bound $\omega$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The achieved rate is 55.6 Mbit/s at 250 Mbaud; the efficiency ($\eta$) is estimated around 0.38.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The security relies on a Semi-Device-Independent (SDI) framework, assuming bounds on the average vacuum component and observable correlations ($W$ and $\omega$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate state distributions in phase space, schematics of the experimental setup, and comparisons of certifiable randomness bounds versus mean photon number $|\alpha|^2$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the need for robust SDI frameworks to detailing the mathematical machinery (SDP relaxations) used for entropy bounding, culminating in an experimental demonstration using integrated photonics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Semi-device-independent QRNG frameworks represent a particularly attractive approach, combining strong security guarantees with high randomness generation rates while relying only on reduced and practical physical assumptions. A recently proposed approach based on photon-number constraints is particularly suited to photonic implementations, where these assumptions can be easily assessed experimentally. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a quantum random number generator within this framework, enabling the direct computation of lower bounds on the certifiable Shannon entropy via semidefinite relaxation techniques. When combined with entropy accumulation methods, this approach enables finite-size randomness certification without assuming independent and identically distributed rounds. We realize the protocol using a four-state coherent-state constellation symmetrically distributed in phase space and measured by heterodyne detection, certifying 0.223 bit per measurement, which is the highest value reported to date for a continuous-variable semi-device-independent QRNG. The implementation combines a low-loss integrated photonic heterodyne receiver with a simple transmitter assembled from commercial components, providing a practical and high-speed architecture for semi-device-independent randomness generation.

</details>
