**Summary.** The paper develops a sophisticated theoretical framework using Population Eigenstates (PESs) to describe high-spin fermionic atoms in optical lattices governed by an SU(d) spin-exchange model. By projecting the dynamics onto this PES basis, the authors derive effective Hamiltonians that accurately capture complex collective spin behavior and quantum correlations when coupling to external fields like light.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work extends quantum many-body physics beyond the standard spin-1/2 limit by utilizing SU(d) symmetry, providing a powerful theoretical tool for understanding complex collective spin behavior in ultracold atomic systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central goal is systematically constructing eigenstates for the SU(d) spin-exchange model governing high-spin fermions in optical lattices.

**Main result.** The Population Eigenstate (PES) framework provides a natural basis that allows for describing collective spin dynamics and accurately modeling coupling to light, even when the total collective spin length is not conserved.

**Method.** The authors employ systematic construction of eigenstates using PESs, deriving effective Hamiltonians via second-order Schrieffer–Wolff transformations projected onto these population manifolds.

**Model / system.** The system involves ultra-cold fermionic atoms with high spin ($s \ge 1$) in a 1D optical lattice, modeled by the SU(d) spin exchange (SE) Hamiltonian derived from the Fermi-Hubbard model in the strongly interacting limit.

**Key observables.** Spin squeezing parameter ($\xi^2$), collective spin length ($\langle\hat{J}^2angle$), and population distribution among different spin sectors ($\langle\hat{P}_{E=0}(\Lambda)angle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** High spin $s \ge 1$, strong interaction limit ($U \gg J$), quasi-momentum $q$, and coupling phase $\phi$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the strongly interacting regime for deriving the SE Hamiltonian, and effective Hamiltonians are derived using second-order perturbation theory.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare spin dynamics ($\xi^2$, $\langle\hat{J}^2angle$) between the full model, the PES-derived effective Hamiltonian, and a restricted Dicke manifold approximation for various coupling phases.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the SE model and introducing the PES basis (commuting with population operators) to deriving effective Hamiltonians via Schrieffer–Wolff transformations. It then analyzes the structure of spin eigenstates ($\Lambda$) within this basis, culminating in applying these tools to study dynamics under light coupling.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the $\mathrm{SU}(d)$ spin exchange model describing ultra-cold fermionic atoms with spin $s\ge 1$ in a one-dimensional optical lattice. The model emerges from the Fermi-Hubbard model in the strongly interacting regime with one atom in each lattice site. The central result of this work is the systematic construction of SE eigenstates in terms of magnetic sub-level populations. This representation provides a natural description of high-spin fermionic systems, where the underlying $\mathrm{SU}(d)$ symmetry gives rise to extensive degeneracies. We illustrate the usefulness of this framework for deriving effective Hamiltonians for a system weakly coupled to light through spin-orbit interactions, using a second-order Schrieffer--Wolff transformation projected onto the introduced population eigenbasis. These effective models provide a controlled description of the collective spin dynamics and capture the role of population redistribution among different collective spin length sectors induced by interactions. The agreement with the exact Fermi--Hubbard with light coupling dynamics confirms the consistency of the population eigenstates framework as a basis for describing high-spin quantum many-body systems.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces the 'minimum entanglement drop' as a novel and powerful monotone to quantify genuine multipartite entanglement, moving beyond limitations of traditional measures. It functions as a structural probe that can map out the underlying connectivity graph of entangled qubits by measuring sensitivity to particle loss. While highly effective for distinguishing topologies, its diagnostic power is limited by certain highly robust quantum states.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides advanced diagnostic tools for characterizing complex quantum correlations beyond simple scalar measures. The focus on topological fingerprinting makes it highly relevant for understanding entanglement in physical architectures or noisy quantum channels.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is developing a robust, computationally tractable measure for quantifying genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) that satisfies all necessary theoretical postulates.

**Main result.** The minimum entanglement drop, defined using negativity or tangle, serves as a powerful structural probe capable of differentiating graph topologies and tracking network evolution. However, it fails to detect entanglement in highly robust states like the 5-qubit error-correcting code.

**Method.** The authors propose defining an entanglement monotone based on the minimum reduction (drop) in global one-to-group entanglement when tracing out a single particle. This is formalized using concepts derived from generalized monogamy inequalities and negativity/tangle measures.

**Model / system.** The work analyzes general $n$-qubit quantum states, focusing on characterizing their internal connectivity structure (e.g., comparing Line vs. Star graph topologies) and analyzing the evolution of entanglement under environmental noise.

**Key observables.** Minimum entanglement drop ($D_{\min}$), minimum negativity drop ($	ext{D}_{S_{q_1}}$), Tangle ($	au$), Negativity ($\mathcal{N}$), and Concurrence ($C$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Number of qubits ($n$), noise parameter ($\gamma$), and the specific graph topology (Line vs. Star).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method is primarily a heuristic structural probe, and its diagnostic sensitivity vanishes for certain highly robust, symmetrically correlated states.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate how the minimum drop uniquely reveals underlying graph topologies (e.g., distinguishing Line from Star graphs) and show the analytical scaling of $D_{\min}$ for noisy W states versus particle number or noise strength.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first identifying the limitations of existing measures, proposing the minimum entanglement drop as a novel monotone, rigorously proving its properties (especially in the tripartite case), demonstrating its utility as a structural probe to map connectivity fingerprints, and finally analyzing its performance on specific state classes like W states under noise.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantifying genuine multipartite entanglement remains a significant challenge. We propose a multipartite entanglement monotone defined by the minimum entanglement drop -- the reduction in global one-to-group entanglement upon tracing out a single particle. We formulate a computationally efficient variant using tangle and negativity to ensure non-vanishing values for W-class states, and rigorously prove it is a valid monotone under local operations and classical communication. In the tripartite regime, the minimum tangle drop is physically equivalent to the minimum pairwise concurrence. We establish an operational framework where the entanglement drop acts as a structural probe: by assessing sensitivity to qubit loss, it identifies inseparable clusters, extracting connectivity fingerprints that uniquely differentiate graph topologies within the same local Clifford equivalence class. Integrating this mapping with classical shadows enables efficient experimental estimation and dynamic tracking of entanglement network evolution. We derive exact analytical solutions for n-qubit W states under environmental noise, revealing robust scaling behaviors. Finally, we acknowledge limitations, noting that diagnostic sensitivity strictly vanishes for highly robust states such as the 5-qubit error-correcting code.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the fate of primordial quantum information encoded in scalar perturbations as they generate gravitational waves. By analyzing decohered Gaussian states, the authors show that residual scalar coherence survives and manifests as measurable non-classical correlations—like tensor discord and connected covariance—in the induced gravitational wave background. These unique phase-sensitive signatures offer new targets for future space-based GW observatories.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete theoretical framework for how non-local quantum correlations (coherence) can be imprinted onto classical background signals (GWs), offering new diagnostic tools beyond simple power spectrum measurements.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To determine if residual quantum information from primordial scalar perturbations can survive decoherence and manifest as detectable signatures in secondary gravitational-wave backgrounds.

**Main result.** Residual scalar anomalous coherence can generate nonzero tensor discord, connected covariance, and phase-sensitive strain correlations even after the initial scalar entanglement has vanished.

**Method.** The authors derive explicit transfer relations linking the scalar anomalous coherence to the induced tensor covariance matrix using a Gaussian state description.

**Model / system.** The study models Scalar-Induced Gravitational Waves (SIGWs) generated at second order from decohered two-mode Gaussian scalar states, analyzing how quantum correlations propagate through nonlinear gravitational interactions.

**Key observables.** Gaussian tensor discord ($D_h(k)$), connected covariance ($\kappa(k)$), and phase-sensitive strain correlators ($\Gamma(k, q)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Decoherence strength ($\epsilon_{	ext{dec}}$) and the frequency/wavenumber spectrum of the source.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis works to leading non-trivial order in scalar perturbations and provides an order-of-magnitude scaling estimate for detectability, not a full sensitivity curve.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares various coherence measures (negativity, discord) showing persistence in the separable regime. Figure 2 illustrates the derived SIGW spectrum ($d_k$) and the connected covariance statistic ($\kappa(f)$).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem of quantum information loss during decoherence, derives transfer relations between scalar coherence and tensor observables, calculates specific diagnostics like discord and connected covariance, and discusses their potential detection using future interferometers.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Scalar-induced gravitational waves are usually treated as a classical stochastic background sourced by phase-random curvature perturbations. We show that this description can miss residual quantum information. Starting from a decohered two-mode Gaussian scalar state, we derive explicit transfer relations between the scalar anomalous coherence and the covariance matrix of induced tensor modes. For a localized scalar power spectrum, the ordinary tensor power is sourced by scalar power contractions, whereas the opposite-mode tensor coherence is sourced by scalar anomalous-coherence contractions. This coherence can generate nonzero tensor discord and a connected tensor-power covariance even after scalar entanglement has vanished. We identify the connected covariance and phase-sensitive strain correlations as probes of primordial quantum coherence in secondary gravitational-wave backgrounds, and discuss their possible relevance for future space-based interferometers and pulsar timing arrays.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces Universal Optimal Tracking (U-TRACK), a sophisticated method for designing Dynamical Decoupling sequences that actively correct residual errors block-by-block. By optimizing these novel XUR pulse structures, the authors demonstrate superior noise suppression compared to traditional methods like XY4 or UR40 on superconducting qubits. This establishes U-TRACK as a practical and highly robust tool for extending quantum coherence times in noisy hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** For a theoretical physicist in this area, the development of an algorithm that moves beyond simple periodic repetition to dynamically compensate for accumulated errors represents a significant conceptual leap in quantum control theory. The combination of optimization techniques (GA + GRAPE) applied to physical constraints is highly relevant.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is designing robust Dynamical Decoupling (DD) sequences to suppress environmental noise and prevent error accumulation during long idle periods in quantum computation.

**Main result.** A novel Universal Optimal Tracking (U-TRACK) approach yields XUR pulse sequences that dynamically compensate for residual errors at every block, significantly outperforming conventional periodic schemes like XY4 or UR40, especially under low-frequency noise.

**Method.** The authors use a combination of gradient optimization (GRAPE) and global search techniques (Genetic Algorithm) to optimize the phases of multiple pulse blocks simultaneously, ensuring high fidelity across intermediate checkpoints.

**Model / system.** The work is demonstrated on superconducting-qubit platforms (e.g., transmon processors). The underlying physics involves controlling qubit evolution under noise sources like frequency detuning and amplitude errors ($\epsilon, \delta$).

**Key observables.** Process fidelity ($F$) measured over long idle times; average fidelity ($ar{F}$) calculated across parameter error grids $(\epsilon, \delta)$; robustness profiles against Random Telegraph Noise (RTN).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Noise regimes defined by the switching rate $\lambda$ of RTN (e.g., low-frequency vs. high-frequency); pulse parameters include amplitude errors ($\epsilon$) and detuning ($\delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The U-TRACK method assumes that error compensation can be achieved block-by-block, leading to non-periodic optimal sequences; simulations often rely on specific pulse shapes like DRAG pulses.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the fidelity decay of UR40, XY4, and U-TRACK4 across various noise regimes (static, low-frequency RTN), demonstrating U-TRACK's superior sustained performance. Later figures detail process fidelity vs. error parameters ($\epsilon, \delta$) for multiple blocks.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the limitations of standard DD methods, proposes and optimizes the U-TRACK framework using global optimization algorithms, validates its performance against various noise models (static, time-dependent RTN), and finally compares it experimentally/numerically against established sequences like XY4 on superconducting hardware.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a widely used and resource-efficient technique for error suppression, but conventional DD relies on periodically repeating a short pulse block to refocus the qubit state during idle periods. Imperfections in this block cause residual errors to accumulate, ultimately degrading state recovery over long idle times. Here, we introduce a universal optimal tracking approach that extends the original tracking concept to a fully state-independent setting for designing DD sequences. By monitoring the qubit's evolution at predefined waypoints during optimization, the method dynamically compensates residual errors while preserving regular refocusing. Experimental demonstrations on a superconducting-qubit platform confirm the suppression of error accumulation under static control imperfections, in agreement with numerical predictions. Complementary simulations further show that optimal-tracking-based sequences maintain strong performance under time-dependent noise. These results establish optimal tracking as a practical and hardware-agnostic approach to designing short, robust DD sequences suitable for noisy quantum devices.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces Vibe Calibration, an autonomous system using LLM agents to automate the complex and expert-dependent process of calibrating large superconducting quantum processors. By formalizing expert knowledge into structured 'Skills,' the system achieves significant speedups and robustness compared to manual operation. This work establishes a reusable, auditable infrastructure for scaling quantum hardware operations.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it tackles the operational bottleneck of quantum hardware by treating calibration not as a set of fixed scripts but as an abstract, reusable, agentic workflow that can be generalized across different physical architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The calibration complexity of superconducting quantum processors is a major bottleneck for scaling toward fault-tolerant quantum computing, as conventional scripts are brittle and expert judgment is limited.

**Main result.** The system autonomously completed calibration on a 112-qubit processor in 4.7 hours, achieving a $4–5	imes$ speedup over manual methods while demonstrating transferable core decision logic across devices.

**Method.** An autonomous calibration system, Vibe Calibration, orchestrates complex workflows by distilling expert tacit knowledge into reusable, auditable 'Skills' structured as decision trees.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a superconducting quantum processor featuring 112 frequency-tunable transmon qubits. The methodology involves using Large Language Model agents to execute these Skills via parameterized measurement commands and quantitative acceptance criteria.

**Key observables.** $T_1$ relaxation time, Ramsey dephasing time ($T_{R2}$), Rabi frequencies, S21 readout response, and visibility.

**Important parameters / regimes.** 112 qubits; 4.7 hours (autonomous runtime); $4–5	imes$ speedup over manual calibration.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is that expert knowledge can be formalized into reusable Skills, allowing the system to pursue the *purpose* of a measurement rather than just mimicking specific human actions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the three-phase evolution from human supervision to full autonomy (Fig. 1), detail the decision tree structure of a qubit-characterization Skill (Fig. 2, Fig. 4), and compare autonomous vs. manual characterization results for $T_1$ and $T_{R2}$ on the 112-qubit device (Fig. 3).

**Paper structure.** The paper details a phased development: initial single-qubit calibration, scaling to 16 qubits, and culminating in the full 112-qubit system. The structure emphasizes distilling expertise into Skills, executing multi-step pipelines (Spectrum $ightarrow$ Power Rabi $ightarrow$ SingleShot $ightarrow$ T1 $ightarrow$ Ramsey), and demonstrating generalization.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Superconducting quantum computing is one of the most mature solid-state platforms for quantum computation, with processors exceeding one hundred qubits. Yet further scaling toward fault-tolerant quantum computing is increasingly constrained by calibration complexity. Conventional scripts are brittle to anomalous signals, and expert judgment is bounded by cognitive bandwidth and serial operation time, failing to keep pace with system scale. Here we report Vibe Calibration, an autonomous calibration system orchestrated by large language model agents, which distills expert tacit knowledge into reusable Skills. Each Skill is organized as a decision tree that packages parameterized measurement commands, quantitative acceptance criteria, and audit records, enabling autonomous execution and self-healing. We capture this knowledge through a three-phase human-in-the-loop distillation process and fine-tune a large language model on validated trajectories. On a 112-qubit processor with frequency-tunable transmons, the system autonomously completes calibration of 108 out of 112 qubits in 4.7 hours, achieving a 4--5$\times$ speedup over manual calibration of the full 112 qubits. A cross-validated comparison with expert manual calibration on a 16-qubit subset shows agreement on 14 out of 16 qubits. More importantly, the model demonstrates transferable calibration workflows across devices. While low-level control scripts require minor interface adaptation for different hardware platforms, the core decision logic and task orchestration generalize to new processors, demonstrating a reusable laboratory interface rather than a memorized script.This work demonstrates, for the first time, fully autonomous calibration of a hundred-qubit superconducting processor through reusable and auditable Skills, removing a critical barrier to scalable quantum hardware operation.

</details>

**Authors:** Lei Li, Zhi Li  
**Type:** theory · **Category:** quantum information and computing · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.23082v1>

**Summary.** This paper develops a novel approach for Quantum Secret Sharing tailored for non-maximal access structures. It characterizes these complex QAS using information theory tools and proposes a hybrid scheme that combines quantum entanglement distribution with classical sharing. The result is a provably perfect and efficient secret sharing protocol applicable to specific hyperstar network topologies.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on quantum information theory rather than condensed matter physics, the rigorous mathematical framework used to analyze resource constraints (efficiency) and perfect security in quantum protocols is highly relevant to understanding error correction and state preparation in complex quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of constructing efficient and perfect quantum secret sharing (QSS) schemes for non-maximal Quantum Access Structures (QAS). It aims to overcome resource consumption issues inherent in current QSS protocols.

**Main result.** A universal, efficient, and perfect quantum secret sharing scheme is proposed for a specific class of non-maximal QAS (the hyperstar with three hyperedges) by combining quantum entanglement distribution with classical secret sharing techniques.

**Method.** The methodology involves characterizing forbidden and intermediate sets within the non-maximal QAS using concepts like quantum mutual information. The construction utilizes entangled states and Pauli operators to encode and reconstruct the secret state.

**Model / system.** The model is Quantum Secret Sharing, where a quantum state $|	ext{K}angle$ is shared among participants according to an access structure $\Gamma$. The specific structures analyzed are derived from hyperstars with three hyperedges.

**Key observables.** Quantum Mutual Information $I(A:K)$, Von Neumann Entropy $S(K)$, and the ability of authorized vs. unauthorized subsets to recover the secret state $|	ext{K}angle$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The structure type (hyperstar with three hyperedges), the threshold parameters $(k, n)$, and the entanglement properties derived from Schmidt decomposition.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often assumes pure-state encoding for the QAS realization. The final PQSS scheme relies on combining quantum sharing over a representative element QAS ($R_i$) with a perfect classical secret sharing component.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the flowchart of the proposed PQSS scheme for a minimal authorized subset based on $\Gamma_3$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first characterizing non-maximal QAS (defining forbidden/intermediate sets), then establishing theoretical links between these sets and information leakage via mutual information. Finally, it constructs and proves the security of the hybrid PQSS scheme for specific hyperstar substructures.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum secret sharing is one of the core security technologies in the field of quantum communication. Aiming at the problems of high quantum resource consumption and the difficulty in balancing security and efficiency existing in current quantum secret sharing schemes under non-maximal quantum access structure(QAS), this paper focuses on the judgment criteria of non-maximal QAS and the construction methods of efficient and perfect quantum secret sharing schemes on a kind of non-maximal QAS, i.e. hyperstar with three hyperedges. Firstly, we characterizes the forbidden sets and intermediate sets within this non-maximal QAS, and provides a characterization for non-maximal QAS realizable by pure-state encoding. Secondly, the representative element QAS of hyperstar with three hyperedges is defined, which serves as a substructure of this hyperstar QAS, and belongs to non-maximal QAS. Furthermore, we propose a universal, efficient, and perfect quantum secret sharing scheme based on this hyperstar QAS using corresponding classical secret sharing scheme as an auxiliary. By deploying lightweight quantum resources to representative element access structures, the proposed scheme reduces the difficulty in quantum state preparation and distribution, and enhances its security and resource utilization efficiency.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a novel, hardware-aware quantum approach to enhance histopathologic cancer detection by extracting robust edge features from medical images using superconducting and trapped-ion quantum processors. By developing configurable circuits and implementing a multi-stage noise mitigation pipeline, the authors demonstrate high inter-platform consistency and achieve strong classification accuracy on real NISQ hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous testing of quantum algorithms on multiple physical hardware backends (superconducting vs. trapped ion) while implementing advanced noise mitigation techniques is highly relevant for understanding the feasibility of near-term quantum machine learning applications.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge of performing reliable histopathologic cancer detection from complex tissue images using near-term quantum hardware.

**Main result.** The proposed quantum edge detection method achieves high inter-platform consistency ($r \approx 0.93–0.94$) and reaches 79.80% classification accuracy on real hardware, outperforming prior QFT baselines.

**Method.** It employs configurable quantum circuits (DG-CSWAP/DG-DST) to estimate multi-directional edge responses via overlap measurements, coupled with a three-stage NISQ error mitigation pipeline.

**Model / system.** The work is tested on five diverse quantum processors via Amazon Braket (superconducting and trapped-ion), operating under Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) constraints.

**Key observables.** Inter-platform Pearson correlation ($r \approx 0.93–0.94$), classification accuracy (79.80%), and the corrected edge estimate $e_{	ext{corr}}^c$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The use of angle encoding $|\psi(p)angle = R_y(	heta) |0angle$ for pixel values, and the specific parameters for noise mitigation stages.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the quantum edge map derived from shot-based measurements can serve as a robust feature input to classical deep learning models (ResNet-50).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the end-to-end pipeline, the 6-qubit DG-CSWAP circuit structure, and comparative results showing classification performance improvements over baselines on real hardware.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem, details two quantum circuits (DG-CSWAP/DG-DST) for edge estimation, rigorously applies a three-stage NISQ mitigation pipeline, validates consistency across five different QPU platforms, and finally demonstrates classification performance using a ResNet-50.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Histopathologic cancer detection is challenging due to tissue variability, staining differences, and subtle visual distinctions between disease classes. We propose two quantum algorithms for this task: a configurable dual-gradient CSWAP circuit (DG-CSWAP) that computes multi-directional edge responses in a single execution via per-pixel local Ry encoding, and a hardware-efficient destructive swap circuit (DG-DST) natively matched to quantum processing unit (QPU) gate sets at substantially lower circuit complexity. We prove algebraic equivalence between DG-CSWAP and DG-DST, enabling a two-circuit QPU validation strategy. A three-stage NISQ mitigation pipeline, including readout error correction, bias subtraction, and slope regression, reduces single-pixel hardware MSE by ~8x. Validated on five quantum processors via Amazon Braket, the method achieves inter-platform Pearson r ~ 0.93-0.94 across all local-simulator pairs. Compared to a prior Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) based amplitude-encoding baseline requiring 12-qubit global state preparation and a three-model ensemble (85.55% on PatchCamelyon), the proposed method uses shot-based measurements, executes on real quantum hardware, and achieves 79.80% accuracy with a single ResNet-50. A Lite configuration delivers a 17x preprocessing speedup at a 2.59% accuracy cost. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantum hardware implementation study with noise mitigation for histopathologic image classification.

</details>

**Summary.** This work rigorously investigates when state-dependent entropy measurements, arising in the context of holographic quantum error correction, correspond to actual local bulk geometries. It establishes a hierarchy of necessary and sufficient conditions—requiring matching first and second-order differential constraints—to prove this geometric compatibility. This bridges advanced topics in quantum information theory with differential geometry.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous mathematical framework connecting quantum information measures (entropy/area) derived from holographic codes directly to fundamental geometric properties of spacetime metrics in AdS space.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is determining the nonlinear geometrizability of state-dependent proto-area data derived from approximate holographic recovery processes.

**Main result.** Geometrizability requires satisfying both first-order (linear) and second-order (quadratic) consistency conditions, which are necessary and sufficient for local metric reconstruction under regularity assumptions.

**Method.** The analysis employs tools from differential geometry, including the geodesic X-ray transform, Jacobi equations, and jet calculus to establish rigorous mathematical criteria for geometric realization.

**Model / system.** The framework is set in the context of AdS/CFT holography applied to quantum error correction codes. The input data is the state-dependent proto-area ($	ext{SPA}$), which measures entropy differences related to boundary regions.

**Key observables.** Proto-Area Map ($	ext{SPA}$), first and second order obstructions ($\Pi_{\mathfrak{g}a_1}$, $\mathcal{O}_2$), and the reconstructed metric two-jet $(h_1, h_2)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis depends on the regularity of the logical state family ($\Sigma$) and the approximation level (finite network vs. continuum).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Assumptions include 'recovery-regularity' for the state manifold and the applicability of split-regularity hypotheses to ensure smooth local geometric structures.

**Figures summary.** Figures summarize geometrizability criteria across different levels (network, first jet, two-jet) and compare various bounds on reconstruction errors.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops from finite network realization problems using linear algebra constraints to the continuum limit, establishing necessary conditions via Jacobi equations for the second jet, and concluding with explicit reconstruction formulas modulo boundary diffeomorphisms.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

State-dependent proto-area data produced by approximate recovery need not be compatible with a single local bulk metric. Using recovery maps calibrated on the code channel and held fixed along a logical-state family, we derive exact finite-resolution criteria and, near the hyperbolic disk, necessary and sufficient conditions for a regular proto-area two-jet to arise from a metric two-jet on a time-reflection-symmetric asymptotically AdS$_3$ slice. Finite networks give a polyhedral realization problem with primal and dual certificates, stable reconstruction, and explicit witnesses of nongeometry. In the continuum, the geometric tangent space is the range of the rank-two geodesic X-ray transform. A metric-forced Jacobi equation determines the normal Hessian of the renormalized boundary-length image and yields a gauge-invariant quadratic obstruction. Under a split-regularity hypothesis, nearby geometric data form a local graph; the two-jet criterion itself is unconditional for regular data. Hamiltonian-skewed codes realize both first-order nongeometry and a response whose first obstruction appears only at quadratic order. The compatible metric perturbation is reconstructed modulo boundary-fixing diffeomorphisms.

</details>

**Summary.** This work applies Density Functional Theory to study few-electron atoms confined by a Gaussian potential, calculating not only energies but also various information-theoretic measures like Shannon entropy. The results reveal that confinement parameters strongly dictate the system's structure, showing characteristic minima/maxima in localization indicators and mapping these trends onto the Fisher-Shannon plane.

**Why it may be interesting.** The integration of quantum information theory (entropy measures) directly into electronic structure calculations for confined systems provides novel diagnostics to quantify electron-electron interaction strength and spatial localization beyond standard energy calculations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the electronic structure and associated information measures of few-electron atoms confined by a spherically symmetric Gaussian potential using Density Functional Theory (DFT). The goal is to understand how confinement parameters affect energy, localization, and correlation effects.

**Main result.** Changes in potential width ($R$) cause specific trends in observables: $S_r$ exhibits minima while $S_p$ and $I_r$ attain maxima. Furthermore, the Fisher-Shannon plane reveals progressive electronic density compression, indicating weakening relative electron-correlation effects.

**Method.** The research employs DFT formalism, solving the Kohn-Sham equation using a generalized pseudo-spectral (GPS) method. Correlation is treated via Wigner or LYP functionals, and information measures like Shannon entropy ($S_r, S_p$) and Fisher information ($I_r$) are calculated.

**Model / system.** The system models few-electron atoms/ions ($	ext{H}, 	ext{He-like } Z=2-18, 	ext{Li}, 	ext{Be}$) confined by a Gaussian Potential $V_{	ext{conf}}(r)$. The effective potential incorporates the external confinement alongside standard Coulomb and exchange-correlation terms.

**Key observables.** Ground/excited state energies ($E$), Shannon entropy in position ($S_r$) and momentum ($S_p$) spaces, Fisher information ($I_r$), and various correlation measures ($	ext{Srcorr}, 	ext{Spcorr}, 	ext{Stcorr}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gaussian potential parameters ($V_0$, $R$), atomic number ($Z$), and the functional choice (Wigner vs. LYP). Analysis focuses on intermediate regimes of $R$ where confinement effects are strongest.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations rely on DFT approximations, specifically using work function-based exchange potentials and parameterized correlation functionals (Wigner/LYP). The GPS method is used for solving the KS equation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate energy dependence on $R$ vs. $V_0$, excitation energies ($1s2s$), and how various information measures ($	ext{Ir}_{	ext{corr}}$, etc.) vary non-monotonically with $R$ and $Z$. The Fisher-Shannon plane is used to map localization trends.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes energy calculations across different atomic species under Gaussian confinement, followed by a detailed investigation of information measures ($S_r, S_p, I_r$) and correlation terms. Key findings are presented through comparative analysis across varying potential parameters ($R, V_0$) and atomic numbers ($Z$).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Energies of H, He-like ($Z=2-18$) ions, Li, and Be are investigated under a spherically symmetric Gaussian potential through a density functional formalism. The radial Kohn-Sham equation has been solved by invoking a work function-based exchange potential. The effect of electron correlation is analyzed by incorporating two functionals: a local parameterized Wigner functional and a non-linear gradient- and Laplacian-dependent Lee-Yang-Parr (LYP) functional. The generalized pseudospectral method is employed to provide accurate numerical eigenfunctions and eigenvalues. This allows nonuniform, optimal spatial discretization fulfilling the Dirichlet boundary conditions. This work demonstrates a possible manipulation of energy by controlling dot parameters. Apart from ground states, exploratory results are also reported for low-lying excited state $1s2s$ ($^{1,3}S$) of He atom. Companion calculations are also performed for various information-theoretic measures, such as Shannon entropy in position ($S_{r}$), momentum ($S_{p}$) spaces, and Fisher information in position space ($I_{r}$). The behavior of correlation functionals in presence of Gaussian potential is examined critically. We find that energy increases, $S_{r}$ exhibits minima, while $S_{p}$, $I_{r}$ attain maxima for a decrease in the width of potential, whereas an increase in potential depth further amplifies these effects across all properties. The Fisher-Shannon plane reveals a progressive localization as well as the compression of electronic density, and thereby indicates a weakening of relative electron-correlation effects. In the Collin's conjecture, it gives rise to a non-linear loop-like feature. Much of the results are presented here for the first time.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and simulation study on controlling Exceptional Points (EPs) in OAM photonics using the geometry of a helicoidal waveguide. By tuning the twist rate ($\Omega$), researchers can force the system into an EP, which is confirmed by observing characteristic signatures like eigenvalue coalescence and phase rigidity collapse. This provides a robust blueprint for designing next-generation photonic devices based on non-Hermitian physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges geometric control (topology/geometry) with non-Hermitian physics in photonics, offering a highly controllable platform for realizing exotic quantum phenomena that are relevant to integrated quantum optics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper proposes a novel method to control Exceptional Points (EPs) in Orbital-Angular-Momentum (OAM) photonics using geometric parameters derived from the helicoidal background.

**Main result.** They demonstrate that the EP location can be precisely tuned by controlling the geometry (twist rate $\Omega$), providing measurable, falsifiable signatures like linear tracking of the EP with residual detuning.

**Method.** The analysis involves reducing the wave dynamics to an effective two-mode non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and applying input-output formalism to map theoretical predictions onto observable spectral maps.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled using OAM modes propagating in a helicoidal background, governed by an effective Schrödinger equation derived from the Laplace-Beltrami operator. The dynamics are captured by an effective two-mode Hamiltonian describing coupling between opposite-OAM modes ($\pm m$).

**Key observables.** Eigenvalue coalescence, phase-rigidity collapse ($r_j 	o 0$), linear tracking of $	ext{EP}$ vs. residual detuning ($\Delta_0$), and branch exchange upon parameter looping.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The helicoidal twist rate ($\Omega$ or $	au$) acts as the primary control parameter, compensating for a residual detuning ($\Delta_0$). The EP condition requires balancing geometric detuning with non-Hermitian losses/gains ($|\Delta\gamma| \sim 4|g|$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on reducing the system to an isolated two-mode doublet, assuming spectator modes remain spectrally separated. It primarily uses semiclassical or coupled-mode approximations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the coalescence of eigenvalue branches (Fig. 2), the collapse of phase rigidity at the EP (Fig. 5), and the linear relationship between $	ext{EP}$ location and external detuning ($\Delta_0$) (Fig. 6, Fig. 10c).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from deriving the effective Hamiltonian in a helicoidal background to establishing the EP condition via two-mode reduction. It then validates this using multimode spectral tests, introduces advanced diagnostics like phase rigidity and topological looping, and concludes with device simulations on both reciprocal and asymmetric coupling platforms.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Exceptional points (EPs) are non-Hermitian spectral singularities where eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce. We propose a geometry-controlled route to EPs in orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) photonics. In an effective torsion-free helicoidal background, the twist supplies a signed, real chiral splitting between opposite-OAM modes, while openness, gain, loss, leakage, or channel coupling, supplies the non-Hermiticity. The EP is reached when the geometric detuning compensates for a residual mode splitting and the linewidth contrast meets the non-Hermitian balance condition; the twist rate is thus the control parameter, not the source of non-Hermiticity. We obtain the OAM slope both for a confined quantum problem and, in the paraxial regime, for a helically twisted guide, and embed the OAM doublet in a multimode mode-space model to show that the EP survives spectator modes. Eigenvalue coalescence, phase-rigidity collapse, linear EP tracking with residual detuning, and branch exchange under geometric encircling provide falsifiable signatures. An OAM-resolved input-output response maps these onto spectroscopy-level observables, including spectral maps and three-dimensional Riemann-surface visualizations. A device-level paraxial simulation of two distinct photonic platforms, one reciprocal and one asymmetric-coupling Wiersig-type platform, reproduces the predicted exceptional point and its linear geometric tracking.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors theoretically investigate a hybrid optomechanical system combining plasmonic and WGM cavities coupled to a molecule. They demonstrate that tuning the inter-cavity coupling and detuning allows for the controlled generation of deterministic chaos via molecular vibrations. This establishes the system as a promising, room-temperature platform for on-chip chaotic light sources.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly bridges cavity QED/optics with molecular physics by demonstrating how engineered coupling mechanisms can induce complex, non-linear dynamics (chaos) in a solid-state platform at ambient temperatures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to achieve deterministic chaotic dynamics for on-chip light generation and random signal applications at room temperature, overcoming limitations of conventional cavity optomechanics.

**Main result.** The hybrid molecular optomechanical system was shown to exhibit a controllable period-doubling route to chaos, identifying it as a viable platform for room-temperature chaotic light sources.

**Method.** The study uses semiclassical equations of motion and characterizes the dynamics by computing the largest Lyapunov exponent ($\lambda_{\max}$) via the Benettin algorithm.

**Model / system.** The system is a hybrid setup coupling a plasmonic nanocavity, a WGM microcavity, and a molecular vibrational mode. The dynamics are modeled using an effective Hamiltonian involving three coupled modes.

**Key observables.** Largest Lyapunov exponent ($\lambda_{\max}$), phase-space trajectories (strange attractors), spectral content of light/vibrations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** WGM detuning ($\Delta_a$), plasmon--WGM coupling ($J$), and plasmon--vibration coupling ($g_c$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is performed in the semiclassical limit, treating the molecular vibrations classically while retaining quantum descriptions for cavity fields.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the system schematic, phase diagrams mapping chaotic regimes based on control parameters ($\Delta a$ vs $g_c$, etc.), and time/phase-space evolution showing transitions to chaos.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the physical setup and Hamiltonian, derives the coupled nonlinear equations of motion, analyzes stability using Lyapunov exponents across parameter spaces, and concludes by mapping out controllable chaotic regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Chaos is central to secure communication and physical random-number generation. Conventional cavity-optomechanical implementations, however, usually rely on weak single-photon optomechanical coupling and low-frequency mechanical modes, so access to deterministic chaotic dynamics often requires large driving power and careful suppression of thermal noise. Here we theoretically study a hybrid molecular optomechanical system formed by coupling a plasmonic nanocavity to a whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microcavity. The plasmonic nanocavity provides terahertz-scale single-photon optomechanical coupling to a molecular vibration, while the WGM resonator offers a low-loss photonic channel that mitigates the short plasmon lifetime. By integrating the semiclassical equations of motion and evaluating the largest Lyapunov exponent, we map the nonlinear dynamical regimes in the parameter spaces of WGM detuning, plasmon--WGM coupling, and plasmon--vibration optomechanical coupling. We show that increasing the plasmon--vibration coupling drives the system from self-sustained oscillations to chaos through a period-doubling cascade. At moderate coupling strengths, isolated chaos windows can be opened or closed by tuning the WGM detuning and the inter-cavity coupling. These results identify molecular optomechanics as a controllable room-temperature platform for on-chip chaotic light generation and random-signal applications.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces the integrated imaginary scattering eigenphase $G(\gamma)$ as a novel, global diagnostic tool to detect Exceptional Points (EPs) in open PT-symmetric systems. By analyzing the S-matrix eigenphases, it shows that $G(\gamma)$ exhibits a unique inflection point preceding the EP, confirming that peak gain/loss asymmetry and state coalescence are governed by distinct physical conditions in open environments.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, model-independent spectroscopic technique for characterizing non-Hermitian degeneracies (EPs) in open quantum systems using only phase measurements, which is highly relevant to modern photonics and metamaterials research.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To find a direct, phase-sensitive signature of Exceptional Points (EPs) in open PT-symmetric systems that does not rely on identifying individual resonant states.

**Main result.** The integrated imaginary scattering eigenphase G(gamma) provides a robust global diagnostic for EPs; its inflection point precedes the EP and coincides with maximum gain/loss asymmetry, demonstrating independent physical mechanisms.

**Method.** Analysis is performed entirely at the level of the Scattering Matrix (S-matrix), tracking the evolution of complex scattering eigenphases ($	heta_n$) across the PT-symmetry-breaking transition.

**Model / system.** The model is a one-dimensional PT-symmetric quantum dimer with balanced gain and loss, coupled to continuum leads. The analysis is formulated generally for any wave system describable by an S-matrix (photonic, acoustic, microwave).

**Key observables.** Scattering Matrix elements ($r, t, r', t'$), complex scattering eigenphases ($	heta_n$), and the integrated imaginary scattering eigenphase $G(\gamma)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The non-Hermitian strength parameter $\gamma$, which controls the transition from PT-exact to PT-broken symmetry.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is formulated entirely at the level of the S-matrix, making the results universally applicable across different wave systems.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the evolution of transmission resonances (Fig. 2) and track resonance positions/widths vs. $\gamma$ (Fig. 3). Crucially, they show the imaginary parts of eigenphases ($	heta_{Im, n}$) developing localized structures of opposite sign near EP (Fig. 5), and plot $G(\gamma)$ showing its characteristic inflection point before saturation (Fig. 6).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the S-matrix formalism for open PT systems, analyzes the complex eigenphases ($	heta_n$) as a diagnostic tool, develops the global scalar observable $G(\gamma)$, and finally demonstrates that $G(\gamma)$ robustly pinpoints the EP by tracking its unique inflection point.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose and analytically demonstrate that the eigenphases of the scattering matrix provide direct, phase-sensitive signatures of exceptional points in open PT-symmetric systems. Using a one-dimensional PT-symmetric quantum dimer with balanced gain and loss, coupled to continuum leads, we track the evolution of the scattering eigenphases across the PT-exact to PT-broken transition. The imaginary parts of the eigenphases develop localized structures of opposite sign as the exceptional point is approached, reflecting the emergence of gain/loss asymmetry in the scattering eigenmodes. We introduce the integrated imaginary scattering eigenphase G(gamma), which condenses this information into a single experimentally accessible scalar. G(gamma) is negligibly small in the PT-exact phase and undergoes a sharp transition -- a pronounced inflection followed by saturation into a plateau -- near the exceptional point. The inflection point of G(gamma) precedes gamma_{EP} and coincides with the maximum amplitude of the transmission resonances, revealing that peak gain/loss asymmetry and eigenstate coalescence are governed by independent conditions in open systems -- a direct fingerprint of their finite coupling to the continuum. Because the analysis is formulated entirely at the level of the S-matrix -- without reference to any specific physical realization -- the results are universally applicable across wave systems, including photonic, acoustic, and microwave platforms where phase-resolved measurements are available.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a response-geometric framework for open quantum systems by decomposing the system's response tensor into symmetric and antisymmetric parts. This allows researchers to geometrically distinguish between local susceptibility (metric sector) and nonreciprocal effects like geometric work (curvature sector). The key finding is that this curvature arises naturally from the misalignment between the system's intrinsic Hamiltonian basis and the environment-induced pointer basis.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful geometric tool to quantify non-reciprocal effects (like directed energy flow or geometric work) in open quantum systems, moving beyond standard equilibrium fluctuation theorems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing a response-geometric framework for open quantum systems by decomposing the stationary-state response tensor into symmetric and antisymmetric sectors.

**Main result.** The theory establishes that geometric work emerges as a measurable signature of nonreciprocal response, extending fluctuation-response relations from equilibrium thermodynamics to non-equilibrium steady states.

**Method.** Linear response theory is used to decompose the stationary-state response tensor into metric (symmetric) and curvature (antisymmetric) components.

**Model / system.** The analysis uses open quantum systems, exemplified by a driven dissipative qubit under pure dephasing. The framework applies generally to systems whose dynamics are governed by competition between Hamiltonian evolution and environmental dissipation.

**Key observables.** Local susceptibility (governed by the symmetric sector), geometric work curvature (from the antisymmetric sector), and state distinguishability (quantified by the Bures metric).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Basis misalignment ($	heta$ or $g$), which quantifies the incompatibility between the Hamiltonian eigenbasis and the environment-selected pointer basis.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes that the stationary state can be parameterized by external control variables, allowing for a geometric description of response. It notes that full integrability (Kähler geometry) remains an open question.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spatial organization and distinct nature of the determinants associated with the work curvature ($F$), susceptibility ($\det G$), and Bures metric ($\det g_{Bures}$) in parameter space.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the framework by decomposing the response tensor, showing how equilibrium recovers purely metric geometry (vanishing antisymmetric sector), and then applying this to non-equilibrium systems where both metric and symplectic structures coexist due to basis incompatibility.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a response-geometric framework for open quantum systems by decomposing the stationary-state response tensor into symmetric and antisymmetric sectors. The symmetric sector defines a metric-like response tensor governing local susceptibility, while the antisymmetric sector defines a curvature two-form associated with nonreciprocal response and geometric work. We show that the work curvature is precisely the antisymmetric component of the response tensor, establishing a fluctuation--response relation that extends the geometric structure of equilibrium thermodynamics to nonequilibrium steady states, and reveals a response geometry with both metric and symplectic sectors. In equilibrium, the antisymmetric sector vanishes by reciprocity, recovering the familiar metric geometry of thermodynamic response. Open quantum systems admit a broader structure in which reciprocal and nonreciprocal responses coexist on the same control manifold. We illustrate this with a driven dissipative qubit under pure dephasing, where finite curvature emerges from the misalignment between the Hamiltonian eigenbasis and the pointer basis selected by the environment, without requiring strong driving or engineered reservoirs. Comparison with the Bures metric shows that response geometry and information geometry characterize distinct properties of the stationary-state manifold: the former governs susceptibility and geometric work, the latter quantifies state distinguishability. Geometric work thus emerges as a measurable signature of nonreciprocal response in open quantum systems.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors analyze a quantum Otto cycle in a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model, demonstrating that the system naturally possesses decoupled 'idle levels.' By tuning the non-Hermitian parameter ($\eta_0$), they show this idle-level mechanism allows for independent control over efficiency, driving the engine into an efficient heat engine regime and confirming non-Hermiticity as a powerful tool in quantum thermodynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete realization of an advanced quantum thermodynamics concept—the idle-level engine—using non-Hermiticity as a tunable resource to surpass standard thermodynamic limitations in spin models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates a quantum Otto cycle using an idle-level heat engine architecture realized within a physical spin model to demonstrate non-Hermiticity's role in controlling thermal machine performance.

**Main result.** Tuning the non-Hermitian parameter ($\eta_0$) drives the system from a dissipative regime ($W<0$) into a genuine heat engine mode ($W>0$), simultaneously enhancing both output work and efficiency towards the Carnot limit.

**Method.** The analysis employs the non-Hermitian canonical thermodynamic framework, calculating equilibrium properties using the biorthogonal eigenbasis for the four strokes of the Otto cycle.

**Model / system.** The system is a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model featuring a staggered imaginary magnetic field. The Hamiltonian naturally decouples into working levels (dependent on external fields) and idle levels (independent of external fields).

**Key observables.** Net work ($W$), engine efficiency ($\eta = W/Q_h$), heat absorbed ($Q_h$), and the energy spectrum.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The non-Hermitian parameter $\eta_0$ is the primary control knob, which must be kept within the PT-unbroken phase ($|\eta_0| < 1$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The work-efficiency synergy is demonstrated for the quasistatic Otto cycle; finite-time cycles are assumed to degrade performance. The adiabatic process requires $\eta_0$ to remain away from the exceptional point ($\eta_0 = 1$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the transition of net work ($W$) from negative (dissipative) to positive (engine) as $\eta_0$ increases, and show that efficiency ($\eta$) enhances monotonically with $\eta_0$. Figure 4 details how idle-level occupation differences modulate absorbed heat ($Q_h$).

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and its energy level decoupling. It then applies the non-Hermitian canonical framework to calculate thermodynamic quantities for the four strokes of the Otto cycle, culminating in demonstrating the idle-level control mechanism that enhances work and efficiency.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study a quantum Otto cycle in a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model with a staggered imaginary magnetic field. The energy spectrum of this system naturally decouples into a pair of working levels that depend on the external field and a pair of idle levels that are completely independent of it, thereby providing the first concrete microscopic realization of the idle-level quantum heat engine architecture proposed by de~Oliveira and Jonathan [Phys. Rev. E 104, 044133 (2021)] in a physical spin model. Tuning the non-Hermitian parameter eta_0 drives a continuous transition from a dissipative regime with negative net work and net heat absorption from the hot reservoir into a genuine heat engine mode, while simultaneously enhancing both output work and efficiency. As eta_0 increases within the stable PT-unbroken phase, the engine efficiency rises significantly, reaching a substantial fraction of the Carnot limit. This effect originates from the compression of the idle-level gap, which redistributes the level occupation weights in the hot and cold equilibrium states and thereby modulates the absorbed heat. The numerator of the net work expression is independent of eta_0, but the denominator depends on eta_0 indirectly through hyperbolic cosine functions -- this is the mathematical root of the idle-level control mechanism. We provide a detailed analysis of the robustness of these findings against parameter variations, a critical comparison of the non-Hermitian control with the Hermitian limit, and a concrete experimental proposal for trapped-ion quantum simulators. Our results demonstrate that non-Hermiticity serves as an indispensable tool for steering both the operation mode and the performance of a quantum engine.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes collective Mpemba-type relaxation in degenerate bosonic modes coupled to a thermal bath. By examining weak-coupling Markovian, strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett, and non-Markovian limits, the authors show that the coupling structure dictates distinct decay channels. The results highlight how reservoir memory and internal dynamics can lead to complex, multiple transient reorderings of relaxation timescales.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for understanding how collective dissipation in many-body bosonic systems can lead to non-trivial, history-dependent relaxation phenomena like the Mpemba effect, which is crucial for quantum thermodynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates collective Mpemba-type relaxation, which involves the crossing of energy decay timescales, in a system of degenerate bosonic modes coupled to a common thermal reservoir.

**Main result.** The coupling structure leads to distinct relaxation channels (incoherent vs. coherent), and the specific physical regime (Markovian vs. non-Markovian) dictates whether crossings are simple exponentials or exhibit complex transient reorderings.

**Method.** The analysis employs mean-field reduction techniques to derive effective master equations for different coupling regimes, comparing energy decay ($\Delta E(t)$) with full state diagnostics like the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

**Model / system.** The system consists of $M$ degenerate bosonic modes coupled via an interaction Hamiltonian to a common thermal reservoir. The dynamics are analyzed across weak-coupling Markovian, strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett, and non-Markovian limits.

**Key observables.** Energy difference $\Delta E(t)$, Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence ($	ext{DKL}$), relaxation rates ($\gamma$ vs. $M\gamma$), and the Mpemba crossing time ($t_	imes$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Number of modes ($M$), coupling strengths, reservoir memory effects (Lorentzian spectrum), and initial state preparation parameters ($\Delta n_0$, $\Delta \alpha$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies heavily on mean-field approximations derived by tracing out $M-1$ modes from the full system Hamiltonian.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate clean Mpemba crossings, anti-Mpemba inversions, and complex transient reorderings showing multiple crossings in both energy and KL divergence diagnostics across different coupling regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically progresses by first establishing the weak-coupling Markovian result (two distinct decay channels), then extending to the Caldeira-Leggett regime (introducing quadrature dynamics), and finally incorporating reservoir memory effects via non-Markovian kernels.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate collective Mpemba-type relaxation in a degenerate family of bosonic modes coupled to a common thermal reservoir. Starting from a fully symmetric M-mode description and employing a representative mean-field reduction, we derive effective master equations for weak-coupling Markovian, strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett, and weak-coupling non-Markovian regimes. In the weak-coupling Markovian limit, relaxation separates into an incoherent thermal channel decaying at rate gamma and a collective coherent channel decaying at rate M gamma, yielding an explicit Mpemba crossing time determined by the initial-state preparation. In the strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett regime, transient quadrature dynamics enriches the relaxation pattern, delaying crossings in the overdamped sector and generating multiple crossings in the underdamped sector. In the non-Markovian regime, reservoir memory reshapes the same channel-competition mechanism through time-dependent decay rates and a Lamb shift, producing delayed and clustered crossing windows. Numerical results based on the energy and the Kullback-Leibler divergence reveal Mpemba and anti-Mpemba behavior, criterion dependence, and multiple transient reorderings induced by collective coherence, quadrature dynamics, and reservoir memory.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes how modifying the underlying connectivity of a sandpile model—by rewiring its directed network—alters its statistical behavior. The authors find that 1D structures exhibit sharp, critical transitions in load distribution, whereas 2D structures show smoother changes. This highlights the sensitivity of transport properties to network topology and suggests the Gini coefficient as a powerful diagnostic tool for such transitions.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical SOC dynamics, the study's use of network topology modification and critical transitions based on global measures like the Gini coefficient provides transferable concepts for understanding non-equilibrium phase transitions in complex quantum systems or engineered quantum networks.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how systematically rewiring a directed network affects the avalanche statistics and structural properties of the sandpile model.

**Main result.** In 1D, rewirings cause a sharp transition in load inequality (Gini coefficient) at $\sim 85\%$ rewiring. In contrast, 2D systems show a smoother change, maintaining power-law energy release even when fully rewired.

**Method.** The authors simulate the Bak-Tang-Wiesenfeld sandpile model on networks that are systematically modified by controlled rewiring algorithms to ensure continuous energy dissipation.

**Model / system.** The system is the BTW sandpile model applied to directed graphs, initially starting as a 1D linear chain and extended to 2D lattices. The process involves iteratively replacing network links while maintaining an acyclic structure (DAG).

**Key observables.** Gini coefficient of load distribution, avalanche energy PDF ($\Delta E$), betweenness centrality, average shortest path length $\langle L angle$, and the critical rewiring proportion ($f_c^r$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The fraction of rewired links ($f_r$) is the primary control parameter, analyzed in both 1D and 2D geometries.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Rewiring rules are strictly enforced to guarantee that energy can always leave the system, preventing trapped energy or network breakage.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the evolution of total energy, stationary grain distributions, and the PDF of energy release events as a function of rewiring steps ($n_R$ or $f_r$). The Gini coefficient vs. $f_r$ plots highlight sharp (1D) versus smooth (2D) transitions.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the sandpile dynamics by first establishing the controlled rewiring process, then comparing 1D and 2D results across various metrics (Gini, $\langle L angle$, centrality), culminating in a discussion of size effects and the utility of the Gini coefficient as a diagnostic tool.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Several studies have considered sandpile dynamics not over regular grids, but over networks. In this case, avalanches redistribute grains not between neighboring sites in a geometrical sense, but between connected sites, in a topological sense. However, depending on how nodes are connected, grains may never leave the system, preventing energy release. In this work, we study the simplest case, the BTW model in one and two dimensions, rewiring the nodes so that at every rewiring step, the energy release is always possible, and study avalanche statistics as a function of rewiring. In the 1D case, a transition is observed in the Gini coefficient of the load distribution per node at about 85% the number of possible rewirings, a transition which is not evident with other measures, such as the size distribution of avalanches or the mean distance between nodes in the network. In the 2D case, energy release follows a power law even when the grid is fully rewired, while the Gini coefficient, unlike the 1D case, decreases at a steady rate, with a smoother transition. The effect of network size N is studied, finding that there is a transition for the Gini coefficient at the thermodynamic limit N \to \infty for both the 1D and 2D cases, transition which is also observed in the betweenness centrality, but not in other topological measures. Finally, the dependence of the results with the load per rewiring iteration, and the avalanche threshold is studied.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes using Shapiro steps in an excitonic Josephson junction as a direct method to verify superfluidity in electron-hole bilayers. By analyzing double-bilayer graphene and TMDs, the authors predict clear voltage plateaus that signal macroscopic phase coherence. This approach allows for mapping out the BCS-BEC crossover physics in these neutral quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work bridges concepts from superconductivity (Josephson junctions) into the realm of excitonic quantum materials, providing a concrete, measurable diagnostic tool for exotic many-body phases like exciton superfluids.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is obtaining direct, unambiguous evidence for zero-magnetic-field exciton superfluidity in electrically neutral electron-hole bilayers.

**Main result.** The authors propose using Shapiro steps in a Josephson junction formed by an excitonic Dayem bridge to directly probe phase coherence. They show this signature can be observed across the full BCS-BEC crossover regime in double-bilayer graphene (DBG).

**Method.** The theoretical framework models the system as a modified Josephson junction, deriving current-phase relations and predicting observable Shapiro plateaus from combined DC+AC driving currents.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on exciton bilayers, specifically double-bilayer graphene (DBG) and transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). The physics is analyzed using Josephson junction dynamics adapted for neutral excitons in a Dayem bridge geometry.

**Key observables.** Resolvable Shapiro plateaus in the I-V characteristics; nonmonotonic evolution of the first step width as density is tuned across the BCS-BEC crossover.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Particle density ($n$), interlayer distance ($d$), interparticle spacing ($r_0$), and the ratio governing the single-valued current-phase relation ($\xi_h \gtrsim L/3.5$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The junction is modeled in the overdamped limit, neglecting capacitance; geometric amplification ($\alpha = W/w \gg 1$) is assumed.

**Figures summary.** Figure 2 shows the critical Josephson current ($I_{JJ}^c$) dependence on interparticle spacing for DBG. Figure 3 illustrates $I$-$V$ characteristics showing Shapiro steps, and Figure 4 demonstrates step visibility via density tuning.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the physical problem (probing neutral superfluidity) and proposes the Josephson junction diagnostic. It then develops the theoretical model using coupled equations for current balance and voltage dynamics. Finally, it presents results comparing DBG and TMDs, highlighting how Shapiro steps confirm superfluidity signatures across density regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Obtaining definitive evidence for zero-magnetic-field exciton superfluidity in electron-hole bilayers remains a longstanding challenge because the condensate is electrically neutral and its phase coherence is difficult to probe directly. We propose a direct test based on Shapiro steps in a Dayem-bridge excitonic Josephson junction. We predict clearly resolvable Shapiro plateaus in experimentally accessible current and voltage regimes for double-bilayer graphene and, in the low-density regime, double-layer transition-metal dichalcogenides. Moreover, by tuning the density across the BCS-BEC crossover we show that the Shapiro response acquires a distinct nonmonotonic evolution. This is determined by the nonmonotonic behavior of the healing length in the crossover from bosonic to fermionic excitations. Observation of these signatures would provide direct evidence of exciton superfluidity and establish exciton bilayers as a platform for neutral Josephson devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work theoretically establishes that the intrinsic quantum geometry of flat-band lattices can drive an excitonic insulator phase. By analyzing fluctuations using a Ginzburg-Landau framework, the authors predict a novel Finite-Momentum Superfluid Density Fluctuation (FMSDF) state under strong interactions. This suggests that geometric constraints dictate dynamic collective electronic behavior in materials like COFs.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete theoretical link between geometric properties (quantum metric) of electronic bands and emergent macroscopic quantum phases (excitonic insulators/superfluids), which is highly relevant for understanding correlated materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to theoretically demonstrate a purely quantum-geometry-driven excitonic insulator (EI) phase and analyze its associated superfluid fluctuations in flat-band systems.

**Main result.** Strong interactions induce a negative effective kinetic coefficient for the amplitude mode, causing softest fluctuations to shift to finite momentum, leading to a Finite-Momentum Superfluid Density Fluctuation (FMSDF) state.

**Method.** The analysis employs mean-field theory on an effective Ginzburg-Landau free energy derived from path integrals and Hubbard-Stratonovich transformations.

**Model / system.** The system models excitons confined to lattice-geometry-induced flat bands (e.g., kagome, Lieb lattices) in a tight-binding model subjected to an out-of-plane Zeeman field.

**Key observables.** Coherence length ($\xi_c$), critical temperatures ($T_{	ext{MF}}$, $T_{	ext{BKT}}$), and the periodic modulation of in-plane magnetization fluctuations (FMSDF).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Dimensionless interaction strength ($2\delta E/gc$), quantum metric components, and Zeeman splitting ($\delta E$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system is assumed to be in the low-energy flat-band subspace, and SOC is negligible compared to the Zeeman field.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate electronic structure with Zeeman splitting and exciton-induced magnetic response; Figure 2 compares $T_{	ext{MF}}$, $T_{	ext{FMSDF}}$, and $T_{	ext{BKT}}$ versus interaction strength.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically derives the effective action for the order parameter using auxiliary fields, analyzes fluctuations by diagonalizing the resulting quadratic action into amplitude and phase modes, and finally connects these fluctuations to observable magnetic responses.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum geometry is instrumental in stabilizing exotic phenomena in systems ranging from topological insulators to superconductors. In dispersionless flat bands, where the kinetic energy is quenched, the quantum metric emerges as the fundamental driver of macroscopic collective phenomena. Here, we theoretically demonstrate that lattice-geometry-induced flat bands, such as those in kagome and Lieb lattices, provide a fertile platform for realizing a purely quantum-geometry-driven excitonic insulator (EI) phase. By applying an out-of-plane Zeeman field to lift spin degeneracy without spin-orbit coupling, we establish a Ginzburg-Landau framework in which the electron-hole wavefunction-overlap directly maps the flat-band quantum metric onto the macroscopic free energy. This mapping plays a key role in both the EI and the associated superfluid phases, with the coherence length and phase stiffness emerging directly from the quantum metric. Our analysis reveals that under strong interactions, the quantum metric induces a negative effective kinetic coefficient for the amplitude mode. Rather than destabilizing the uniform condensate, this softens the amplitude fluctuations at a finite momentum, giving rise to a finite-momentum superfluid density fluctuation (FMSDF) state. This state is observable as a periodically modulated magnitude of in-plane magnetization fluctuations. Our findings establish a rigorous link between flat-band quantum geometry and dynamic collective excitonic states, with promising pathways for realization in covalent-organic frameworks (COFs).

</details>
