**Summary.** This theoretical paper connects the geometry of quantum measurements (SIC-POVM overlaps) to advanced number theory via Stark units. It argues that these overlap phases must be expressible as specific products of square roots of Stark units derived from ray class fields. This establishes a deep, unexpected link between quantum information and algebraic number theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a profound mathematical underpinning for quantum information concepts, suggesting that fundamental physical constraints (like those imposed by SICs) are dictated by deep arithmetic laws governing algebraic units.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the deep mathematical relationship between the overlap units of Symmetric Informationally Complete (SIC) measurements in quantum systems and algebraic units derived from number theory, specifically Stark units.

**Main result.** It conjectures that these overlap units are always products of integral powers of square roots of Stark units originating from specific ray class fields attached to the base field's maximal ring of integers.

**Method.** The analysis combines advanced algebraic number theory (ray class fields, Stark units) with quantum information theory concepts (SIC-POVMs and the Weyl–Heisenberg group structure).

**Model / system.** The physical system is defined by SIC-POVMs in a Hilbert space $\mathbb{C}^d$, whose overlaps are analyzed using tools from algebraic number theory, including ray class fields $K_{d;f}\mathbb{L}$.

**Key observables.** Overlap units ($\theta_{j,k}$), Stark units (algebraic units derived from zeta functions), and the dimension $d$ of the Hilbert space.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension $d$, which is related to fundamental discriminants $\Delta_0$; various moduli defining ray class fields ($f|f_0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The work relies heavily on conjectures regarding Stark units and the structure of Galois groups relating these number-theoretic objects to quantum overlaps.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate field inclusion diagrams, lattice structures for divisors related to moduli $d$, and geometric representations (like 'flower' structures) of subgroups within the Weyl–Heisenberg group.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the connection between SICs and algebraic units. It then uses Galois theory and class field theory to constrain the possible structure of these overlaps, culminating in detailed number-theoretic proofs that link the overlap values precisely to Stark unit structures.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

It has been observed that the mutual scalar products of the vectors in a SIC-POVM are given by algebraic units, and at least in some cases by square roots of Stark units. The full picture is somewhat more complicated, especially if non-minimal SIC-POVMs are considered. We present a mixture of exact and numerical evidence suggesting that the overlap units are always products of integral powers of square roots of Stark units from ray class fields all of which are attached to the maximal ring of integers in the base field. In the non-minimal case a lattice of such ray class fields is involved. In every second dimension (counted in a certain way) some of the overlap units equal $\pm 1$, and we show that this follows from a special property of the ray class fields. Our observations are complementary to but consistent with the claim that the overlap units can be calculated directly from the Shintani--Faddeev modular cocycle.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a novel technique using helical neutron wavefronts to resolve a long-standing ambiguity in neutron scattering: distinguishing the single-particle spatial extent from the transverse coherence length. By analyzing annular intensity profiles, the authors experimentally proved that these two quantities are distinct, measuring a wavepacket size an order of magnitude larger than the beam's coherence length.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful new diagnostic tool in neutron scattering, allowing researchers to disentangle fundamental quantum mechanical properties (single-particle wave function) from statistical ensemble properties (coherence), which is crucial for interpreting complex measurements in condensed matter and quantum physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is experimentally separating the transverse coherence length (related to ensemble correlations) from the intrinsic spatial extent of a single neutron wavepacket, as both cause apparent intensity broadening.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated this separation using helical neutron wavefronts, finding that the single-particle wavepacket extent ($\ge 2 \mu	ext{m}$) is significantly larger than the measured transverse coherence length ($\approx 180 	ext{ nm}$).

**Method.** They utilized the unique intensity profiles generated by helical states (carrying Orbital Angular Momentum) to isolate measurements sensitive only to single-particle properties versus those sensitive to ensemble averaging.

**Model / system.** The experiment uses neutron beams, specifically generating and analyzing helical wavefronts. The theoretical framework involves modeling the beam as an incoherent ensemble of neutrons, each described by a single wavepacket $\psi_0(\vec{r})$.

**Key observables.** Peak radius ($r_{	ext{peak}}$) of annular intensity profiles from helical beams; measured beam divergence ($	heta$); and the resulting coherence length ($\zeta$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Transverse Coherence Length ($\zeta \approx 180 	ext{ nm}$); Single-Particle Wavepacket Extent ($w \ge 2 \mu	ext{m}$); Beam Divergence ($	heta \approx 1.1 	ext{ mrad}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the ability to model and measure intensity profiles using helical states, which allows for a distinct mathematical separation of coherence effects from wavepacket size.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate diffraction patterns for different OAM modes ($\ell$), showing how $r_{	ext{peak}}$ relates to both varying wavepacket extent ($w$) and varying beam divergence ($	heta$).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical ambiguity between coherence length and wavepacket size. It then details the methodology using helical wavefronts, presenting calculations for intensity and coherence functions. Finally, it presents experimental results confirming the separation of these two distinct physical quantities.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Distinguishing transverse coherence length from single-particle wavepacket extent is fundamentally challenging, as both manifest through spatial broadening of observed intensity profiles in conventional experiments. Here we introduce a method based on helical neutron wavefronts that enables this separation. Helical neutron states produce annular intensity profiles whose peak radius depends on the transverse wavepacket extent, while coherence length only contributes to profile broadening. In our experimental geometry we measure a beam divergence of ~1.1 mrad, corresponding to a transverse coherence length of ~180 nm. In contrast, the same measurement places a lower bound of >= 2 um on the spatial extent of the individual neutron wavepackets, more than an order of magnitude larger than the coherence length. These results provide direct experimental evidence that transverse coherence length and single-particle wavepacket extent are distinct physical quantities, resolving a longstanding source of confusion in the neutron literature.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces FlashVAN, a novel, physics-inspired transformer designed for efficiently simulating frustrated spin glass systems. It addresses the computational bottlenecks of traditional methods by integrating sparse attention and hardware acceleration (FlashAttention). The resulting framework accurately calculates thermodynamic properties like free energy and overlap distributions across various temperatures for models like SK and EA.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the development of highly efficient, structure-aware neural network samplers (FlashVAN) represents a significant methodological advance in applying deep learning tools to complex many-body physics problems that often require sampling or expectation value calculations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is developing scalable, efficient methods to sample the Boltzmann distribution for frustrated spin glasses, overcoming limitations in previous machine learning approaches.

**Main result.** The proposed FlashVAN framework achieves up to two orders of magnitude speedup over vanilla variational autoregressive networks, enabling simulations on unprecedentedly large systems while accurately resolving key thermodynamic properties.

**Method.** It employs a physics-inspired transformer architecture featuring sparse attention and tailored positional embeddings, optimized with FlashAttention kernels for hardware efficiency during autoregressive sampling.

**Model / system.** The system studied is the spin glass, modeled by Hamiltonians such as the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model and the Edwards-Anderson (EA) model on 2D or 3D lattices. The state space involves binary spins $\sigma \in \{\pm 1\}^N$.

**Key observables.** Free energy ($F$), ground-state energy ($\langle e_0 angle$), overlap statistics ($p(q)$), and the Boltzmann distribution $p(\sigma)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$) or inverse temperature ($eta$), system size ($N$ or lattice dimensions $L$), and sparsity window size ($W$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes that the physics-inspired attention mechanism can effectively encode the local interaction topology of the spin system, and it relies on variational inference to approximate the true distribution.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the architecture, optimization workflow (minimizing KL-divergence), convergence of free energy/ground-state energy under temperature annealing, and computational speedup comparisons against prior art.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces FlashVAN by addressing scaling issues in variational methods. It details the physics-inspired attention and positional embeddings, presents results on SK and EA models showing superior performance across various temperatures and system sizes, and concludes with complexity analysis comparing it to naive transformer approaches.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Efficient sampling of the Boltzmann distribution in frustrated spin glasses is central to statistical mechanics and combinatorial optimization. Despite advances in machine-learning-based approaches, two issues persist: limited understanding of why variational models fail to benefit from increased scale, unlike the monotonic scaling law of large language models; and high computational cost on large systems that negates advantages over classical sampling methods. Here, we develop a physics-inspired transformer with interpretable sparse attention and spin-tailored positional embeddings to address these challenges. By further leveraging FlashAttention for parallel ancestral sampling, it achieves up to two orders of magnitude speedup over vanilla variational autoregressive networks, enabling neural-network simulations of spin-glass systems to unprecedented sizes on a single GPU. It can resolve full probability distributions, free energies, and overlap statistics across temperatures, for Sherrington-Kirkpatrick and 2D or 3D Edwards-Anderson models, where existing machine-learning methods encounter limitations at certain temperatures. This framework thus establishes a scalable paradigm for frustrated spin-glass systems.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents an efficient Bell State Measurement protocol tailored for Rotation-symmetric cat (RS-cat) bosonic codes. By using only simple linear optics and photon number detectors, the method extracts both phase and photon-number modulo information. The results demonstrate that this measurement is highly robust, achieving near-deterministic success even when accounting for realistic photon loss mechanisms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses a key primitive (BSM) for advanced quantum computation architectures (bosonic codes), providing concrete, resource-efficient measurement protocols applicable to continuous-variable quantum information processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is developing an efficient Bell state measurement (BSM) protocol for Rotation-symmetric cat (RS-cat) codes, which is crucial for long-distance quantum communication and Fusion-based Quantum Computation (FBQC).

**Main result.** Under ideal conditions, the proposed BSM protocol becomes deterministic for arbitrary symmetry order N with sufficiently large amplitudes. Furthermore, post-selection can enhance the success probability even in the presence of photon loss.

**Method.** The protocol utilizes only a Half Beam Splitter (HBS) and Photon-Number-Resolving Detectors (PNRDs), exploiting the characteristic photon-number structure induced by the code's rotational symmetry to extract both modulo and phase information for discrimination.

**Model / system.** The system involves RS-cat codes, which are bosonic quantum error-correcting codes characterized by a discrete rotational symmetry of order N. These codes are built from finite-energy superpositions of coherent states in phase space.

**Key observables.** Detected photon-number patterns $(n_c, n_d)$, the normalized difference $X = (n_c - n_d) / (n_c + n_d)$, and the success probability under loss.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Symmetry order N, amplitude $\alpha$, photon loss rate $\eta$, and post-selection threshold $\tau$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes ideal loss-free conditions for determinism proofs, but also numerically evaluates performance under finite photon loss ($\eta=10^{-3}, 10^{-2}$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the success probability vs. $\alpha$ (lossless case), failure rate vs. $\eta$ showing improvement with $N$, and histograms of the discriminant $X$ demonstrating distinguishability and regions rejected by post-selection.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces RS-cat codes, details the HBS/PNRD BSM protocol using symmetry properties to extract phase information via $X$, proves determinism in the loss-free limit, and concludes with numerical evaluations showing robustness against photon loss and benefits from post-selection.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Rotation-symmetric cat (RS-cat) codes are a bosonic-code platform for quantum information processing, combining finite-energy realizability with robustness against photon loss through their discrete rotational symmetry. For applications in long-distance quantum communication and fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC), efficient Bell state measurement (BSM) is a key primitive. In this work, we consider a BSM protocol for RS-cat codes using only a half beam splitter (HBS) and photon-number-resolving detectors (PNRDs). By exploiting the characteristic photon-number structure induced by the discrete rotational symmetry of RS-cat codes, our protocol extracts both photon-number modulo and phase information for Bell-state discrimination. We show that, under ideal loss-free conditions, the proposed BSM protocol becomes deterministic for arbitrary symmetry order $N$ for sufficiently large amplitudes $α$. We further numerically evaluate the success probability under photon loss and identify the loss regime in which higher-order RS-cat codes provide an advantage. Finally, we show that post-selection can enhance the success probability.

</details>

**Summary.** This study uses combined structural and spectroscopic techniques on LaCrSb3 to investigate its unconventional magnetism. The key finding is that the FMR spectrum requires a model incorporating two interacting magnetic sublattices (FM and AFM). This strongly supports a complex spin structure in this layered ferromagnet, moving beyond simple single-sublattice descriptions.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a concrete example of how advanced spectroscopy (FMR) can reveal underlying complex magnetic order (coexisting FM/AFM sublattices) in correlated materials, linking macroscopic measurements to microscopic Hamiltonian parameters.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the unconventional magnetism and magnetic excitations within the layered metallic ferromagnet LaCrSb3, aiming to understand its complex spin structure beyond simple ferromagnetic models.

**Main result.** FMR spectroscopy strongly suggests the presence of at least two interacting magnetic sublattices (one FM and one AFM) below a characteristic temperature T*, which is quantitatively explained by a phenomenological model.

**Method.** The research combines multiple experimental techniques, including X-ray diffraction, static magnetization measurements, and high-frequency/electron spin resonance (FMR/ESR) spectroscopy. Theoretical analysis involves fitting the data to a phenomenological Hamiltonian using Linear Spin Wave Theory (LSWT).

**Model / system.** The system is LaCrSb3, a layered metallic ferromagnet exhibiting strong magneto-elastic coupling and complex magnetic transitions ($T_C \simeq 126$ K, $T^* \sim 95$ K). The theoretical model treats the magnetism as arising from interacting orthogonal ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic sublattices.

**Key observables.** Temperature dependence of lattice parameters ($\alpha_V$), magnetization M(T), and the observation of two distinct, non-degenerate FMR resonance branches below T*.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Ferromagnetic transition temperature $T_C \simeq 126$ K; Spin reorientation temperature $T^*$; Exchange coupling parameters ($J_{1b}, J_{2c}$, etc.) fitted to the model.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the observed two-branch FMR spectrum necessitates a minimum of two interacting magnetic sublattices (FM and AFM). The model itself is phenomenological.

**Figures summary.** Figures show XRD patterns confirming structural stability but magnetoelastic coupling; temperature dependence plots illustrate anomalies near $T_C$; and critical figures display the field/frequency evolution of FMR spectra, revealing multiple resonance branches at low temperatures.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically presents evidence from structure (XRD) and bulk magnetism ($M(T)$), followed by detailed spectroscopic analysis (ESR/FMR). The core argument builds towards proposing and validating a two-sublattice model using LSWT to explain the observed multi-branch excitation spectrum.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

LaCrSb$_{3}$ is a metallic ferromagnet with a layered crystal structure demonstrating intriguing electronic and magnetic properties, such as large anomalous Hall effect, strong canting of the spin lattice, and a peculiar spin-reorientation transition. Here, we report the results of the temperature-dependent x-ray diffraction, static magnetization, and in particular electron spin resonance (ESR) and ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) experiments carried out over a wide range of frequencies, magnetic fields, and temperatures. Though x-ray data reveals no structural transition down to 15 K, a strong magneto-elastic coupling is detected across the ferromagnetic transition at $T_{\rm C} \simeq 126$ K. ESR results indicate a presence of the quasi-static short-range correlations extending far above $T_{\rm C}$, which is a typical fingerprint of the low-dimensional magnetism. The frequency-field diagram of the FMR modes mapped below $T_{\rm C}$ strongly suggests presence of two magnetic sublattices in LaCrSb$_{3}$. A quantitative understanding of the FMR excitations was achieved within a phenomenological model of interacting orthogonal ferro- and antiferromagnetic sublattices which was earlier proposed to explain unusually strong spin canting observed by neutron diffraction [E.~Granado et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 89, 107204 (2002)]. The FMR results corroborate this scenario and call for the development of the underlying microscopic model of unconventional magnetism in LaCrSb$_{3}$.

</details>

By combining these experiments with DFT calculations, the authors demonstrate that spin-split bands only appear when both noncollinear magnetic order and strong Spin-Orbit Coupling coexist. This establishes a fundamental mechanism for generating unconventional magnetism in itinerant electron systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed interplay between crystal symmetry, magnetic ordering, relativistic effects (SOC), and electronic band structure, which are core concepts in modern condensed matter theory relevant to topological materials and magnetism.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC) is the essential symmetry-breaking mechanism required to induce spin-split Fermi surfaces in compensated antiferromagnets, moving beyond systems where splitting occurs nonrelativistically.

**Main result.** SmBi realizes a cooperative, relativistic route to spin-split Fermi surfaces, requiring both noncollinear magnetic order and SOC; this reconstruction is observed across two successive AFM transitions but not in the control material SmSb.

**Method.** The research combines ultrahigh-sensitivity ac magnetostriction measurements (detecting quantum oscillations), detailed magnetic symmetry analysis, and first-principles DFT calculations including SOC.

**Model / system.** The physical system is Samarium Bismuth (SmBi), which undergoes two sequential antiferromagnetic transitions ($	ext{PM} 	o 	ext{AFM-I} 	o 	ext{AFM-II}$). Theoretical analysis maps candidate noncollinear magnetic structures to specific symmetry groups.

**Key observables.** Quantum oscillation frequencies ($\alpha, eta, \delta, \epsilon$, etc.), temperature dependence of magnetostriction coefficients ($\lambda'/	ext{dH}$), and the emergence/splitting of Fermi surface branches.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperatures near $T_N \approx 9	ext{ K}$ and $T^* \approx 7	ext{ K}$; magnetic fields up to $\sim 100	ext{ T}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the observed QO features are bulk electronic properties, not surface states; DFT calculations require careful alignment of the Fermi level due to $4f$ electron treatment.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate crystal structures and proposed magnetic orders (Type-I/III); $\lambda'/	ext{dH}$ vs. T show distinct changes across transitions; FFT contour plots map the temperature evolution and splitting of QO branches ($\alpha'$ into $\mu$ and $
u$).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes experimental quantum oscillation data across two magnetic transitions, correlates these findings with theoretical predictions based on symmetry analysis (MSG/MPG), and uses DFT calculations to confirm that SOC is necessary for the observed spin splitting in noncollinear phases.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Spin-split electronic structures in compensated antiferromagnets are commonly sought in the nonrelativistic limit, where magnetic order lifts spin degeneracy without spin-orbit coupling (SOC). Whether SOC can instead be the indispensable symmetry-breaking ingredient remains largely unexplored. Here we combine quantum oscillations detected by ultrahigh-sensitivity ac magnetostriction, magnetic-symmetry analysis and first-principles calculations to resolve the bulk Fermi-surface evolution of SmBi across two successive antiferromagnetic (AFM) transitions. New oscillation branches emerge below TN and undergo a further reconstruction below T*, whereas isostructural SmSb shows no comparable change. For the candidate noncollinear orders of SmBi, breaking global parity-time symmetry is insufficient in the nonrelativistic limit because residual spin-space symmetries protect twofold band degeneracy; conversely, SOC alone cannot lift the degeneracy of the centrosymmetric paramagnetic (PM) phase. Only the coexistence of noncollinear order and SOC locks spin to the lattice and removes the residual protection. SmBi therefore realizes a cooperative, relativistic route to spin-split Fermi surfaces, broadening unconventional magnetism beyond systems whose splitting is already present in the nonrelativistic limit.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper examines the Principle of Common Cause (PCC) applied to joint probabilities measured on two identical quantum particles. It finds that due to the required permutation symmetry of observables, a single common cause variable is either non-existent or trivial. This suggests that explaining all observed correlations requires assuming effective distinguishability between the particles.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly tackles fundamental issues at the intersection of quantum foundations and causality (PCC), which is crucial for understanding how local hidden variables might manifest in multi-particle quantum systems, even when measurements are commutative.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether joint probabilities measured on two identical quantum particles can be explained by a single common cause, contrasting this with non-identical particles and addressing the constraints imposed by quantum mechanics.

**Main result.** The analysis concludes that either symmetric common causes do not necessarily exist (suggesting hidden distinguishability), or any existing symmetric screening variables are trivial, meaning no single common cause can explain all measured correlations.

**Method.** It applies the Probabilistic Common Cause (PCC) framework to joint probabilities derived from measurements on identical particles, comparing results obtained by assuming particle labels versus using label-free event descriptions.

**Model / system.** The system involves two identical quantum particles whose observables must be permutation-symmetric. The analysis uses projectors related to spatial and internal spin degrees of freedom within a tensor-product Hilbert space.

**Key observables.** Joint probabilities $p(A, B)$ derived from measurements; screening variables $C$ used in the common cause factorization.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The requirement for permutation symmetry on observables and the structure of the joint probability distributions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is testing the applicability of the PCC framework to quantum correlations, particularly when restricted by particle indistinguishability (permutation symmetry).

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the provided notes.

**Paper structure.** The paper moves from discussing non-identical particles and Bell violations to focusing on identical particles. It compares labeled vs. event-based common cause approaches, ultimately concluding that the constraints imposed by quantum indistinguishability severely limit or eliminate the possibility of a single common cause variable.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Violations of Bell's inequalities imply that joint probabilities generated by non-commutative measurements on two (non-identical) quantum particles do not have a single common cause. But joint probabilities generated for such non-identical particles via commutative measurements do have non-trivial common cause variables. We focus on commutative measurements and consider two identical quantum particles, whose density matrices and observables (hermitian operators) are necessarily permutation-symmetric. It is natural to demand that the common cause describing joint probabilities is also permutation symmetric, i.e., it acts symmetrically on both particles. Looking at various ways of defining joint probabilities from the same measurement data, we conclude that either symmetric common causes need not exist (i.e., that the particles can be hiddenly distinguishable), or that symmetric screening variables exist, but they are trivial, i.e., no single common cause can explain all single-measurement correlations.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces the concept of the 'quantum metric bound state,' establishing that when perfect localization fails due to disorder, the spatial decay rate of confined waves is universally limited by the bulk quantum metric. By deriving this rigorous lower bound using advanced spectral methods, it provides a powerful, predictive design principle for engineering wave confinement in synthetic platforms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work connects fundamental concepts from algebraic geometry (quantum metrics) directly to measurable physical properties like mode decay length in engineered photonic or electronic systems, providing a powerful new diagnostic tool for wave engineering.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To establish a universal, model-independent geometric lower bound for the spatial decay length of defect-induced bound states in flat-band lattices when perfect localization conditions are broken by generic impurities.

**Main result.** The exponential decay length ($\xi_b$) is rigorously proven to be lower-bounded by the bulk quantum metric ($\ell_{QM}$), establishing $\xi_b \gtrsim C \cdot \ell_{QM}$.

**Method.** The analysis uses Green's function formalism, complex momentum continuation (pole structure analysis), and Bernstein-type inequalities applied to band projection operators.

**Model / system.** The study models light confinement in photonic lattices, using the Lieb lattice as a primary example. The physics is governed by a tight-binding Hamiltonian analyzed via Schrödinger-like equations with local impurities breaking perfect symmetry.

**Key observables.** Confinement Length Scales ($\xi_b$), Quantum Metric Length ($\ell_{QM}$), and the decay rate derived from pole singularities in the complex momentum plane.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The bound depends on the algebraic degree $N$ of the projection operator, leading to a scaling $\xi_b \gtrsim 4/N^2 \cdot \ell_{QM}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Assumes weak-guidance conditions and that the flat band projection operator belongs to a rational trigonometric space for the rigorous bounding techniques.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare decay lengths in three regimes (dispersive, CLS, Quantum Metric Bound State) and show simulations confirming the geometric floor set by $\ell_{QM}$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the problem of confinement breakdown to deriving a mathematical lower bound using advanced spectral theory (Bernstein-type inequalities), culminating in demonstrating that this metric provides a universal, predictive design principle.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The spatial confinement of defect-induced bound states is conventionally governed by the effective mass in dispersive bands. More recently, Compact Localized States (CLSs) arising from exact destructive interference have been utilized to achieve confinement in flat bands. However, CLSs rely on pristine lattice symmetries and fine-tuned defect profiles. The introduction of a generic local impurity inevitably breaks these strict phase-matching conditions, resulting in extensive bound states whose fundamental length scale has remained an open question. Here, we establish a third regime of confinement: the quantum metric bound state. We provide a rigorous mathematical proof demonstrating that in the absence of kinetic energy and CLS protection, the exponential decay length of these states is lower-bounded by the quantum metric of the unperturbed flat band. We demonstrate the tightness of this geometric limit by constructing a family of highly tunable flat-band generators, and we verify its universality across diverse realistic architectures. Ultimately, this classification establishes the independently measurable quantum metric as a predictive design principle for engineering confined modes in synthetic wave platforms.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes a refined model for particle dispersal by combining subdiffusive fractional Brownian motion with stopping times whose rates are drawn from a Gamma distribution. This heterogeneity successfully generates the heavy-tailed power-law decay necessary to describe rare, long-distance events while retaining the localized clumping characteristic of the underlying subdiffusion process.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on physical dispersal, the mathematical techniques used—analyzing heavy tails arising from multiplicative noise or randomized rates in anomalous diffusion processes—are highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics problems involving complex particle interactions or energy dissipation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a model for dispersal kernels that accurately describe both localized clumping and rare, long-distance dispersal events by generating heavy tails.

**Main result.** By introducing heterogeneity in the stopping rate (making it Gamma-distributed), the resulting radial density function exhibits a power-law decay $g(r) \sim r^{-1 - a/H}$, confirming a heavy-tailed distribution.

**Method.** The analysis involves deriving and performing asymptotic analysis on the radial probability density function by combining subdiffusive fractional Brownian motion (fBm) with randomized exponential stopping times.

**Model / system.** The system models particle dispersal using subdiffusive fBm ($H < 1/2$) where the stopping time rate ($\lambda$) is drawn from a Gamma distribution. This combination generates the required heavy-tailed statistics for realistic environmental modeling.

**Key observables.** Radial probability density function $g(r)$ and its tail behavior, specifically the power-law decay $r^{-1 - a/H}$ as $r 	o \infty$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Hurst exponent ($H$), Gamma distribution parameters ($a, b$), and the diffusion parameter ($\sigma$). The regime of interest is subdiffusion ($0 < H < 1/2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on approximations valid in the large-$r$ limit (e.g., $t \gg b$) and assumes that the underlying movement follows fBm.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare simulation results for randomized vs. constant stopping rates, showing clear heavy tails only when rate randomization is included. Hill plots and Mean-excess plots are used to diagnose this tail behavior.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the failure of simple models (exponential decay) for long-distance dispersal, proposes randomizing the stopping rate parameter ($\lambda \sim 	ext{Gamma}$), derives the asymptotic power-law tail $g(r) \sim r^{-1 - a/H}$, and validates this result through both analytical methods and numerical simulations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Subdiffusive fractional Brownian motions produce localized aggregation when particles are stopped at exponentially distributed times. In applications where clumping and long-distance dispersal events are observed simultaneously, such as in some instances of seed dispersal, this model fails to describe the tails of the data. The resulting redistribution kernel has only an exponentially decaying tail, whereas a heavier tail is needed for modeling the long-distance dispersal observed. Here we propose a model in which subdiffusive particles stop at exponentially distributed times, but with a rate parameter that is Gamma distributed. This heterogeneity in stopping rates causes the density of final radial positions to have a heavy-tailed distribution. Our model retains the strong localized clumping characteristic of subdiffusive fractional Brownian motion while simultaneously generating the heavy tails required for realistic long-distance dispersal.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes stochastic Turing patterns in reaction-diffusion systems, showing that integrating fluctuations over time reveals a hidden large-scale order. This emergent structure exhibits effective hyperuniformity, meaning long-wavelength density variations are suppressed by a finite kinetic floor. The methodology uses advanced statistical tools like the structure factor analysis within the Linear Noise Approximation.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the concept of emergent organization via filtering (time integration) is analogous to how quantum correlations or entanglement can be revealed by time evolution measurements in open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how robust, large-scale spatial organization emerges from stochastic Turing patterns when considering time integration of fluctuating local populations.

**Main result.** Time integration acts as a dynamical filter that reveals an emergent effective hyperuniformity in the density fluctuations, characterized by a $1/R$ decay in variance over intermediate scales.

**Method.** The analysis uses the Linear Noise Approximation (LNA) applied to stochastic reaction-diffusion equations and analyzes the time-integrated structure factor in Fourier space.

**Model / system.** The model is a generic two-species stochastic reaction-diffusion process, exemplified by the Levin-Segel predator-prey system, evolving on a lattice with periodic boundary conditions.

**Key observables.** Time-integrated demographic fluctuations ($\Xi(X)_r(T)$), structure factor $S(X)_q(T)$, and intensive variance $	ext{var}(X)(R; T)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The ratio of diffusion rates ($
u/\mu$) relative to the deterministic instability point, and the integration time $T$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the Linear Noise Approximation (LNA) and assumes that the system reaches a steady state for the structure factor in the long-time limit ($T 	o \infty$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the emergence of patterns in time-integrated vs. instantaneous snapshots, showing variance decay as $1/\ell$ over increasingly broad regions near instability.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the mathematical framework using LNA for stochastic fluctuations, derives the structure factor for time-integrated configurations, and then applies this to the Levin-Segel model to demonstrate the transition from instantaneous noise to long-range hyperuniform order.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Demographic noise generates stochastic Turing patterns even when reaction-diffusion systems are deterministically stable. We show analytically and verify numerically in the Levin-Segel model that temporal integration of configurations reveals emergent large-scale organization. The intensive number variance in a window of size $R \gg 1$ approaches a finite reaction-kinetic floor as $1/R$, over a spatial range growing by orders of magnitude near the Turing instability. This yields an effectively hyperuniform, fine-tuning-free regime previously unidentified in non-conserved multispecies stochastic systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper determines the precise small-drift scaling law for the rate at which random walks set new records. By utilizing Mellin transforms on a harmonic sum identity, the authors show that this record rate's exponent is continuously controlled by the skewness of the step distribution via the positivity parameter $ho$. This unifies results across Gaussian, heavy-tailed, and skewed random walk regimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly quantum mechanical, the rigorous mathematical framework connecting asymptotic scaling laws (like record rates) to underlying distributional symmetries ($\alpha, eta$) is highly relevant for understanding critical phenomena or non-equilibrium dynamics in complex quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how the rate at which a random walk or Lévy flight sets new records (the record rate, $\lambda(\mu)$) depends on small positive drift ($\mu$). It specifically analyzes this dependence as the drift approaches zero.

**Main result.** The record rate exhibits an asymptotic power-law scaling $\lambda(\mu) \sim K\mu^{(1-ho)/
u}$, where the exponent is continuously tuned by the skewness of the underlying step distribution through the positivity parameter $ho$.

**Method.** The analysis heavily relies on using Mellin transforms applied to the harmonic sum derived from the Spitzer–Baxter identity, allowing for a unified treatment across different types of random walks.

**Model / system.** The model is a general random walk $S_n$ with i.i.d. steps $\xi_i$, which can be characterized by their limiting stable law index ($\alpha$) and skewness ($eta$). The analysis covers both diffusive (Gaussian) and heavy-tailed Lévy flight regimes.

**Key observables.** The record rate $\lambda(\mu)$, the expected maximum $E(M_N)$, and the exponent governing the small-$\mu$ decay of these quantities.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Drift ($\mu$), stable law index ($\alpha \in (1, 2]$), positivity parameter ($ho = P(Y>0)$), and skewness ($eta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results are exact for Gaussian and strictly stable steps but extend to the domains of attraction at the leading power level. The analysis assumes the applicability of Mellin transform techniques to factorize the relevant harmonic sums.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates record setting in a biased random walk as $\mu 	o 0$. Figure 2 shows the poles of the Mellin transform, distinguishing the leading law from correction terms. Figure 3 and 4 map the exponent's dependence on skewness ($eta$) across different stable indices ($\alpha$).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the connection between the record rate and a harmonic sum via the Spitzer–Baxter identity. It then employs Mellin transforms to analyze this sum in the small-drift limit, deriving the leading power law dependence on $\mu$ and showing how skewness controls the exponent through $ho$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A random walk with small positive drift $μ$ sets new records at a rate $λ(μ)$ that vanishes as $μ\to 0$. For centered steps attracted to a stable law $Y$ with index $1 < α\leq 2$ and positivity parameter $ρ= P(Y>0)$, we find $λ(μ) \sim Kμ^{(1-ρ)/ν}$, $ν=1-1/α$, as $μ\to 0$. The result is exact for Gaussian and strictly stable steps, and extends at the leading-power level to their domains of attraction. The exponent is set by the asymmetry only through $ρ$, sweeping the interval $[1,\,1/(α-1)]$ as the skewness varies. It recovers the Gaussian linear law with slope $\sqrt{2}$ and, for symmetric heavy tails, the power $μ^{α/2(α-1)}$; beyond the stable tail ratio, distributional details enter through the prefactor $K$, which is explicit for strictly stable steps. The result follows directly from one Mellin transform of the harmonic sum in the Spitzer-Baxter identity, which factorizes into a kernel transform and a Riemann $ζ$ factor whose poles deliver at once the leading law, its prefactor, and a correction ladder, unifying diffusive, heavy-tailed, and skewed walks. The same transform also yields the expected maximum, recovering Kingman's heavy-traffic law for queues and Siegmund's corrected-diffusion constant as adjacent poles.

</details>

**Summary.** This work evaluates Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for cyberattack detection using limited qubits. The study demonstrates that forcing high-dimensional network data into a small quantum state via amplitude encoding severely limits the model's representational capacity compared to classical neural networks. The authors conclude that future quantum advantage requires abandoning aggressive feature compression in favor of broader Hilbert space representations.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on cybersecurity, the core technical challenge—quantifying the expressibility gap between quantum circuits and classical models when data is compressed—is highly relevant to understanding resource limitations in variational quantum algorithms for complex physical simulations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the structural limits of Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for detecting network anomalies in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era.

**Main result.** Aggressive data compression via Amplitude Encoding into a small number of qubits severely restricts the VQC's expressiveness, leading to performance ceilings significantly below classical benchmarks.

**Method.** The authors developed and tested a 4-qubit VQC using amplitude encoding on the NSL-KDD dataset, comparing its performance against classical MLPs and analyzing optimization convergence.

**Model / system.** The model is a hybrid quantum-classical circuit consisting of state preparation (Amplitude Encoding), a trainable parameterized ansatz (RealAmplitudes), and Z-basis measurement. It operates on NISQ devices simulated via statevector simulators.

**Key observables.** Binary classification accuracy (88% achieved vs 97% classical MLP); in-sample diagnostic accuracy (9%); mode collapse behavior.

**Important parameters / regimes.** 4 qubits, 24 trainable parameters, 16 principal components (from PCA), COBYLA/SPSA optimizers.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary limitation is the aggressive dimensionality reduction imposed by amplitude encoding; furthermore, the results do not isolate the encoding from ansatz depth or optimizer budget.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate t-SNE projections of class overlaps and confusion matrices comparing VQC performance against classical baselines (Tiny MLP).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically details data preprocessing (PCA, Target Encoding), constructs the 4-qubit VQC pipeline, evaluates it using multiple optimizers, compares results to classical MLPs, and concludes by proposing a shift towards uncompressed angle encoding.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

This paper investigates the effectiveness and structural limits of Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for detecting network anomalies in the era of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) systems. Using the official 20\% research subset of the NSL-KDD dataset, a 4-qubit classifier featuring a 24-parameter trainable ansatz was developed, utilizing amplitude encoding to embed 16 principal components. On a held-out partition of this subset, the model achieved a consistent binary-classification accuracy of 88\%. A comparative evaluation with two fundamentally different optimizers, COBYLA and SPSA, found that the observed performance plateau is not attributable to convergence to local minima, a result we interpret as consistent with an encoding-related expressibility limit rather than an optimization artifact. An architectural parity comparison with a classical neural network (a Tiny MLP with four nodes, achieving 97\% accuracy) highlighted the expressiveness gap associated with data overcompression into restricted quantum states. The model was trained on a class-balanced set spanning the 22 raw NSL-KDD attack categories and evaluated in-sample as a probe of representational capacity: under this configuration the VQC reached only 9\% accuracy and exhibited a degenerate mode collapse onto a small subset of classes. We interpret this behavior as consistent with the loss of linear separability induced by excessive compression in the quantum probability space, while explicitly noting that our experiments do not isolate the encoding from the ansatz depth, optimizer budget, and measurement-decoding scheme (see Limitations). Motivated by these observations and by Cover's theorem, we outline an alternative paradigm: a 16-qubit VQC with angle encoding that expands the Hilbert-space representation rather than relying on aggressive classical dimensionality reduction.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proves a super-polynomial quantum advantage for testing whether a Boolean function is close to being defined by only $k$ variables (a $k$-junta). It achieves this using an efficient quantum tester and establishes the lower bound classically by constructing hard distributions based on error-correcting codes. This work significantly advances the understanding of computational limits in property testing.

**Why it may be interesting.** Although focused on computational complexity theory, the techniques used—especially constructing hard distributions and proving query complexity gaps—are foundational to understanding the limits of information extraction from complex physical measurements or noisy data sets in quantum physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper establishes a super-polynomial quantum advantage for solving the tolerant $k$-junta testing problem in an adaptive setting.

**Main result.** It shows that the problem can be solved with $	ext{poly}(k)$ quantum queries, while any classical algorithm requires at least $k^{\Omega(\log k)}$ queries under specific parameter regimes.

**Method.** The quantum advantage is demonstrated using a specialized non-adaptive quantum tester adapted from prior work. The corresponding classical lower bound relies on constructing hard distributions for 'yes' instances based on error-correcting codes and applying Yao's minimax lemma.

**Model / system.** The model involves black-box access to a Boolean function $f: \{0, 1\}^n 	o \{\pm 1\}$, which is tested for its proximity (tolerance) to being defined by only $k$ variables (a $k$-junta).

**Key observables.** Query complexity (number of oracle calls), correlation $	ext{corr}(f, J_T)$, and the parameters defining closeness ($\varepsilon_1$) and distance ($\varepsilon_2$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The regime requires $0 \le \varepsilon_1 < \varepsilon_2 \le 1/2$, particularly focusing on small gaps $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_2 - \varepsilon_1$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The quantum tester used is non-adaptive, and the super-polynomial classical lower bound requires a sub-constant gap between $\varepsilon_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$.

**Paper structure.** The paper reviews standard junta testing, introduces tolerant testing for noisy data, presents Theorem 1 establishing the quantum advantage via both an efficient quantum tester and a novel classical lower bound based on hard distributions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We establish the first super-polynomial quantum advantage for the tolerant junta testing problem in the adaptive setting. Specifically, we show that within a certain parameter regime, tolerant $k$-junta testing with high precision can be solved using $\mathrm{poly}(k)$ quantum queries, whereas any classical algorithm requires at least $k^{Ω(\log k)}$ queries.   The problem of tolerant $k$-junta testing is as follows: given parameters $(k, ε_1, ε_2)$, with $0\le ε_1<ε_2 \le 1/2$, and black-box access to a Boolean function $f$ (defined on $n$ variables), distinguish whether $f$ is $ε_1$-close to some $k$-junta or $ε_2$-far from every $k$-junta.   We show the quantum advantage for a range of parameters close to $1/2$, for example, $ε_1 = 1/2-1/k$ and $ε_2 = 1/2-1/(2k^2)$. The (non-adaptive) quantum tester we use was given by a recent work of Bao, Liu, Yao, Ye, and Zhang (SOSA 2026). We slightly adapt their analysis to show that it holds in the above parameter regime. On the other hand, our classical lower bound requires substantial new ideas. Inspired by the lower bound techniques of Chen and Patel (FOCS 2023), we introduce a new hard distribution of ``yes'' instances (i.e., instances with distance at most $ε_1$ to $k$-juntas) that is based on planting an ``approximate-junta'' as follows: we randomly pick $k$ out of $n$ coordinates, and for each fixing of the $k$ coordinates, the $2^{n-k}$ values in the restricted subcube are drawn randomly except for the set of points in an error-correcting code on which we place the same random bit. We show that this distribution is much closer to $k$-juntas than the uniform distribution, but on the other hand, they are indistinguishable with respect to any classical algorithm making $k^{o(\log k)}$ queries.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the practical challenge of Quantum Key Distribution when communicating parties lack a shared reference frame over noisy channels. The authors introduce two robust methods—PTM analysis and Sequential Basis Matching—to determine optimal local measurement bases. They prove these methods yield equivalent, enhanced key rates compared to standard protocols, significantly improving theoretical performance estimates for real-world quantum links.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it provides a rigorous framework for optimizing communication protocols under realistic, non-ideal environmental constraints (like relative motion in satellite links) that violate idealized assumptions of perfect alignment.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is establishing secret keys via Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) when communication occurs over an unknown, stationary, unital qubit channel without the communicating parties sharing a global reference frame.

**Main result.** Both proposed methods—Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM) analysis and Sequential Basis Matching (SBM)—yield equivalent results, demonstrating that optimized local signaling can recover positive key rates even when standard assumptions about basis alignment fail.

**Method.** The authors propose two complementary theoretical approaches: one using the PTM derived from channel characterization via SVD, and another operational approach called SBM that iteratively optimizes measurement bases based on observed error probabilities.

**Model / system.** The system models QKD over a qubit channel characterized by unknown unitaries ($U_A, U_B$) and unital noise ($\mathcal{N}$). The analysis relies heavily on the Pauli basis representation of quantum states and channels.

**Key observables.** Secret key rates (for BB84 and six-state protocols), Quantum Bit Error Rates (QBERs) in X, Y, and Z bases, and the effective channel's PTM parameters.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The channel noise strength ($\epsilon$), which quantifies the deviation from ideal transmission; the number of measurement shots ($N_s$) for finite-sample analysis.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The quantum channel is assumed to be stationary and unital. The primary challenge addressed is the violation of the shared reference frame assumption, rather than modeling specific physical noise sources like loss or dark counts.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare secret key rates vs. channel parameter $\epsilon$ for standard versus optimized signaling; they also show QBER sets and finite-sample estimations demonstrating convergence to the theoretical PTM rate.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the physical challenge (QKD without shared reference frame). It then details two mathematical approaches: 1) Constructing the effective channel via PTM/SVD, and 2) Implementing SBM for sequential basis optimization. Finally, it compares the results and analyzes performance robustness.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We consider a general and practical scenario of quantum key distribution (QKD) over an unknown, stationary, unital qubit channel. Furthermore, due to practical limitations, e.g., relative movement and rotation of communicating parties, a global shared reference frame cannot be established. This scenario can routinely appear in satellite QKD. We propose two methods to overcome the physical qubit noise and the lack of shared reference frame. The first proposed approach involves constructing the Pauli transfer matrix (PTM) description of the channel, which we achieve without requiring a shared reference frame, by absorbing the lack of shared reference frame in the channel definition. This is followed by the identification of singular vectors of PTM as the Bloch vectors for optimal signal states. In the optimized local bases, the resulting correlations are equivalent, up to outcome relabeling, to those of a Pauli channel, allowing us to show the optimality of the BB84 and six-state QKD protocols under these conditions. The second approach, called the sequential basis matching (SBM) involves sequentially identifying the channel-optimized local bases that enable QKD. We show that both of these approaches result in the same effective key exchange rate for QKD.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper models cryptocurrency market collective behavior using the framework of statistical mechanics, constructing an 'Market Crystal' based on asset correlations. By defining magnetization and energy observables derived from an Ising Hamiltonian, the authors characterize market states as oscillating between highly ordered (ferromagnetic-like) and disordered regimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete example of applying established concepts from condensed matter physics (Ising models, order parameters) to model non-equilibrium complex systems like financial markets, which is a key area in econophysics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to characterize the collective dynamics and emergent states within complex financial systems, specifically cryptocurrency markets.

**Main result.** The market's phase space is organized around a quadratic relationship between energy and magnetization ($E \simeq -1.27M^2 - 0.03$), indicating that strong alignment (high $|M|$) corresponds to low structural energy.

**Method.** The authors employ analogies from statistical mechanics, mapping asset returns onto binary spins ($\sigma_i$) and constructing an Ising-like Hamiltonian ($H = -\sum J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j$).

**Model / system.** The system is the 'Market Crystal,' a spin lattice embedding of 169 cryptocurrencies. Interactions ($J_{ij}$) are determined by historical Pearson correlation coefficients ($ho_{ij}$), forming an Ising Hamiltonian.

**Key observables.** Magnetization ($M(t)$) measures net directional alignment, and Energy ($E(t)$) quantifies structural coherence relative to the correlation matrix.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The lattice size is $13 	imes 13$, and the coupling strengths are derived from empirical correlations over the observation period.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions include treating historical correlations as fixed interaction strengths for the Hamiltonian, and using a heuristic CBFS procedure to embed assets onto a physical lattice structure.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spin configuration on the lattice (Fig 1), the time evolution of magnetization ($M(t)$) and energy ($E(t)$) (Figs 2 & 3), and the resulting phase space plot showing the quadratic relationship between $E$ and $M$, along with marginal histograms confirming bimodality.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the analogy between market dynamics and spin systems, details the construction of the Market Crystal using correlation embedding, defines key observables ($M$ and $E$), analyzes their temporal evolution, and concludes by mapping the phase space structure to reveal underlying ordered regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Collective dynamics in financial markets can emerge through synchronized movements of large groups of assets. Motivated by analogies with interacting many-body systems, we introduce a spin-lattice representation for analyzing collective states in cryptocurrency markets. In this framework, assets are encoded as binary spin variables according to the sign of their returns, while correlations between assets determine effective interaction strengths. A correlation-based breadth-first search (CBFS) procedure embeds 169 cryptocurrencies into a $13 \times 13$ lattice, enabling the construction of an Ising-like Hamiltonian describing the market configuration, which we call the \emph{Market Crystal}. Macroscopic observables such as magnetization and energy provide a statistical-mechanical characterization of collective market states. The resulting phase-space structure highlights regimes of strong alignment and fragmentation among assets, with an energy--magnetization pattern suggestive of predominantly ferromagnetic interactions. This framework offers a statistical-mechanical viewpoint for studying collective behavior in financial systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously compares Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) and Clifford Data Regression (CDR) for mitigating noise in quantum measurements under limited experimental shots. It derives theoretical operating windows showing that the optimal technique switches based on the available shot budget and calibration quality. The findings provide crucial guidelines for designing practical, resource-aware quantum algorithms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous theoretical tools for resource optimization in near-term quantum computation by quantifying the precise finite-shot limits where different error mitigation strategies succeed or fail.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper compares Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) and Clifford Data Regression (CDR) for quantum error mitigation in the finite-shot regime to determine which technique minimizes Mean Square Error (MSE). It establishes operating windows where one method outperforms another based on shot budget.

**Main result.** A finite crossover budget exists, $B_{	ext{PEC=CDR}}(p)$, beyond which PEC dominates CDR's performance. The analysis shows that the optimal strategy depends critically on the available measurement resources (shot budget) and calibration mismatch.

**Method.** The authors derive mean-square-error boundaries for different estimators using small-$p$ expansions, comparing bias terms against variance overheads derived from Pauli observable measurements.

**Model / system.** The analysis is applied to estimating expectation values of Pauli observables (e.g., MaxCut Hamiltonian) in quantum circuits subjected to local depolarizing noise models. The comparison framework involves PEC using quasi-probability inverses and CDR trained on classical data regression.

**Key observables.** Mean Square Error (MSE), finite-shot gain ($\Delta$), bias terms ($b_M(p)$), variance overheads ($\sigma_M^2(p)$), and the crossover budget $B_{	ext{PEC=CDR}}(p)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** First-order CDR calibration mismatch ($\delta_1$), shot budget ($B$), noise strength ($p$), and second-order coefficients ($\delta_2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes local noise models, linearity for the CDR approximation, and relies on small-$p$ expansions to derive asymptotic scaling laws.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the predicted operating regions (PEC dominant vs. CDR dominant) across varying shot budgets and noise levels for specific observables like the MaxCut Hamiltonian.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from general MSE formulations comparing mitigation techniques, derives theorems governing crossover points based on bias/variance trade-offs, provides detailed analysis of calibration mismatch requirements, and concludes with extensive numerical validation across various graph instances and Pauli channels.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum error mitigation on noisy devices is limited not only by residual bias but also by the shot noise and calibration errors introduced by the mitigation procedure itself. We derive finite-shot mean-square-error boundaries for probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), Clifford data regression (CDR), and no mitigation for noisy Pauli-observable estimates. Exact PEC removes the target bias under an exact noise inverse at the price of a quasi-probability variance overhead, whereas population linear CDR can have smaller target-shot variance but retains a calibration floor when the training and target noise responses do not match. This competition yields a finite CDR-dominant operating window whose upper endpoint scales as $B_{\mathrm{PEC}=\mathrm{CDR}}(p)\propto 1/(δ_1^2p)$, where $δ_1$ is the first-order CDR calibration mismatch. We further prove a target-response projection theorem showing that response-blind affine CDR removes the first-order bias only when the target noise response is affine in the ideal target value; otherwise a nonzero projection error gives an irreducible local calibration floor. The same mean-square-error formulation extends to second-order calibration, commuting Pauli Hamiltonians, finite CDR training shots, and residual PEC model bias. A closed-form two-qubit calculation and QAOA simulations support the predicted no-mitigation, CDR-dominant, and PEC-dominant regimes.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a comprehensive framework to measure genuine global contextuality using 'coordination costs,' quantifying the minimum required classical communication and memory. By relating this cost to combinatorial covering numbers ($\chi_G$), it establishes that strong quantum contextuality imposes unavoidable lower bounds on any classical simulation protocol. This advances the understanding of resource separation between quantum and classical physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous theoretical tool—the coordination cost—to quantify the computational resources needed by classical simulators to mimic quantum correlations, which is fundamental for understanding resource limitations in quantum computation and communication protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To establish a quantitative link between genuine global Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality and the minimum classical coordination cost required to simulate quantum correlations.

**Main result.** The paper proves that genuine global KS contextuality lower-bounds a joint classical coordination cost involving communication, memory, and local computation depth ($B+M \ge \log_2 \chi_G(T)$).

**Method.** It develops an abstract framework using compiled task models and resource inequalities derived from covering numbers ($\chi_D^G$) to quantify the required classical resources.

**Model / system.** The analysis uses abstract information-theoretic models, generalizing Bell nonlocality (communication cost) and KS contextuality into a joint coordination cost for arbitrary constraint satisfaction tasks.

**Key observables.** Global contextual covering number ($\chi_G(T)$), depth-restricted covering number ($\chi_D^G(T)$), and the classical resource tuple $(B, M, D)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coordination bits (the common unit of cost), repetition factor ($m$), and flag probabilities ($p_{F,n}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on defining a 'cover-admissible' classical simulator model and assumes the existence of an abstract lifting theorem to transfer bounds from simple KS seeds to global models.

**Figures summary.** Not specified (Notes describe mathematical theorems and derived inequalities rather than figure content).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds logically by first defining the resource cost framework, then introducing specific combinatorial tasks (like twisted hypercubes or Hardy games) to derive concrete lower bounds on $\chi_G(T)$, culminating in an abstract theorem that transfers these bounds from simple contextuality seeds to genuinely global models.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Classical simulations of quantum correlations can fail because no low-communication local hidden-variable model exists, or because no single noncontextual hidden state can explain all compatible measurement contexts. This manuscript studies a third regime: genuine global Kochen-Specker contextuality, where local subsystems are noncontextual and the tested multipartite blocks are generalized-Bell-local, but the whole empirical model admits no global noncontextual hidden-variable explanation. We propose a coordination-cost framework in which communication, memory, and local computation are treated as different ways for a classical simulator to maintain a global classical explanation from locally available information. We introduce coordination bits, global contextual covering numbers, scaling laws for task families, and an abstract lifting theorem showing how classical simulation lower bounds for KS-contextual seed families can be transferred to genuinely global-KS models. As worked examples, we analyze a polarization-path Hardy obstruction and postselected KCBS-type tasks.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces using transformer neural networks to estimate the Coherent Information (CI), which serves as a theoretical upper bound on reliable quantum information transfer. By linking CI maximization to minimizing BCE loss, they create a powerful ML tool for estimating QEC thresholds. This approach significantly improves upon classical decoders and rigorously proves the optimality of advanced soft post-selection techniques.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful ML framework to tackle fundamental limits in quantum computation, offering quantitative tools (CI) that bridge information theory with practical decoder design for noisy qubits.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Determining optimal quantum error correction (QEC) thresholds is computationally hard due to noise susceptibility, requiring methods to quantify the maximum reliable information transfer rate.

**Main result.** The authors show that transformer-based neural networks can accurately estimate the Coherent Information (CI), providing superior threshold estimates and outperforming traditional decoders like MWPM.

**Method.** They develop a transformer model trained using Binary Cross-Entropy loss, establishing a direct link between this loss and the CI. They also introduce novel optimal soft post-selection schemes based on MLD cosets.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on QEC codes, particularly the surface code, analyzing performance under various noise models (depolarizing, phenomenological, circuit-level). The core mathematical tool is the Coherent Information (CI), which quantifies recoverable information.

**Key observables.** Coherent Information (CI), Logical Error Rate ($p_L$), Abort Probability ($p_{	ext{abort}}$), and Noise Thresholds.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Code distance ($d$), noise strength ($p$), and the post-selection parameter ($c$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on establishing that minimizing BCE loss approximates maximizing CI, and that optimal post-selection is governed by MLD cosets.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate CI estimates showing threshold crossings across different noise types; other figures detail the QEC circuit setups (e.g., X/Z readout) and compare error rate scaling between various decoding strategies.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical link between CI and BCE loss, then developing the transformer architecture for estimation, followed by proving the optimality of MLD-based soft post-selection schemes, and finally benchmarking performance across multiple noise models.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

As quantum computers remain susceptible to noise, QEC is essential for preserving logical information during computations. However, the performance of QEC codes breaks down beyond certain noise thresholds, revealing fundamental limits on their ability to protect quantum information. These limits can be characterized using information-theoretic measures such as the coherent information, which quantifies the maximum rate at which logical information can be reliably transmitted through a noisy quantum channel. In this work, we establish a direct connection between the CI and the binary cross-entropy loss used when training neural network decoders. Specifically, we show that the CI constitutes a sharp lower bound on the achievable loss for decoders that track logical operators across noisy channels. To this end, we develop a transformer-based neural network model based on maximum likelihood decoding. We train this network to estimate the CI and evaluate its performance on the surface code under three noise models: code capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise. Our results demonstrate that the network accurately predicts CI and yields threshold estimates that closely match known theoretical limits. When used as a decoder, the network significantly outperforms the minimum weight perfect matching decoder in terms of logical error rate. We also introduce a novel soft post-selection scheme that independently treats uncertainty in both logical operators and relies on confidence-based filtering of the network's output. We prove that such post-selection strategies, based on the MLD cosets, are optimal, and demonstrate their scalability in terms of both logical error rate and abort probability. These findings establish transformer-based architectures as powerful tools for QEC and provide the first numerical evidence supporting the optimality and scalability of MLD-based post-selection.

</details>

**Summary.** This thesis addresses the complexity of building scalable quantum networks by integrating three previously separate domains: routing, link calibration, and hardware programmability. It develops a cross-layer framework that allows protocols to function reliably even with partial knowledge of imperfect physical links. The result is a comprehensive model for programmable quantum repeaters necessary for long-distance quantum communication.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a comprehensive blueprint for realizing quantum internet infrastructure by explicitly linking high-level network protocols (routing) to low-level physical control mechanisms (ISA/calibration), which is crucial for experimental realization using solid-state qubits.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is designing scalable quantum networks by developing integrated protocols for routing, managing link imperfections via calibration, and implementing programmable hardware at the repeater nodes.

**Main result.** The thesis proposes a cross-layer framework where grey-box routing achieves robustness using partial knowledge, while explicit calibration schedules and an Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) enable reliable operation despite hardware drift.

**Method.** The work combines theoretical protocol development with architectural modeling, deriving optimal scheduling algorithms for link calibration and proposing a concrete ISA interface for physical quantum repeaters.

**Model / system.** The system is a quantum network designed for long-distance entanglement distribution. It models components like qubits (e.g., NV centers), entanglement swapping operations, and the interaction between network protocols and underlying hardware control layers.

**Key observables.** End to end fidelity ($\mathcal{F}_{	ext{ete}}$), Blocking Probability (BP), Throughput ($T$), and operational efficiency metrics.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Link fidelity decay rate ($\Gamma_e$), calibration overhead time, network topology parameters, and the size/capability of the programmable node register.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The research moves beyond assuming full or static knowledge of link properties, instead modeling partial knowledge and dynamic hardware limitations as fundamental constraints.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate entanglement generation schemes (MeetInTheMiddle, Sender-Receiver), network topologies (Grid/Cylindrical), and performance comparisons showing how BP and Fidelity vary with node quality ($\xi$) under different routing algorithms.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the need for a cross-layer view; it then details routing strategies using grey-box approaches, followed by developing calibration-aware models for link operation, culminating in the proposal of an ISA for programmable repeater nodes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The quantum internet enables distribution of quantum states across distant nodes, supporting secure communication, distributed computing, and quantum sensing. Unlike classical networks, it is constrained by the no cloning theorem, probabilistic entanglement generation, decoherence, and hardware drift, making classical abstractions inadequate. Scalable quantum networking therefore requires new architectures, protocols, and optimisation methods that explicitly account for these limitations.   This thesis studies the architecture, routing, and operation of quantum networks under realistic constraints, focusing on bipartite entanglement distribution over quantum repeater networks. Key metrics include end to end fidelity, throughput, scalability, and fairness. At the network layer, routing strategies are developed beyond assumptions of homogeneous nodes and full network knowledge. Routing under heterogeneous repeater efficiencies shows how partial knowledge of node quality improves fidelity and reduces path blocking. A grey box routing approach is then introduced, where path selection relies only on topology and end to end estimates, achieving robustness and fairness without detailed link information.   At the link layer, calibration and hardware drift are addressed through a calibration aware model separating activation and calibration phases. For linear repeater chains, an optimal calibration schedule is derived to balance operation time and calibration overhead. This is extended to general topologies with shared links, where a greedy orchestration heuristic is proposed.   Finally, the thesis connects network protocols with hardware via an instruction set architecture for programmable quantum repeater nodes based on NV centers, enabling coherent programmability and linking physical operations to higher layer protocols.

</details>
