**Summary.** This theoretical work explores unconventional superconductivity in Kagome lattices using the $t$-$J$ model. It demonstrates that specific electronic structures, particularly at certain Van Hove Singularities, force the emergence of a Pair-Density Wave (PDW) state. Furthermore, tuning parameters can stabilize a novel chiral interband superconducting phase through complex symmetry constraints.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter, the concept of symmetry-enforced topological phases and competing orders in strongly correlated systems shares conceptual links with understanding complex many-body ground states relevant to quantum simulation platforms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Investigating unconventional superconducting phases, specifically Pair-Density Wave (PDW) and chiral interband superconductivity, in strongly correlated Kagome systems.

**Main result.** The study shows that a PDW state emerges inevitably at the sublattice-pure vHS, and proximity to an $m'$-type vHS stabilizes a distinct chiral interband superconducting state due to phase frustration.

**Method.** Self-consistent mean-field theory is employed alongside Ginzburg-Landau analysis to map out the competition between various pairing symmetries (PDW, Nematic, Chiral).

**Model / system.** The research uses the extended $t$-$J$ model derived from the Hubbard model on the Kagome lattice. The analysis focuses on superconductivity near specific Van Hove Singularities ($p$-type and $m'$-type) at high-symmetry points.

**Key observables.** Superconducting order parameters ($\Delta$), PDW formation, chiral interband pairing strength, and phase diagram regions in the $\mu$-$t'$ plane.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Chemical potential ($\mu$) tuned to specific vHSs; further-neighbor hopping ($t'$); strong correlation limit (large-$U$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is performed within the mean-field approximation and neglects most higher-order hopping terms beyond $t'$.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing PDW regions near the $p$-type vHS, and real-space representations of competing phases like PDW and Chiral order E1.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the emergence of PDW at one type of vHS, then explores competition between various pairing states (Uniform, Nematic, Chiral) when a second distinct vHS ($m'$-type) is introduced via tuning hopping parameters.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The pair-density wave (PDW) state, characterized by Cooper pairing at finite momentum, is a long-sought superconducting phase whose possible realization in Kagome metals is particularly intriguing in the strongly correlated regime. We investigate superconductivity in the extended $t$-$J$ model on the Kagome lattice and show that the symmetry-enforced sublattice structure of the Bloch wavefunctions gives rise to a rich landscape of unconventional pairing states. When the chemical potential is tuned to a sublattice-pure ($p$-type) van Hove singularity (vHS), a PDW state inevitably emerges. Near the $m'$-type vHS, which features opposite mirror eigenvalues to the conventional $m$-type vHS, intraband chiral, uniform, and nematic pairing states compete. When further-neighbor hoppings drive the $p$- and $m'$-type vHSs towards near degeneracy, phase frustration in the interband pairing channel stabilizes a chiral interband state. Our results reveal the previously overlooked $m'$-type vHS as a distinct route to unconventional superconductivity rooted in electronic correlations and mirror-symmetry-constrained Bloch wavefunctions.

</details>

**Summary.** Researchers used a superconducting microwave cavity setup to measure the electrical response of small-angle twisted WSe2. They confirmed the presence of ferroelectricity by observing characteristic hysteresis loops in capacitance and quality factor. This technique provides a high-frequency tool for studying domain-wall dynamics in 2D ferroelectric materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter ferroelectrics, the use of high-frequency cavity measurements to probe domain dynamics is analogous to characterizing dissipation mechanisms in open quantum systems or superconducting qubits coupled to lossy environments.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to probe the signature of sliding ferroelectricity within small-angle twisted WSe2 heterostructures.

**Main result.** Hysteretic responses in both capacitance and cavity quality factor were observed, confirming ferroelectric switching dynamics associated with domain-wall motion at high frequencies.

**Method.** The polarization is probed by embedding the material into a superconducting coplanar waveguide (CPW) cavity and measuring its high-frequency AC response using microwave transmission spectroscopy.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a small-angle parallel stacked WSe2 heterostructure, which exhibits ferroelectricity due to stacking-induced symmetry breaking. This structure acts as the coupling capacitor within an superconducting CPW cavity.

**Key observables.** Hysteretic response in capacitance and internal quality factor ($Q_i$); changes in resonant frequency ($	ilde{S}_{21}$ magnitude/phase).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coercive field ($\sim 0.14 	ext{ V/nm}$ for $0.1^\circ$ twist); operating temperature (e.g., $1.5 	ext{ K}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The measurement technique is sensitive to domain-wall dynamics at high frequencies, and the observed hysteresis originates specifically from the t-WSe2 layer, not the hBN layers.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematic device setups (heterostructure coupled to cavity), measured $	ilde{S}_{21}$ data showing resonant features, and plots demonstrating capacitance and $Q_i$ hysteresis versus applied gate voltage.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the physical setup using superconducting cavities, measures the complex dielectric susceptibility via microwave spectroscopy, analyzes the resulting hysteresis in C and Q, and uses control experiments to confirm the ferroelectric origin of the signal.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Ferroelectricity is a property of materials that exhibit spontaneous charge polarization. Ferroelectricity in 2D materials is interesting because of their applications in memory devices and field-effect transistors. Recently, a new type of ferroelectricity, known as sliding ferroelectricity, has been discovered, in which parallel-stacked bilayers of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) or transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) develop an out-of-plane electric polarization. In this work, we probe the polarization of small-angle parallel stacked WSe$_2$ by measuring its high-frequency AC response, achieved by embedding it into a half-wave superconducting coplanar waveguide cavity. We observe a hysteretic response in the capacitance of the stack and quality factor of the cavity, confirming ferroelectric switching in the system. Our results further reveal relaxation effects associated with ferroelectric domain-wall motion. This cavity-based technique has potential applications in probing domain-wall dynamics in a ferroelectric system at high frequencies.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically analyzes how the thermal Purcell effect modifies heat, linear momentum, and angular momentum exchange between a nanoparticle and an optical cavity. Using fluctuational electrodynamics, the authors show that cavity geometry allows for selective control: heat and torque are enhanced while lateral force is suppressed or vanishes under specific symmetry conditions. This demonstrates precise engineering capability over nanoscale energy transport.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for engineering nanoscale energy and momentum transfer using structured electromagnetic environments, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems where boundary conditions dictate coupling strengths.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how placing a magneto-optic nanoparticle within a Fabry-Pérot cavity modifies the exchange of radiative heat, linear momentum, and angular momentum via the thermal Purcell effect.

**Main result.** Geometric confinement selectively controls energy and momentum transfer: sub-wavelength confinement enhances heat and torque but suppresses lateral force. Furthermore, symmetry dictates that at the cavity center, the lateral force vanishes while heat and torque remain finite.

**Method.** The analysis employs fluctuational electrodynamics, deriving spectral densities for power, force, and torque by calculating cross-correlations involving the cavity-modified dyadic Green's functions.

**Model / system.** The system consists of a magneto-optic nanoparticle (InSb) placed inside an optical Fabry-Pérot cavity formed by two perfectly conducting mirrors. The interaction is governed by fluctuating electromagnetic fields and depends on the particle's polarizability tensor components.

**Key observables.** Radiative heat transfer ($h(\omega)$), linear momentum/lateral force ($f_x(\omega)$), and angular-momentum/torque ($	au_y(\omega)$) spectral densities.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cavity length ($L$), particle-to-mirror separation ($d$), external magnetic field ($B$), and the thermal wavelength ($\lambda_{th}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the electric-dipole approximation, assuming perfectly metallic plates (perfectly conducting boundaries), and ignoring near-field evanescent modes for simplification.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spatial distribution of LDOS components, showing enhancement/oscillation patterns. They also plot exchanged power vs. particle position ($d$) and cavity length ($L$), demonstrating characteristic dependencies like $1/L$ in the small-$L$ limit.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the physical setup and observables using fluctuational electrodynamics, deriving general spectral density expressions for heat, force, and torque. It then analyzes specific geometric limits (e.g., sub-wavelength confinement, cavity center) by exploiting symmetry properties like parity decomposition to derive distinct physical behaviors.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The thermal Purcell effect describes the modification of the local density of states of the fluctuating electromagnetic field induced by a Fabry-Pérot cavity, leading to the enhancement or suppression of radiative transport quantities. Using fluctuational electrodynamics, we investigate nonequilibrium radiative heat, linear-momentum, and angular-momentum exchange between a magneto-optic nanoparticle and a Fabry-Pérot cavity. Analytical expressions for the spectral densities reveal that geometric confinement modifies the electromagnetic local density of states, producing distinct behaviors for different transport quantities. Specifically, sub-wavelength confinement enhances radiative heat and angular-momentum transfer, but suppresses the lateral force. Additionally, interference between cavity modes causes all transfer quantities to oscillate spatially with particle position. At the cavity center, mirror symmetry enforces a parity decomposition of electromagnetic fluctuations resulting in a vanishing lateral force, whereas heat transfer and torque remain finite through combined even and odd modal contributions. These results demonstrate that cavity engineering provides selective control over nanoscale energy and momentum transfer via structured electromagnetic fluctuations.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores the radiative Mpemba effect in a $	ext{VO}_2$ nanoparticle over an $	ext{SiC}$ substrate, leveraging the material's phase-change hysteresis. The authors demonstrate that latent heat acts as a crucial thermal buffer enabling this cooling anomaly. The findings highlight the strong dependence of this effect on near-field radiative coupling.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical thermal physics, the analysis of non-equilibrium energy transfer driven by material state changes (phase transitions) shares mathematical parallels with open quantum systems where environment coupling dictates relaxation dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the radiative analogue of the Mpemba effect—where hotter systems cool faster than colder ones—in a system exhibiting phase-change hysteresis.

**Main result.** The Mpemba effect is shown to be governed by the latent heat contribution acting as a thermal buffer, and its existence depends critically on near-field coupling effects within the phase-change material.

**Method.** The analysis involves analytically deriving onset conditions and mapping the system's phase space using numerical simulations based on coupled heat balance equations.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a VO2 nanoparticle placed above an SiC substrate, utilizing the temperature-dependent hysteresis of the $	ext{VO}_2$ material. The energy exchange is modeled via radiative coupling between the particle and the substrate.

**Key observables.** Intersection time ($	au$) between cooling and heating trajectories; spectral power exchanged ($P_{	ext{sub}\leftrightarrow	ext{dip}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Nanoparticle radius ($R$), separation distance ($d$), and the temperature dependence of specific heat capacity ($C_p$) due to phase transition.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The characteristic time scale for temperature homogenization is assumed much faster than the thermal relaxation time due to radiation; simplified analytical models are used for hysteresis modeling.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the system setup, heatmaps showing $	au$ for ordinary and inverse Mpemba effects across varying parameters, and comparisons of temperature evolution in different phases (dielectric vs. metallic).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the governing heat balance equation, derives the necessary conditions for the Mpemba effect using rate equations, analyzes the role of latent heat via the caloric channel, and then maps out the phase space to demonstrate ordinary, inverse, and passive manifestations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Mpemba effect states that initially hotter systems cool faster than colder ones. While known in convective, conductive, and quantum systems, its radiative analogue is unexplored. Here, this anomaly is realized via phase-change hysteresis of a VO$_2$ nanoparticle near a SiC substrate. After analytically deriving an onset condition, the phase space is mapped. Crucially, latent heat acts as a thermal buffer enabling both ordinary and inverse effects. Near-field coupling governs the relaxation time and enables a passive effect where memory is stored externally via substrate reflection.

</details>

**Summary.** This work unifies the understanding of oscillons by proving they are nonlinear bound states arising from spectral resonances, such as threshold or anti-bound modes. Using perturbative methods on nonlinear field theories in 1+1 dimensions, the authors demonstrate how these localized excitations govern soliton dynamics, particularly when solitons interact with a 'spectral wall'. The findings provide a robust theoretical framework for understanding stable, long-lived non-linear structures.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of nonlinear resonance leading to localized excitations is highly relevant in open quantum systems and AMO physics when considering dissipation or coupling to continuum modes (e.g., cavity decay). The mathematical framework for handling non-normalizable resonances is transferable.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To establish a unified understanding of oscillons, showing they arise as nonlinear bound states bifurcating from spectral resonances like threshold or anti-bound modes.

**Main result.** Oscillons are interpreted as nonlinear bound states originating from the localized interaction with non-normalizable resonance modes (threshold/anti-bound). This mechanism explains soliton stopping and stationary state formation after passing a spectral wall.

**Method.** The analysis uses perturbative expansions of the field equations, deriving effective envelope equations for the oscillon profile. Solvability conditions are adapted to handle non-normalizable modes.

**Model / system.** The study analyzes nonlinear field theories, primarily involving generalizations of the Klein-Gordon equation in (1+1) dimensions ($\phi_{tt} - \phi_{xx} + dU/d\phi = 0$). Specific models include $\phi^4$ theory and the Sine-Gordon model.

**Key observables.** Nonlinear frequency shift ($	ilde{\omega}^2$), oscillon amplitude, stationary state formation location relative to the spectral wall ($x_{sw}$), and mode transition characteristics.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The nonlinearity strength (controlled by $\epsilon$ or coupling constants $c$) and initial excitation amplitudes ($A$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Standard solvability conditions fail due to non-normalizability, requiring the assumption of a localized envelope function. The analysis is primarily restricted to (1+1) dimensions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate spectral structures near resonance points, mapping out regimes where oscillons form based on model parameters ($c$), and show numerical evolution of antikinks demonstrating stationary state formation after passing the spectral wall.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first defining oscillons via threshold modes in vacuum. It then generalizes this to kink backgrounds (wobbleron) using perturbative expansions, deriving an effective envelope equation. Finally, it applies this framework to soliton dynamics near a spectral wall, showing mode transitions from anti-bound states into stable oscillon structures.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show that an oscillon can be understood as a localized discrete resonant (non-normalizable) mode. Specifically, oscillon in the vacuum arises from the threshold mode, which because of nonlinearity gets localized. Following this idea, we find {\it wobblerons} - nonlinear excitations of kinks, that is, oscillons-kink bound state. Now, the oscillon can also originate in an antibound mode, i.e., a discrete, positive energy but non-normalizable mode.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes using the spin polarization of an attached quantum dot as a diagnostic tool to detect Majorana zero modes (MZMs) within a superconducting wire. By rotating the external Zeeman field direction, the authors show that topological states induce a distinct, measurable change in this spin polarization compared to non-topological regimes. This method offers a powerful spectroscopic signature for characterizing topological superconductivity.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly sensitive spectroscopic tool—analyzing spin polarization changes—to probe topological quantum states in solid-state systems, which is crucial for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop a robust method using spin polarization analysis of an attached quantum dot (QD) to definitively detect Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in topological superconducting wires, overcoming ambiguities from trivial resonances.

**Main result.** The detection relies on observing a significant and characteristic change in the QD's effective spin polarization when the Zeeman field direction in the wire is rotated, which contrasts sharply with the constant polarization seen in trivial states.

**Method.** The analysis employs Green's function formalism to calculate the QD spectral density and its spin polarization at the Fermi energy ($\omega=0$) as a function of the external magnetic field rotation angle ($\Theta$).

**Model / system.** The system consists of a quantum dot coupled to a topological superconducting wire, modeled by Hamiltonians incorporating tight-binding terms, Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and tunable Zeeman fields. The analysis uses both full numerical simulations and simplified 'Toy Models' based on chiral operators.

**Key observables.** QD spectral density ($ho_{QD}$), effective spin polarization ($P(\epsilon_F)$) as a function of the Zeeman field angle $\Theta$, and non-linear dependence of $P$ vs. magnetic field magnitude.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Zeeman field rotation angle ($\Theta$), coupling strength between QD and wire, superconducting gap ($\Delta$), and critical topological parameters ($V_{	ext{cr}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often focuses on the spin evolution under Rashba and Zeeman fields, sometimes simplifying or disregarding the full superconducting pairing term for specific diagnostic measurements.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate spectral densities and spin polarization plots showing distinct behavior (large change vs. near-constant) when comparing topological versus trivial wire states as a function of $\Theta$.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the physical system and Hamiltonian, to deriving the necessary Green's function formalism for the coupled QD-wire structure, and finally applying this framework to calculate and interpret the spin polarization diagnostics under varying magnetic field orientations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We demonstrate that analysis of the spin polarization of a quantum dot (QD) attached to the topological wire can provide valuable insights into Majorana zero mode (MZM) formation and topological phase transition. Detection is realized by rotation of the Zeeman field in the wire, while retaining the Zeeman field direction in the dot intact. In the presence of Majorana mode, the effective QD spin polarization at Fermi energy changes significantly when the direction of the Zeeman field in the wire changes from parallel to perpendicular to the wire axis. It can be opposed to the wire in its trivial state, when spin polarization remains practically constant while the magnetic field is rotated. Similar unaltered spin polarization is observed when QD spin sub-level at Fermi energy mimics MZM. Moreover, the characteristic non-linear dependence of the spin polarization on the magnetic field magnitude at its critical value identifies a topological phase transition in the wire. This feature is observed independently on the coupling strength of the wire to the dot and the angle of the Zeeman field.

</details>

**Summary.** This work theoretically predicts that twisted bilayer graphene with large twist angles can become a superconductor due to strong electron correlations. By calculating the screened Coulomb interaction, the authors establish that a d-wave pairing state is stabilized, potentially leading to high critical temperatures under bias voltage.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on graphene, the theoretical framework of solving for correlated ground states via Green's functions and analyzing symmetry-protected instabilities is highly relevant to strongly correlated systems studied in AMO physics or condensed matter theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study predicts superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene (tBLG) at large twist angles, driven by electron-electron interactions.

**Main result.** Superconductivity is stabilized by the screened Coulomb interaction, exhibiting a d-wave order parameter symmetry. The transition temperature ($T_c$) can reach several hundred millikelvin under applied bias voltage.

**Method.** The analysis employs Green's functions and utilizes the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) to screen the bare Coulomb interaction, solving self-consistency equations for the superconducting order parameter.

**Model / system.** The system is twisted bilayer graphene modeled using a continuum approach near Dirac points. The Hamiltonian incorporates interlayer hopping terms, and superconductivity arises from pairing interactions mediated by the screened Coulomb repulsion.

**Key observables.** Superconducting gap ($\Delta$), superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), and the symmetry of the order parameter (d-wave).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Large twist angle ($	heta$), doping level, applied bias voltage ($V/e$), and interlayer hopping parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on RPA for screening interactions and assumes specific structural conditions regarding the superlattice cell size.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the electron spectrum showing a gap in LAtBLG. Other figures likely show $T_c$ dependence on doping or bias voltage, confirming d-wave stability.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the single-particle band structure and gap formation to deriving the interaction Hamiltonian using RPA screening. It then solves the self-consistency equations for both inter-valley (d-wave) and intra-valley pairing channels to determine the most stable superconducting state.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We predict that twisted bilayer graphene with large twist angle and small superlattice cell can be superconducting. Such a bilayer graphene can have a gap in the spectrum. This gap appears due to the hybridization of electrons moving in different layers with Fermi momenta close to the Dirac points which are equivalent to each other in the superlattice Brillouin zone. Small doping of the bilayer introduces charge carries having large density of states. We show that the screened Coulomb interaction is enough to stabilize superconducting state in the material. The symmetry of the order parameter is of the $d$-wave type. Application of the bias voltage increases the superconducting transition temperature. For realistic values of the model parameters the transition temperature can be as large as several hundreds of milikelvin.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces current noise spectroscopy as a superior technique to probe molecular junctions, bypassing thermal broadening limitations inherent in standard IETS. By analyzing voltage-dependent current noise ($\Delta I$), the authors model charge transport through vibrational manifolds to extract detailed molecular parameters like anharmonicities and reorganization energies. This establishes noise signatures as a highly sensitive 'molecular fingerprint' for quantum device characterization.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful experimental realization of probing molecule-electrode coupling dynamics by analyzing noise spectra, which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems where environmental coupling (vibrations) dictates electronic transport rates.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to overcome the limitations of traditional spectroscopy (IETS) by using current noise measurements ($\Delta I$) to achieve high-resolution vibrational fingerprinting in molecular electronic junctions.

**Main result.** The technique successfully maps complex vibrational manifolds and allows for the direct extraction of crucial nanoscale parameters like anharmonicities, dissociation energies, and reorganization energies.

**Method.** The authors employ a fast-convolution-based Landauer-Büttiker transport model fitted to voltage-dependent current noise ($\Delta I(V)$) measurements taken on suspended-wire molecular junctions.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a molecular junction (e.g., $	ext{C}_{10}$ or TPT SAMs) bridging electrodes, whose electronic transport is modeled by incorporating the coupling between electronic tunneling and quantized vibrational energy levels.

**Key observables.** Voltage-dependent current noise ($\Delta I(V)$), which exhibits distinct peak features corresponding to molecular vibrational modes and their overtones.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Mode energies, anharmonicities ($\chi_e$), dissociation energies ($D_e$), and local environment reorganization energies ($E_r$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on modeling the current using rate equations for excited/ground states and assumes that noise measurements are sensitive to transition rates rather than just conductance additions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate typical $I(V)$ and $\Delta I(V)$ curves for C10 and TPT junctions, showing model fits. The paper details how the decay parameter ($s$) controls the line shape of noise peaks, and tables summarize extracted parameters like wavenumbers and reorganization energies.

**Paper structure.** The structure moves from establishing the physical problem (limitations of IETS) to presenting the advanced methodology ($\Delta I$ spectroscopy), developing the underlying quantum transport model (Landauer-Büttiker/rate equations), applying it to extract multiple molecular parameters, and finally interpreting these results as unique chemical fingerprints.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The precise realization of molecular electronic devices requires a comprehensive understanding of charge transport mechanisms and the specific interplay between electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom. While average current measurements (I-V characteristics) and conventional Inelastic Electron Tunneling Spectroscopy (IETS) offer valuable insights, they are fundamentally limited by temperature-dependent line-width broadening. This study presents a high-resolution spectroscopic methodology utilizing suspended-wire molecular junctions (SWMJs) based on self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) of 1-decanethiol (C10) and 1,1',4',1''-terphenyl-4-thiol (TPT). By systematically probing the voltage-dependent current noise ($ΔI$), we demonstrate that electronic noise spectroscopy circumvents thermal degradation by probing transition rates between vibrational manifolds rather than simple additions of conductance channels, which enables sub-thermal feature mapping. Leveraging a fast-convolution-based Landauer-Büttiker transport model fitted to experimental data, we map complex vibrational manifolds, including high-energy overtones. This allows for the direct extraction of crucial nanoscale molecular parameters, including mode energies, anharmonicities ($x_e$), dissociation energies ($D_e$), and local environment reorganization energies ($E_r$). These parameter-dense noise signatures act as a unique molecular fingerprint, establishing noise spectroscopy as a highly sensitive platform for chemical sensing and discrimination in advanced quantum devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work systematically investigates how the inherent chirality of carbon nanotubes dictates their non-equilibrium orbital response, quantified by the Edelstein susceptibility. By employing advanced Green's function techniques and modeling controlled current injection, the authors demonstrate that these CNTs act as highly selective filters, transmitting only electronic states whose angular momentum matches specific crystal quantization rules.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit connection between structural chirality and quantized orbital angular momentum filtering provides a concrete, tunable mechanism for controlling electronic transport properties in nanoscale conductors. This bridges concepts from topological physics (chirality) with quantum transport measurements.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates non-equilibrium orbital response, selectivity, and filtering capabilities governed by structural chirality in carbon nanotubes (CNTs). It aims to show that these effects are dictated by the specific chiral wrapping vector rather than simple geometric parameters.

**Main result.** Chiral CNTs can function as efficient orbital-angular-momentum filters, selectively transmitting electronic states based on their crystal angular momentum. The orbital Edelstein susceptibility ($\chi_{Lz}^z$) depends strongly on chirality and diameter, revealing distinct families of behavior.

**Method.** The research employs the Landauer–Büttiker formalism combined with Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) techniques to calculate current-driven orbital magnetic moments and susceptibilities.

**Model / system.** The physical system is chiral Carbon Nanotubes modeled using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding framework retaining a single $p_z$ orbital per carbon atom. The analysis systematically compares metallic and semiconducting CNTs under different contact geometries (end vs. side).

**Key observables.** Orbital Edelstein susceptibility ($\chi_{Lz}^z$), local orbital magnetic moment ($\mathbf{m}$), and the ratio of azimuthal to axial current ($\langle I_\phi angle / \langle I_z angle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Chiral indices $(n, m)$, nanotube diameter ($d_t$), applied voltage ($V_{SD}$), and contact geometry.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often uses the wide-band approximation for contacts and models idealized coupling conditions to isolate intrinsic electronic responses. The filtering mechanism is linked to the discrete rotational symmetry $C_n$.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate $\chi_{Lz}^z$ dependence on gate voltage, diameter vs. chiral angle space, and conductance as a function of injected angular momentum ($l$) relative to the crystal angular momentum ($m$).

**Paper structure.** The paper develops from calculating the orbital Edelstein susceptibility ($\chi_{Lz}^z$) in general (Chunk 2), establishing its dependence on chirality over simple scaling laws. It then refines this by analyzing current components and effective winding angles (Chunk 3). The focus shifts to comparing metallic vs. semiconducting behavior, showing enhanced response near band edges (Chunk 4). Finally, the most advanced concept is demonstrated: using controlled angular momentum injection via projected contacts to enforce strict orbital-angular-momentum filtering rules ($l \equiv m \pmod{n}$) (Chunks 6 & 7).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) constitute a highly tunable platform for probing the interplay between structural chirality and quantum transport in quasi-one-dimensional systems. Here, we perform a systematic study of the non-equilibrium orbital response across a broad set of metallic and semiconducting chiral CNTs. We find that the orbital Edelstein susceptibility depends strongly on both chirality and nanotube diameter, revealing that the orbital response cannot be captured by a universal scaling law. Instead, distinct families of CNTs emerge, forming characteristic orbital-response branches uniquely determined by the chiral wrapping vector. We further investigate the role of metallic contacts on orbital-current generation and orbital selectivity. While metallic CNTs rapidly recover their intrinsic orbital response away from the contact region, semiconducting CNTs display pronounced oscillatory behavior arising from interference between transport channels carrying different angular momenta injected by wide-band metallic contacts. Finally, by incorporating angular correlations into the contact self-energy, we demonstrate that chiral CNTs can operate as efficient orbital-angular-momentum filters, selectively transmitting orbitally textured electronic states in accordance with the crystal angular momentum of the propagating bands.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study investigates how intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity in bilayer 1T'-WTe2 can be used to electrically tune both conventional and anomalous spin Hall effects. By calculating the spin conductivities using DFT, the authors demonstrate that switching the ferroelectric polarization reversibly changes the sign and magnitude of these transport coefficients. This work proposes a pathway for nonvolatile electrical control in next-generation spintronic memory devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter spintronics rather than fundamental quantum information protocols, the concept of using electric fields (via ferroelectricity) to control quantized transport properties (spin currents) is highly relevant to controlling quantum states and energy dissipation in nanoscale devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is achieving field-free magnetization switching in spintronic devices by tuning both conventional and anomalous spin Hall effects (CSHE/ASHE). The research proposes utilizing intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity to achieve this tunability.

**Main result.** Sliding ferroelectricity enables the reversible switching of signs and magnitudes for both CSHCs and ASHCs in bilayer 1T'-WTe2. This establishes a strong coupling between ferroelectric polarization and spin transport, enabling nonvolatile electrical control of spintronic devices.

**Method.** The study employs Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations, including van der Waals corrections, to compute the Spin Hall Conductivities using the Kubo formula based on band structure analysis and k-resolved Spin Berry Curvature contributions.

**Model / system.** The physical system is bilayer 1T'-WTe2, a transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) exhibiting intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity. The calculations analyze various stacking configurations (AA vs AB stackings) to map out the dependence of spin transport properties on polarization state.

**Key observables.** Spin Hall Conductivities ($\sigma_{yxy}, \sigma_{y	ext{yx}}$), Conventional Spin Hall Conductivity, Anomalous Spin Hall Conductivity, and the magnitude/sign of ferroelectric polarization ($P$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The enhancement factor achieved by bilayer stacking (up to $\sim 2	imes$) and the specific values calculated for conductivity ($\sigma_{yxy} = -96.77 (\hbar/e)	ext{S/cm}$ in bilayer).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on DFT calculations, assuming that the observed spin transport phenomena are governed by band structure topology changes induced by ferroelectric polarization switching.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the atomic structures and BZ schematics for different stacking modes. Key figures show k-resolved Spin Berry Curvature contributions ($\sigma_{zxy}, \sigma_{zyx}, 	ext{and } \sigma_{yyx}$) across various stackings, demonstrating how polarization switching alters these contributions.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the physical context (SHE/ASHE challenge) and then details the theoretical framework using DFT. It systematically analyzes the effect of stacking patterns and ferroelectric sliding on the spin Hall conductivities, culminating in a discussion of the mechanism linking polarization reversal to sign switching in ASHCs.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The spin Hall effect, recognized for its high-speed, low-power, and highly controllable characteristics, is a key enabler for next-generation memory and logic devices. However, a primary challenge lies in achieving 180$^{\circ}$ magnetization switching without an external magnetic field in spin-orbit torque devices. Here, we propose a method to tune the conventional and anomalous spin Hall effects by the intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity. Importantly, the anomalous spin Hall effect can enable the field-free switching of perpendicular magnetization. We find a substantial anomalous spin Hall conductivity of $σ_{xy}^{y}$ = 45.62 ($\hbar$/e)S/cm and $σ_{yx}^{y}$ = 56.84 ($\hbar$/e)S/cm in monolayer 1T'-WTe$_2$. These values are significantly enhanced to $σ_{xy}^{y}$ = -96.77 ($\hbar$/e)S/cm and $σ_{yx}^{y}$ = 104.03 ($\hbar$/e)S/cm in the bilayer 1T'-WTe$_2$. More interestingly, the sliding ferroelectricity enables reversible switching of the signs and magnitudes for both the conventional and anomalous spin Hall conductivities. This originates from the fact that the sliding ferroelectric markedly shifts the relative spin Berry curvature contributions from the valence and conduction bands around the $Γ$-X path. Our findings not only reveal a strong coupling between sliding ferroelectricity and spin transport, but also propose a strategy for the nonvolatile electrical control of spintronic devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper rigorously analyzes the anisotropic Rytova-Keldysh interaction potential governing excitons in 2D materials. By applying advanced mathematical techniques like steepest descent and specialized asymptotic expansions, it derives closed-form expressions for the screening potential across all length scales. The key outcome is a quantitative prediction of the exciton ground-state binding energy that explicitly accounts for material anisotropy.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous analytical tools to calculate fundamental properties (like binding energy) in low-dimensional quantum systems where anisotropy is crucial, bridging complex integral physics with solvable variational models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To provide an analytical foundation for the strongly anisotropic Rytova-Keldysh interaction potential governing excitons in 2D materials, and subsequently derive a closed-form expression for the exciton ground-state binding energy.

**Main result.** The paper derives distinct asymptotic forms for the screening potential: a geometric mean dependence at short ranges and a standard $1/r$ Coulomb decay at long ranges. It provides an analytical formula for the ground state energy capturing the competition between effective mass and dielectric tensors.

**Method.** The analysis employs advanced mathematical techniques including mapping to 1D integrals, applying the method of steepest descent (Laplace's method) for intermediate regimes, and using variational calculations with anisotropic Gaussian wavefunctions.

**Model / system.** The system is excitons confined in ultrathin two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors exhibiting significant in-plane dielectric anisotropy. The interaction potential is modeled by the generalized Rytova-Keldysh screening potential.

**Key observables.** Exciton ground-state binding energy ($E_{	ext{gs}}$), and the anisotropic screened potential $V(r, \phi)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Screening lengths ($r_x, r_y$), effective masses ($m_x, m_y$), and dielectric tensors ($\epsilon_x, \epsilon_y$). Regimes include short-range, intermediate-range (strong anisotropy), and long-range.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on approximations like small-argument Taylor expansions for special functions and assumes the applicability of Laplace's method in certain spatial regimes.

**Figures summary.** Not specified by notes; however, the text describes analyzing potential contours (elliptical at short range, circular at long range) and deriving energy equations.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the screened potential across different length scales: first establishing the exact 1D integral form, then deriving closed-form asymptotic expressions for the short-range limit using special functions, followed by analyzing the intermediate regime via steepest descent, and finally confirming the long-range behavior matches standard 3D unscreened Coulomb interaction.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The classic Rytova-Keldysh potential describes the non-local dielectric screening of Coulomb interactions in ultrathin two-dimensional (2D) materials. Recently, the corresponding potential for arbitrary in-plane anisotropy was derived in integral form, with numerical studies suggesting that an effective isotropic approximation remains robust for highly directional systems. In this paper we provide the analytical foundation for these observations by mapping the complete spatial landscape of the strongly anisotropic Rytova-Keldysh interaction. By applying the method of steepest descent and momentum-space coordinate scaling to the exact one-dimensional integral representation, we derive closed-form asymptotic expressions for the potential across all spatial regimes. We find that the intermediate-range screening exhibits a non-trivial amplitude scaling driven by the direction of weakest polarizability, while the short-range limit produces an anisotropic logarithmic well governed by the geometric mean of the principal polarizabilities. Finally, utilizing this short-range confinement, we implement an anisotropic Gaussian variational ansatz to solve the Wannier equation, providing a closed-form analytical expression for the exciton ground-state binding energy that explicitly captures the competition between the effective mass and dielectric tensors.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces the concept of a Supercurrent Gauge Field (SGF) that allows for the generation of magnetic-field-like effects in Josephson junctions using only electric currents. By demonstrating this, the authors show that both quantum interference and the Josephson Diode Effect can be controlled entirely electrically, opening pathways for compact superconducting quantum devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a powerful analogy between magnetic flux quantization and supercurrent phase winding, offering an all-electric means to probe fundamental superconducting phenomena like momentum transfer and diode behavior without external magnets. This is highly relevant for developing compact quantum devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research aims to eliminate the historical dependence of Josephson quantum interference and the Josephson Diode Effect (JDE) on external magnetic fields.

**Main result.** They demonstrate that a supercurrent gauge field (SGF), generated purely by electric currents, can induce both macroscopic quantum interference patterns and the JDE, establishing an all-electric control mechanism.

**Method.** The study combines theoretical modeling based on Ginzburg-Landau theory with detailed transport measurements in planar Josephson junctions using varying current configurations.

**Model / system.** The physical platform consists of planar Josephson junctions made from materials like Bi2O2Se and bilayer graphene. The physics is modeled by treating the supercurrent gauge field (SGF) as an effective replacement for the magnetic vector potential A in the superconducting order parameter phase gradient.

**Key observables.** Supercurrent Interference Patterns (SIPs), Josephson Diode Effect (JDE) asymmetry ($I_{	ext{C}}^+$ vs $I_{	ext{C}}^-$), and Negative Differential Resistance (NDR).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Bias current, control currents ($I_1, I_2$), external magnetic fields ($B_x, B_y$), and temperature.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the physical equivalence between the SGF generated by supercurrents and an externally applied magnetic field. It also models the system using Ginzburg-Landau theory approximations for current density.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the emergence of JDE in asymmetric current configurations (field-free), show how control currents can modulate interference patterns mimicking flux sweeping, and detail the dependence of JDE on external fields and temperature.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the problem (B-field reliance), then introducing the SGF concept via theoretical modeling (Ginzburg-Landau/gauge invariance), demonstrating its realization through current injection in asymmetric junctions to show field-free interference, and finally confirming the universal nature of JDE using this electric control.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Josephson effect, a hallmark of superconducting phase coherence, drives modern quantum technologies. However, Josephson-based quantum interference has hitherto been tethered to magnetic fields, despite phase coherence being a quintessential, intrinsic trait of superconductivity. Moreover, the Josephson diode effect (JDE) is typically viewed as an anomalous phenomenon indicative of broken symmetries in exotic phases of matter. Here, in planar Josephson junctions made with $\mathrm{Bi}_2\mathrm{O}_2\mathrm{Se}$ and bilayer graphene, we demonstrate that the JDE is a missing universal property of the Josephson effect. Simultaneously, we present an all-electric technology that replaces magnetic flux for controlling and measuring supercurrent interference. Central to our approach is a supercurrent gauge field (SGF), generated and amplified through high-kinetic-inductance superconductors and novel device architectures. By establishing the physical equivalence between the SGF and a magnetic field, we eliminate the reliance on external fields in quantum interference and reveal a universal, field-free JDE mechanism with broad implications for detecting broken-symmetry states. Finally, we show that the SGF offers capabilities beyond those of a conventional magnetic field by experimentally demonstrating a magnetic-free, phase-sensitive technique to construct and characterize finite-momentum superconductivity, opening new frontiers for exploring novel phases of matter and superconducting quantum architectures.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes using a solid-state transcapacitor (TCAP) as a next-generation logic element to overcome the energy limits of CMOS transistors. By exploiting electro-mechanical coupling in ferroelectric materials, TCAPs can achieve significant reductions in switching energy and delay through capacitive power recycling. The work provides extensive theoretical and simulation evidence supporting this pathway for ultra-low-power computing.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical electronics, the underlying physics—coupling between polarization switching, mechanical stress, and charge modulation—touches upon complex many-body interactions in condensed matter systems that are relevant to understanding emergent quantum phenomena or highly non-linear material responses.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is overcoming the energy scaling limitations of conventional CMOS transistors for advanced logic, memory, and interconnects in AI systems.

**Main result.** A novel solid-state transcapacitor (TCAP) utilizing ferroelectric or piezoelectric materials can achieve significantly lower energy consumption (potentially 100x reduction) by enabling capacitive power recovery rather than relying on dissipative transport current.

**Method.** The authors employ a combination of analytical modeling, multi-physics simulations (COMSOL), and circuit simulation (SPICE) to characterize TCAP operation across various coupling mechanisms.

**Model / system.** The core system is the TCAP, realized by modulating polarization/capacitance in ferroelectric or piezoelectric channels using an external gate stressor. The physics involves coupling between electric fields, mechanical strain, and polarization dynamics, governed by Landau-Khalatnikov type equations.

**Key observables.** Energy consumption ($E_{tr}/E_{tc}$), delay ($	au_{tr}/	au_{tc}$), Charge Gain (CG), Voltage Margin Gain (VMG), and the ON/OFF Ratio for memory applications.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Operating voltage scales, polarization density ($P_s$), coercive voltage ($V_c$), and coupling coefficients (e.g., electrostrictive tensors).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The models often rely on simplifying assumptions, such as approximating the charge-voltage dependence with a $	anh$ function for simulation convergence.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare CMOS vs. TCAP inverter characteristics, show hysteresis shrinkage due to gate voltage, and illustrate multi-physics simulations of stress/polarization evolution in ferroelectric materials.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically introduces the energy crisis in computing, proposes the TCAP concept based on solid-state physics (ferroelectrics/piezoelectrics), derives key performance metrics like Charge Gain and Transcapacitance, and validates these concepts through detailed simulation comparisons against CMOS.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Today's transistors dictate the voltage and charge scales for both logic and memory. While AI systems are recognized to be limited by memory energy, the dominant share of the energy is expended in the intrachip interconnects whose voltage and charge scales are set by transistors. The energy scaling challenges of transistors can be attributed to simultaneously meeting high current density, high current/impedance modulation, and the inability to lower voltages. Hence, a new logic element that lowers the voltage and charge needs is a priority, not only for lowering logic power but also memory access power. Here, we propose a novel 3-terminal logic element for low energy computing, a solid-state transcapacitor (TCAP). A TCAP is a solid state displacement current modulator realized by a gate which controls the charge-voltage relationship of the channel. Unlike transistors, TCAPs eliminate the dissipative transport current, are not bound by the Boltzmann current modulation limit, and operate with displacement currents limited only by the polarization response and contact resistance. Hence, TCAP circuits may simultaneously overcome the voltage, current density, and current modulation limits of CMOS. We describe a solid state TCAP using a piezoelectric transcapacitor in which a gate-controlled stressor modulates the capacitance of a polar channel via electromechanical coupling. This device achieves inversion and gain, essential for logic, and is functionally equivalent to a 1T-1C memory cell, enabling dense memory. Using voltage scaling, capacitive energy recovery, and high polarization densities of polar materials, the logic based on TCAP offers a pathway to 100 fold lower energy consumption with a delay comparable to ultimately scaled CMOS devices. This approach provides a new potential pathway for low-energy computing beyond the limits of transistors using electro-mechanics and multiferroics.

</details>

**Summary.** This work applies nonlinear dynamics and fractional calculus to a financial model to test if long-memory economic fluctuations exhibit a predictable, discrete spectral fingerprint called a frequency comb. The results show that such a deterministic structure emerges only when specific parameters and fractional exponents fall within narrow, stable regimes. This suggests a profound link between memory effects in finance and underlying harmonic organization.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly quantum, the mathematical framework of using fractional calculus and spectral analysis to characterize deterministic structure in complex systems mirrors techniques used in open quantum systems modeling or characterizing non-Markovian dynamics where long-term memory effects are crucial.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether long-range memory financial systems can exhibit a deterministic, discrete spectral fingerprint analogous to a frequency comb.

**Main result.** Under specific parameter and fractional-order conditions, the system's steady-state power spectrum organizes into a clear, equidistant frequency comb structure. This suggests that complex economic cycles might possess an underlying deterministic periodicity rather than being purely stochastic.

**Method.** The authors employed numerical integration of a nonlinear, fractional-order financial model followed by Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) spectral analysis to diagnose the presence and stability of the comb.

**Model / system.** The system is based on a three-dimensional nonlinear financial model involving interest rate ($x$), investment demand ($y$), and price index ($z$). This model is generalized using Caputo fractional derivatives ($	ext{D}^{q_i}$) to incorporate long-range memory effects into the dynamics.

**Key observables.** The primary observable is the power spectrum, specifically looking for discrete, equally spaced spectral lines (the frequency comb). Other observables include Lyapunov exponents and phase portrait geometry.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Structural parameters include saving amount ($a$), investment cost ($b$), and demand elasticity ($c$). Crucially, the fractional orders ($q_1, q_2, q_3$) dictate whether the comb appears or if the system transitions to chaos.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the observed spectral structure is governed by a single bounded, two-lobed motion in the phase space. The use of the Caputo fractional derivative formulation is central to the model.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate time series, FFT spectra showing the comb under varying parameters ($a, b, c$), and how the comb's existence depends on the specific ranges of the fractional orders ($q_1, q_2, q_3$).

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by defining the nonlinear financial model, generalizing it to fractional order dynamics, performing extensive parameter sweeps across structural constants ($a, b, c$) and memory exponents ($q_i$), and analyzing the resulting spectral signatures.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Frequency combs are discrete, equally spaced, phase-coherent spectral lines that emerge from nonlinear mode coupling in physical systems. We show that the incommensurate fractional-order financial model of Huang, Li, Ma, and Chen, whose Caputo derivatives encode macroeconomic long-range memory, generates an analogous structure in its steady-state spectrum. The comb appears only over specific values and ranges of the saving amount $a$, the investment cost $b$, and the demand elasticity $c$, outside which the spectral lines lose their equal spacing. It persists across extended parameter regimes and stays invariant to perturbations in the initial interest rate $x_0$ and investment demand $y_0$, while distinct spectral regimes appear at different initial price levels $z_0$. The comb is generated only when the fractional-order exponents $q_1$, $q_2$, and $q_3$ associated with interest rate, investment demand, and price index are above the critical threshold values. At even higher values of these exponents, the frequency comb transitions into chaos. These findings show that the long-run cyclic structure of a memory-bearing financial economy organises into a discrete, deterministic spectral fingerprint rather than a stochastic continuum.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper investigates tunneling through a barrier in a Rarita-Schwinger semi-metal, which possesses multiple spin sectors. By comparing single-sector transmission to coherent mixtures, the authors demonstrate that directional asymmetry can emerge even if the underlying band structure is isotropic. This effect is attributed entirely to phase differences between internal wave components, establishing an analogy to the Imbert-Fedorov effect in quantum transport.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete theoretical mechanism showing how phase accumulation in internal degrees of freedom (spin components) can induce measurable transport asymmetries, which is relevant for understanding quantum interfaces and non-Hermitian effects in condensed matter systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to identify fingerprints of an Imbert-Fedorov-like effect in the quantum tunneling transmission through a barrier within a Rarita-Schwinger semi-metal.

**Main result.** Directional asymmetry in tunneling ($T(k_y) 
eq T(-k_y)$) can occur even in idealized, isotropic multiband systems, arising purely from phase differences between internal wave components rather than explicit band anisotropy.

**Method.** The authors analytically derived transmission amplitudes by solving the scattering problem for a multi-component spinor wavefunction across a square barrier using mode-matching techniques.

**Model / system.** The system is a Rarita-Schwinger semi-metal, which supports two distinct propagating spin sectors ($m=1/2$ and $m=3/2$) forming Dirac-like cones. Tunneling occurs through an idealized square potential barrier.

**Key observables.** Tunneling transmission probability $T(k_y)$ and the asymmetry function $A(k_y) = T(k_y) - T(-k_y)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The spin projections ($m=1/2, m=3/2$), the barrier height ($V_0$), and the incident transverse momentum ($\kappa_y$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to a rotationally symmetric case for analytical tractability; the effect is shown to persist even when the underlying Hamiltonian is mirror symmetric.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate energy dispersion cones, compare transmission for single-sector vs. coherent mixtures, and plot the asymmetry function $A(\kappa_y)$ showing non-zero values away from normal incidence.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the multichannel nature of the system, calculates transmission amplitudes for both single-channel and coherent mixed-incidence cases, and then rigorously demonstrates that the directional asymmetry arises solely from interference terms involving different scattering/propagation phases between the spin sectors.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study tunneling through a square barrier in a rotationally symmetric Rarita-Schwinger semi-metal and identify fingerprints of an Imbert-Fedorov-like effect in the tunneling transmission. The problem is intrinsically multichannel at all energies because there exist two propagating sectors with spin projections $m=1/2$ and $m=3/2$. We derive the transmission amplitudes analytically and compare the single-channel and coherent mixed-incidence cases in the two channels. Interestingly, we observe that tunneling at high energy shows a bias towards scattering into spin projection $3/2$ contributions. For single-channel injection, we find that the transmission remains symmetric under a mirror transformation of the incident angle. In contrast, for the coherent superposition, we find a directional asymmetry in the transmission probability $T(k_y)\neq T(-k_y)$. Importantly, this effect does not originate from an anisotropy of the dispersion. Instead, it arises from the phase structure of the multicomponent scattering states. The two spin projection sectors exhibit different scattering and barrier-propagation phases, which enter as interference terms when both channels appear as a coherent superposition. This interference term is identified as the cause of the broken mirror symmetry. We therefore discover an analog of the Imbert-Fedorov effect, at the level of interface-induced phase differences between internal wave components. Our result demonstrates that asymmetric tunneling can already occur in transport experiments, even in an idealized, isotropic multiband system, and should therefore not be automatically attributed solely to explicit band anisotropy.

</details>

Using STM/AFM and DFT, the authors show that sulfur promotes clean sulfur deletion to form perylene, offering a powerful design principle for molecular synthesis.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on molecular materials science, the use of controlled voltage pulses to induce specific bond cleavages and structural transformations at the single-molecule level mirrors concepts in controlling quantum states or chemical reactions using external fields.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether selective skeletal editing of heterocyclic cores can be achieved by judiciously choosing the heteroatom, comparing oxygen-containing versus sulfur-containing rings.

**Main result.** Tip-induced reactions on sulfur-containing analogues ($	ext{DNT}$) predominantly result in facile sulfur deletion to form perylene, contrasting with oxygen analogues ($	ext{DNO}$), which show mixed rearrangement and deletion products.

**Method.** The research combines single-molecule scanning probe microscopy (STM/AFM) experiments with detailed Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations of potential energy landscapes.

**Model / system.** The system involves dinaphtho[1,8-bc:1',8'-ef]oxepine ($	ext{DNO}$) and its sulfur analogue ($	ext{DNT}$), adsorbed on surfaces like $	ext{Cu}(111)$ or $	ext{NaCl}$. The process is driven by applying voltage pulses from the microscope tip.

**Figures summary.** Figures show STM/AFM images of adsorbed molecules ($	ext{DNT}$), evidence of product formation (perylene), and DFT potential energy diagrams comparing reaction barriers for $	ext{O}$ vs. $	ext{S}$ elimination.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from demonstrating initial tip-induced chemistry on oxygen analogues to systematically testing the role of heteroatom substitution by analyzing sulfur analogues, supported by comparative computational modeling.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Skeletal editing enables precise structural modifications of molecules at late stages of a synthetic sequence, with applications in drug discovery and materials science. We recently demonstrated skeletal editing on the single-molecule scale. Voltage pulses applied by the tip of a scanning probe microscope to an oxygen-containing seven-membered heterocycle led to both oxygen deletion and ring-contraction rearrangement reactions. An open question is whether selective skeletal editing of a heterocyclic core can be achieved by an appropriate choice of the heteroatom. Here, we show that tip-induced reactions of an analogous sulfur-containing seven-membered ring results in sulfur deletion in virtually all cases. Our results demonstrate that the combination of tip-induced chemistry and heteroatom selection in the molecular design is a powerful strategy for single-molecule skeletal editing, with the potential to enable diverse structural transformations of heterocyclic frameworks.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper applies advanced statistical mechanics tools to model virus-host interaction networks. By analyzing how network properties change upon node removal, the authors identify 'transition-like' behavior using thermodynamic quantities like heat capacity. This demonstrates that a rigorous thermodynamic framework can be successfully applied to predict structural stability and dynamic changes in complex biological systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** While applied to biology, the methodology—using concepts like heat capacity and susceptibility derived from graph spectra to locate phase transitions or structural reorganization points—is directly analogous to techniques used in studying quantum many-body systems and complex energy landscapes.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to understand how virus-host interactions affect network stability by analyzing structural transitions using thermodynamic concepts.

**Main result.** The analysis reveals transition-like behavior in spectral thermodynamic functions (like heat capacity and susceptibility) when nodes are removed, suggesting a thermodynamic framework is useful for studying these complex biological networks.

**Method.** The authors employ statistical physics tools, calculating network parameters like Graph Temperature, Magnetization, Susceptibility, and Heat Capacity derived from the adjacency spectrum.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a virus-host interaction network (for species like *H. sapiens*), represented as a weighted, directed graph with connections between host biomolecules and viruses.

**Key observables.** Network Density (D), Assortativity Coefficient, Graph Temperature (T), Magnetization (M), Susceptibility ($\chi$), and Heat Capacity ($C$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Node removal strategy (targeted vs. random); confidence scores for interactions; spectral eigenvalues ($\lambda_i$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that structural changes in the network can be mapped onto thermodynamic concepts, such as using fixed spin assignments ($s_j$) for magnetization calculations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the evolution of metrics like density and susceptibility under targeted vs. random node removal; heat capacity curves show multiple peaks indicating different spectral scales within the network structure.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from characterizing rank-frequency distributions (Zipf's law fitting) to analyzing structural robustness via node removal, culminating in a full thermodynamic analysis using spectral properties to pinpoint critical transition points.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Understanding virus-host interactions is crucial for predicting the stability of networks under various perturbations. In this study, we present an analysis of virus-related networks for several organisms (Homo sapiens, Mus musculus, Gallus gallus), encompassing directed and weighted connections. We compute a range of network parameters, including topological characteristics and thermodynamic quantities derived from adjacency spectra, to gain insights into the structural robustness and dynamic behavior of the networks. To assess stability, we model two distinct node removal scenarios: targeted elimination of the most influential nodes and random removal. Our findings reveal transition-like behavior in spectral thermodynamic functions and characteristic changes in structural measures, contributing to evaluating the potential of a thermodynamic framework for studying virus-host networks and advancing a deeper understanding of their dynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** This work pioneers AFM pseudospintronics by utilizing the sublattice degree of freedom in antiferromagnets that lack conventional spin splitting. The key mechanism identified is a partial pseudospin–spin coupling, which allows for switching polarization by reversing the Néel vector. This leads to measurable effects like NV-controlled tunneling and large nonvolatile magnetoresistance.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the use of symmetry breaking (NV reversal) to control electronic transport properties via internal degrees of freedom (sublattice pseudospin) is relevant to open quantum systems where multiple coupled order parameters govern dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a new paradigm for spintronics, termed AFM pseudospintronics, that operates in antiferromagnets (AFMs) without relying on the conventional requirement of spin splitting.

**Main result.** The study demonstrates that sublattice degrees of freedom can be exploited via partial pseudospin–spin coupling to achieve Néel-vector-controlled transmission and a large nonvolatile pseudomagnetoresistance effect.

**Method.** Theoretical analysis involving tight-binding models, Fourier transforms applied to Friedel oscillations (FOs), and calculation of tunneling magnetoresistance ratios.

**Model / system.** The system is a honeycomb AFM modeled by a tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating sublattice pseudospin ($\hat{	au}$) and real spin ($\hat{\sigma}$). The physics hinges on the coupling between these degrees of freedom in zero spin-splitting collinear AFMs.

**Key observables.** Sublattice-resolved Friedel oscillation amplitude ratio ($R_s$), Néel vector (NV)-controlled transmission, and nonvolatile pseudomagnetoresistance (PMR).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Pseudospin polarization ($ar{\sigma}_z^s = \Lambda_s/\epsilon$), doping level ($\epsilon$), and junction potential ($V_0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes interfaces are along zigzag directions to simplify scattering processes, allowing the conservation of spin and valley in tunneling calculations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spin-degenerate band structure and pseudospin polarization; they show sublattice-resolved FOs (intravalley/intervalley) used to extract the ratio $R$; and finally, they depict the NV control over junction transmission and PMR magnitude.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical framework by introducing the Hamiltonian and the concept of partial pseudospin–spin coupling. It then derives measurable quantities like the amplitude ratio from FOs, demonstrating local probing of the NV state. Finally, it applies this understanding to predict large nonvolatile PMR effects in junctions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Antiferromagnets (AFMs) are promising for high-density spintronics due to their zero net magnetization, yet conventional AFM spintronics relies on spin splitting-a requirement that excludes many collinear AFMs with compensated spin sublattices. Here we exploit the sublattice degree of freedom in a honeycomb AFM with zero spin splitting. We uncover a coupling between spin and sublattice: the out-of-plane pseudospin polarization is spin-dependent, a mechanism we term partial pseudospin-spin coupling. This allows switching of the pseudospin polarization by reversing the Néel vector. Introducing an impurity into a specific sublattice induces Friedel oscillations with a sublattice-resolved amplitude ratio dictated solely by the pseudospin polarization, which is directly measurable by spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy. Furthermore, we demonstrate Néel-vector-controlled transmission and a large nonvolatile tunneling magnetoresistance in an all-in-one AFM junction, with pronounced resonant enhancement in gate-tunable two-dimensional devices. Our work establishes a new paradigm-AFM pseudospintronics-that utilizes the sublattice pseudospin in zero-spin-splitting AFMs, extending spintronics beyond the conventional spin-splitting paradigm.

</details>

**Summary.** This work presents a comprehensive, physics-based blueprint for an in-memory neuromorphic processor using multi-level memristive synapses. By performing analog matrix multiplication directly where weights are stored, it bypasses the energy limitations of data movement inherent in conventional digital computing architectures. The resulting architecture is highly scalable and extremely energy efficient for modern AI workloads like LLMs.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on AI hardware, the underlying physical modeling of state evolution ($\dot{x} = f(x, v)$) derived from charge/ion dynamics shares mathematical parallels with non-equilibrium statistical mechanics used to model complex material states.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Overcoming the von Neumann bottleneck in data-intensive AI workloads by integrating memory and computation onto a single chip.

**Main result.** The proposed memristive crossbar fabric achieves energy efficiency orders of magnitude better than digital accelerators for LLM inference by performing MAC operations in the analog domain.

**Method.** Developing physics-based models derived from ionic transport (Nernst–Planck) to characterize multi-level conductance states, and then applying these devices in a full neuromorphic architecture.

**Model / system.** The system is a memristive crossbar fabric built using $	ext{HfO}_2$-based resistive synapses, capable of storing quasi-continuous analog weights. It implements computation via Kirchhoff's laws ($\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{G}^	op\mathbf{v}$) in the physical domain.

**Key observables.** Energy per token ($E_{	ext{tok}}$), Throughput ($	ext{tok}/	ext{s}$), Number of distinguishable conductance levels ($L_{th}$), and Output Current ($\mathbf{I}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Device parameters include the dynamic range ($ho = G_{max}/G_{min}$) and the read-noise floor ($\sigma G_{th}$); architectural scaling involves 3D stacking depth ($T$) and cell area ($a_{	ext{cell}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes that weight movement energy dominates digital costs, justifying the in-memory approach; performance figures are projections based on ideal device behavior.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the physical cross-section of 3D BEOL integration, the overall memristive-FPGA system architecture, and comparative roofline analyses showing superior scaling over digital methods.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from fundamental physics modeling (ionic transport) to device characterization (level count, noise), then details the analog computation primitives (VMM, self-attention), and concludes with architectural blueprints for full LLM inference engines.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Building on resistive communication, this paper presents a physics-based design of an on-chip neural network with multi-level memristive synapses supporting a dense spectrum of conductance states. Derived from ionic transport physics, we develop a state-variable model and quantify storable sub-levels under thermal noise, drift, and quantized conductance. We assemble these devices into a 1T1R crossbar fabric, derive the linear algebra of analog vector-matrix multiplication (VMM) under wire resistance, and design a differential synapse for signed weights. A multilayer pipeline executes inference, backpropagation, and weight updates physically in the analog domain. We derive the in-situ outer-product learning rule, its discretization onto the conductance lattice, and the resulting quantization noise. We provide energy, area, capacity, and inter-tile models, showing this substrate is ideally suited for large language models (LLMs). Our design eliminates weight movement, surpassing binary ReRAM and traditional CMOS. We detail the material stack (HfO_2-based), the FEOL/BEOL CMOS foundry-integration flow, a self-contained SPICE model, the complete memristive-FPGA neuromorphic system, and an in-memory self-attention engine with current-mode translinear softmax. Finally, a ternary BitNet datapath shows projected per-token efficiency orders of magnitude better than advanced CPUs or GPUs. The result is a self-contained hardware-native blueprint for a high-density, analog, in-memory neural processor.

</details>
